detail.abstract: Does language reshape what people eat? This paper identifies the causal effects of Mandarin proficiency and dialect distance on household food consumption in China, separating a humancapital "modernization channel" from a cultural-capital "local-network channel." Using three independent micro-datasets, the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS 2010 and 2014), the China Labor-force Dynamics Survey (CLDS 2014), and the China Health and Nutrition Survey (CHNS 1989-2015), we employ a three-layer identification strategy, with each layer relying on different identifying assumptions: two-stage least squares (2SLS) in the CFPS, instrumenting Mandarin proficiency with family language and county Mandarin share; an Atkin (2016)-style cross-dialect migrant design in the CHNS with community-by-wave fixed effects; and a bilingual dose-response analysis in the CLDS. Mandarin proficiency raises per-capita food expenditure by 13.85% and lowers animal-oil use, a pattern that replicates across datasets. Within the same community-year, cross-dialect migrants consume 0.93 fewer food types and 0.65 percentage points less protein energy than local residents and take roughly thirty years to assimilate; a 1989 direct-recall item shows that only 49.4% of cross-province migrants retain home foodways, against 90.7% of nonmigrants. We also report a cautionary null: province-level Mandarin penetration appears strongly correlated with dietary diversity but loses all significance once province fixed effects are added, signaling ecological-fallacy risk in cross-province studies. An Ashenfelter-Krueger correction further shows that the OLS-2SLS gap is partly classical measurement-error attenuation, with an implied reliability ratio of 0.27-0.66. Mandarin promotion thus accelerates dietary modernization while potentially eroding dialect-encoded local food knowledge, implying scope to coordinate language and nutrition policy under the "Greater Food Vision.

detail.abstract: Marketing mix modeling (MMM) has regained attention as firms seek privacy-compliant approaches to evaluate marketing effectiveness based on aggregated data. While prior research has primarily focused on statistical estimation methods, guidance on how to design, implement, and use MMM in practical decision-making remains limited. This paper conceptualizes MMM not merely as a statistical model but as a decision system embedded in marketing planning processes. We develop a set of design principles that address recurring challenges in real-world MMM deployments, including problem scoping, variable construction under data constraints, handling of interdependent marketing actions, model robustness under multicollinearity and seasonality, and the integration of MMM with complementary validation methods. The proposed framework organizes MMM activities along the planning process-scoping, data construction, modeling, interpretation, and continuous use-and provides practical heuristics and failure modes observed in applied settings. In particular, we emphasize that (1) MMM should be operated as a continuously updated system for brand management, (2) marketing actions must be modeled with explicit recognition of their structural interdependence, and (3) model outputs should be validated through additional methods such as experiments or auxiliary planning tools. By bridging methodological insights and practical deployment, this paper contributes a structured framework for improving the reliability, interpretability, and usability of MMM in managerial decisionmaking.

title: Standing Out from Adjacent Reviews: How Content Similarity Affects Review Helpfulness
affiliations: Wuhan University, Wuhan University, Xi’an Jiaotong University and Wuhan University

detail.title: Standing Out from Adjacent Reviews: How Content Similarity Affects Review Helpfulness
detail.abstract: Prior research and practice have largely examined review content characteristics in isolation to enhance review helpfulness, overlooking that perceived helpfulness is context dependent. This oversight poses a broader platform design challenge: how to structure information environments as consumers browse reviews sequentially. Drawing on the information diagnosticity and variety-seeking perspectives, we introduce adjacency-based content similarity and argue that platforms can enhance overall helpfulness by reducing local redundancy. Using around 3 million TripAdvisor hotel reviews and Doc2Vec to measure this similarity, we find that reviews are perceived as less helpful when highly similar content appears adjacently; this effect is attenuated for high-reputation reviewers and amplified for hedonic (vs. utilitarian) products, and is driven primarily by similarity in content on experience-related attributes. Complementary online experiments establish causality and identify perceived uniqueness as the mediating mechanism. We further replicate the main pattern in other contexts (e.g., restaurants, video games, and consumer goods). This study advances understanding of review helpfulness by highlighting the role of sequential information structures and offers direct implications for platforms' algorithmic feed design, particularly through review reordering and curation to mitigate local redundancy.

title: Defensive Hybrid Intelligence: An Integrative Theory of Intelligence Production Under Adversarial Information Conditions

detail.title: Defensive Hybrid Intelligence: An Integrative Theory of Intelligence Production Under Adversarial Information Conditions

detail.abstract:
Background: Established models of intelligence production: the intelligence cycle, the target-centric model and the OODA loop – were conceived for an environment in which collection was scarce, analysis was human, and adversarial manipulation of the information space was peripheral rather than central. The convergence of large language models, ubiquitous open-source data and industrialised influence operations has inverted each of these assumptions.

Purpose: This article develops Intelligence Theory 2026, an original conceptual framework organised around the construct of Defensive Hybrid Intelligence (DHI). The framework integrates artificial intelligence, open-source intelligence, information fusion, explainable AI, human–machine teaming and intelligence governance into a single theoretical architecture for strategic decision-making under adversarial information conditions.

Methods: The study employs qualitative conceptual research combining theory synthesis, a concept-centric structured review of ten thematic literatures, comparative theoretical synthesis and formal framework construction. Constructs are defined, causal relationships specified, and testable propositions derived.

Results: The framework identifies four interacting layers – sensing, fusion, judgement and governance – connected by explicit feedback loops, and repositions cognitive defence from an afterthought to a structural property of the intelligence enterprise. Six propositions specify the conditions under which hybrid human–AI configurations outperform either fully automated or fully human analytic arrangements.

Contribution: The article extends intelligence theory beyond process description towards an integrative, governance-aware model that treats epistemic security as a first-order design requirement.

Implications: The framework offers agencies, corporate intelligence functions and AI developers a common vocabulary for designing accountable, explainable and manipulation-resistant intelligence systems.

detail.abstract: Financial dashboards are good at showing data and poor at explaining it. This paper describes FinSight AI, an opensource web dashboard that pairs the LLaMA 3.3 70B model, served through the Groq inference API, with a live MongoDB Atlas transaction store so that an analyst can question the data in plain English and receive answers grounded in the actual database contents. On every request, the backend aggregates the user's transactions into a compact statistical context-monthly revenue and expense series, category totals, the largest credits and debits, and portfolio-level risk-and injects it into the model's system prompt, which keeps responses tied to real values rather than model guesses. A lightweight rule engine scores each incoming transaction from 0 to 100 using amount and recipient heuristics and flags entries at or above a threshold of 40; the language model then supplies natural-language explanations of the flags on demand. The prototype, built on React 18, Node.js/Express, and JWT plus Google OAuth 2.0 authentication, loads its five dashboard endpoints in under 800 ms and returns AI analyses in 1.5-3 s on a free-tier database. We report the design, the prompt-construction method, observations from a seeded 60transaction dataset, and an honest account of the prototype's limitations. The full source code is public under the MIT license.

title: How Physical Assets Enter Digital Capital Markets Contents

detail.title: How Physical Assets Enter Digital Capital Markets Contents
detail.abstract:
Real estate has long been identified as a prime candidate for digitalization and tokenization, yet adoption has remained limited despite sustained technological progress. This report argues that the constraint is not blockchain maturity, market infrastructure, or financial engineering, but the absence of durable informational foundations at the asset level. Most real estate assets cannot yet be evaluated, governed, or transferred efficiently because their data does not persist in verifiable, reusable forms across lifecycle phases, ownership changes, and regulatory regimes.

At the core of the problem is asset legibility: the ability of an asset to explain itself credibly without reconstruction. Real estate accumulates value, risk, and obligations over decades, yet its informational record routinely fragments as projects move from design to construction, operations, and transaction. When continuity breaks, diligence becomes forensic, valuation confidence widens, and risk must be priced conservatively. The report establishes that preserving continuity—through structured, traceable, and verifiable information—is a prerequisite for financial efficiency, not an operational luxury.

Building on this foundation, the report reframes trust as an engineering problem, not a relational one. In markets defined by long-lived assets, infrequent transactions, and distributed stakeholders, reputation does not scale. Trust must instead be produced through systems that enforce provenance, auditability, controls, and repeatability. Without engineered trust, automation and decentralization amplify uncertainty rather than reduce it. Technologies such as tokenization, smart contracts, and AI remain dependent on the quality and governance of their inputs.

The report then challenges prevailing assumptions about liquidity. Liquidity is not created by platforms, fractionalization, or issuance mechanics; it is an outcome of readiness. Assets become liquid only when they are understandable and verifiable without bespoke investigation. Tokenization does not circumvent this requirement—it exposes it. Financial instruments function more effectively when they are state-aware, responding to verified changes in asset condition rather than static disclosures. Absent reliable state, oracles, pricing mechanisms, and risk models fail to align financial abstraction with physical reality.

Finally, the analysis extends beyond individual assets to portfolios, markets, and cities. Markets form when assets are comparable and legible; capital prices clarity more than novelty. At scale, the same informational failures that impede private transactions also undermine urban condition, infrastructure planning, and public-private alignment. The report concludes that integrating physical assets into digital capital markets requires not better financial products, but better informational infrastructure—systems designed to preserve asset understanding over time. Only when assets are continuously legible can digital finance operate with the confidence, efficiency, and institutional credibility required for scale.

title: AI-Powered Analysts
affiliations: University of Maryland-College Park - Robert H. Smith School of Business,  and University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business

detail.title: AI-Powered Analysts
detail.abstract: We examine how brokerages' institutional adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), measured from AI skill requirements in research-related job postings, shapes sell-side analyst work. AI adoption varies across brokerages and is predicted by peer adoption, organizational capacity, analyst human capital, and institutional demand. Comparing the same analyst-firm pair over time, analysts at higher-adoption brokerages issue more accurate earnings forecasts. The gains are larger when forecasts rely more on public, machine-readable information: early in the cycle, for firms with lower information asymmetry and more readable disclosures, and among technically trained analysts. Using intraday decision fatigue, we show that AI substitutes for analysts' cognitive effort within the forecasting task: it attenuates fatigue-related accuracy losses and herding. Freed capacity is redeployed toward relationship building with management and investing clients. Forecasts by analysts at higher-adoption brokerages elicit stronger price reactions, and adopters shift hiring toward senior analysts. Institutional AI thus benefits analyst research by conserving the scarce cognition it runs on, with gains that surface in forecast quality, market pricing, and the composition of the analyst workforce.

title: The Case for Digital Economies: What It Means for Africa

detail.title: The Case for Digital Economies: What It Means for Africa

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no conflicat of interest

detail.abstract:
Timothy Sturgeon's Upgrading Strategies for the Digital Economy (2019) makes a claim that sounds modest until you sit with it: firms in less-developed economies have, in his words, “profound” potential to benefit from modularity, open innovation, and digital platforms, provided they focus on industrial niches where domain knowledge matters more than raw scale. It is a hopeful argument, built on a genuinely useful taxonomy, and this paper does not dismiss it. What this paper does is put that claim next to three countries that have, by any reasonable measure, actually built functioning digital economies — Singapore, Australia, and Norway — and ask a blunt question. Did any of them get there the way Sturgeon says less-developed economies now can?

The short answer is no, not quite. Each of the three built its digital economy through a specific, expensive, and patiently sustained combination of state capacity, capital, and time that Sturgeon's paper never prices into its optimism. That is not a reason to dismiss Sturgeon's framework — the taxonomy of modularity, platforms, and platform layering remains genuinely useful, and this paper says so plainly. It is a reason to treat the leap from that taxonomy to “profound opportunities for LDC firms” as a hypothesis still waiting for its evidence, and to look at what the three country cases below suggest that evidence would actually require.

title: Entrepreneurial Experimentation as a Behavioral Logic: The Entrepreneurial Experimentation Logic (EEL) and Lean Startup Practice Archetypes (LSPA)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract:
Purpose
This paper develops a behavioral theory of entrepreneurial experimentation. Although experimentation has become central to venture creation, the field lacks a coherent explanation of how entrepreneurs enact it through cognition, behavior, organizing, and framing. The study introduces the Entrepreneurial Experimentation Logic (EEL), using a systematic review of Lean Startup and related experimentation approaches to identify the behavioral mechanisms underlying entrepreneurial experimentation.

Design/methodology/approach
A systematic literature review examined two questions: 1) How do scholars characterize the Lean Startup? and 2) Which related practices reflect similar experimentation logics under different labels? The review synthesized 60 peer-reviewed studies published through 2025 using descriptive and thematic analysis to identify recurring concepts, behavioral mechanisms, and patterns across the literature.

Findings
The review identified 22 Lean Startup characterizations and 31 analogous terms that share a common behavioral logic of hypothesis testing, experimentation, and iterative learning. These findings informed the Entrepreneurial Experimentation Logic (EEL), comprising four interrelated dimensions: cognitive logic, behavioral routines, organizational capabilities, and framing practices. The study also introduces the Lean Startup Practice Archetype (LSPA) typology—Scientific Practitioners, User-Centered Designers, Growth Hackers, and Strategic Experimenters—which explains distinct behavioral enactments of entrepreneurial experimentation across contexts.

Originality/value
Rather than cataloging definitions, this paper develops a behavioral theory of entrepreneurial experimentation. The EEL and LSPA provide a coherent conceptual foundation for comparative, longitudinal, and empirical research while improving construct clarity across entrepreneurship scholarship. The review also offers practical guidance for applying experimentation concepts more consistently in research, teaching, and entrepreneurial practice.

detail.abstract: Organizational learning theory offers rich accounts of single-, double-, and triple-loop learning. It rarely evidences whether higher-order learning endures once the structured interventions that occasion it are withdrawn. This study addresses that gap by asking how entrepreneurial teams govern and sustain learning in the year following a Lean Startup intervention, the National Science Foundation's I-Corps™ program. Using a 12-month follow-up, qualitative case design, and the Gioia methodology, this work analyzes interviews with eight teams that completed the program and remained active. Learning did not decay once teams removed the external scaffolding. Teams sustained double-loop learning by reframing assumptions and mindset. More consequentially, they developed learning governance through evidence thresholds, interview targeting, structured reflection, and decision rules that reshaped how they learned. This study distinguishes continued experimentation from triple-loop learning, arguing that only the latter modifies the rules that govern learning. It positions learning governance as an emergent organizing capability that shapes adaptation under uncertainty. This work extends triple-loop learning theory and connects it to dynamic capabilities. By tracing how governed learning becomes a durable capability rather than an episodic event, the study advances a longitudinal process model of persistent entrepreneurial learning. It clarifies what counts as evidence of higher-order learning.

title: After the Lords Report: A Transitional Options Matrix for Existing Skilled Workers under Earned Settlement

detail.title: After the Lords Report: A Transitional Options Matrix for Existing Skilled Workers under Earned Settlement
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the design of transitional arrangements for existing participants in long-term migration pathways undergoing structural reform. Using the United Kingdom's proposed "Earned Settlement" reforms as a case study, it asks a narrower but practically important question: if government decides to alter settlement conditions for an existing cohort, what forms of transition are available, and what justifications are required to reject them?

The article argues that public debate has often treated the issue as a binary choice between complete grandfathering and full retrospective application of new rules. In practice, the policy design space is substantially broader. Drawing upon parliamentary committee evidence, public-law principles, and comparative transition mechanisms used elsewhere in immigration and regulatory policy, the paper develops a Transitional Options Matrix identifying multiple intermediate approaches capable of reducing disruption while preserving the Government's ability to pursue prospective reform.

The matrix includes full saving provisions, notice-based cut-off dates, stage-based protection for near-completion cases, capped extensions, transitional credits for time already completed under existing rules, protected interim status, fiscal ring-fencing measures, dependant safeguards, fee mitigation mechanisms, and targeted cohort approaches. Each mechanism is analysed not as a policy recommendation in itself, but as a less intrusive alternative against which blanket retrospective restructuring should be evaluated.

The paper argues that the existence of workable intermediate mechanisms alters the burden of justification resting upon government. Where less disruptive and administratively operable alternatives exist, policymakers should explain why these options are inadequate before adopting measures that retrospectively alter established completion horizons and long-term reliance interests.

The article therefore reframes the settlement debate from one concerning whether transition is necessary to one concerning the form that transition should take. Its central claim is that proportionality analysis in migration policy should not be confined to judicial review proceedings after implementation, but should instead be incorporated into legislative design at the point of reform.

Originally published by the Electronic Immigration Network (EIN) on 2 July 2026.

detail.abstract: The current model of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) finance is fundamentally jeopardized by institutional short-termism, fragmented regulatory oversight, and a pervasive lack of verifiable impact measurement (Measurement, Reporting, and Verification, or MRV). This failure, central to the contemporary 'WEF Crisis,' necessitates a new, autonomous financial architecture. This report proposes a Dual-Stream Sustainable Tokenomics Model designed to bypass these systemic flaws by simultaneously accelerating regenerative capital flow toward all 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and programmatically defunding low-ESG, high-polluting enterprises. The core mechanism involves the deployment of Negative Externality Tokens (NETs), which act as a programmatic Pigouvian liability, enforced by resilient Divestment DAOs (D-DAOs). This creates an autonomous, persistent financial penalty that forces polluting entities to internalize environmental costs, effectively 'starving' unsustainable capital streams . Concurrently, the issuance of Real-World Asset (RWA) tokens and Impact Credits (ICs), underpinned by Decentralized Ledger Technology (DLT) and real-time Digital MRV (dMRV) 1, provides verifiable transparency and necessary liquidity 3 for sustainable projects across all SDGs—from poverty alleviation (SDG 1) to climate action (SDG 13). The shift to adaptive DAO 3.0 governance 4 ensures policy persistence and resilience against institutional inertia, establishing a self-sustaining financial stream decoupled from fluctuating political and financial cycles.

detail.abstract: The Dutch Medicines Pricing Act (Wet geneesmiddelenprijzen, WGP) establishes price caps for medicines to control pharmaceutical expenditures. While the WGP has contributed to lower medicine costs, concerns have emerged that reduced prices may undermine supplier participation and increase medicine shortages. This study examines the relationship between price cap reductions, supplier dynamics, and medicine shortages using comprehensive longitudinal data on prescription clusters (PRKs) in the Netherlands. We find that, over the past decade, price caps have declined, the number of suppliers per PRK has decreased, market concentration has increased, and shortage exposure has risen. Exploiting substantial price cap reductions (≥10%) and comparing affected PRKs with matched control clusters, we show that price cap decreases increase the market share in shortage by 1.34 percentage points on average, equivalent to approximately 4.9 additional shortage days per PRK per year. At the same time, price cap reductions are associated with declines in the number of suppliers and active suppliers by 1.81% and 3.00%, respectively. These effects are particularly pronounced among low-priced, low-revenue, multi-source, and price-constrained medicines. Additional analyses reveal substantial heterogeneity across market conditions, with the strongest effects observed among medicines with limited economic margins and weaker supplier incentives. The findings remain robust across alternative identification strategies, shortage definitions, time windows, and smaller price cap shocks. Overall, our results highlight an important trade-off between pharmaceutical cost containment and supply resilience, suggesting that pricing policies should consider their potential effects on supplier participation and medicine availability.

detail.abstract: Discovering causal relationships from observational data forces a choice between accuracy and scale: state-of-the-art differentiable methods achieve near-perfect F1 below d=150 but collapse to zero edges beyond, while scalable alternatives sacrifice the DAG constraint that defines causal directionality. causalscale (v3.2.0) addresses this trade-off. The package unifies seven engines: ClusterAware (exact DAG constraints for d≤200), DAGMA (strongest lowdimensional solver, F1 up to 0.989), Causal Transformer (200<d≤500), LowRankGNN (correlationreconstruction F1 at genome scale, d≤17,787; note: distinct from DAG-structure F1), plus MultiScale, MultiModal, and Ensemble, under automatic dimension-based selection.

detail.abstract: We incorporate bonds, including green bonds, alongside traditional monetary assets in the construction of a broad Divisia monetary aggregate for the United States using the Törnqvist-Theil discrete time approximation for the continuous time Divisia Index. The user costs for calculating this index are risk-adjusted and forecasted for capital uncertain assets. The analysis reveals a significant and positive correlation between a broad Divisia monetary aggregate for the US, including green bonds, and the detrended output gap. In contrast, a simple sum construct over the same assets exhibits statistical relevance only during the brief covid-19 pandemic period. We assert that a monetary aggregate which has green bonds incorporated in its construction serves as a valuable tool in monetary policy for analysing aggregate demand in the United States. This novel addition to the central banks' toolkit has the potential to provide central banks with econometric information to support monetary policy decisions whilst also incorporating information related to any transition toward environmental projects financed by designated green bonds, as highlighted by Bank of England 2018. Further research is recommended to extend this work to include other countries and to evaluate in other monetary policy frameworks.

title: Bayes Factors and Moderate Deviations in High-Throughput Screening
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, George Mason University and

detail.title: Bayes Factors and Moderate Deviations in High-Throughput Screening
detail.abstract: A high-throughput screen is a decision problem reported as a testing problem, with a threshold that ignores the size of the study and the price of a false lead. Feature screening, hyperparameter search and large-scale A/B testing are all instances; we take genome-wide association studies as the running example, but the argument needs only an estimate and a standard error per candidate. Starting from Wakefield's approximate Bayes factor (ABF), we give a decision-theoretic account of ranking, calibration and design, organised around one observation: the genome-wide threshold sits at z ≍ {log(m 2 n)} 1/2 , the moderatedeviation scale, where the deviation rate function is universal. That universality, rather than asymptotic normality, is what licenses a Bayes factor built from an estimate and a standard error; its validity requires log(m 2 n) = o(N 1/3), which fails at early-GWAS sample sizes. Four results follow. The prior under which Bayes factor and p-value rankings agree is exactly the exchangeable standardised effects model of adaptive shrinkage. The ABF obeys a Schwarz identity, giving log 10 p T ≈-log 10 m-1 2 log 10 n+c: Bonferroni supplies the m and omits the √ n. The threshold decomposes as Donoho and Johnstone's universal threshold plus an Occam factor, and on the Donoho-Jin phase diagram a study sits on the detection boundary and far below the exact-recovery boundary. Finally E H0 [ABF-1 ] = 1 exactly, so the ABF is an e-value and the pipeline is anytime-valid. The economics are stark: budget allocation is worth 32×, correcting the winner's curse repairs a 14% overstatement in the tail lift of a deployed score (and sixteen points of replication power in genomics), and the threshold-the question the literature has argued about-is worth about 7%.

detail.abstract: Retirees face three constraints that the canonical 4% rule does not address jointly: an inviolable consumption floor (essential living expenses), an early-retirement desire to spend more, and a limited accumulated principal. We study ARAWS, an adaptive rule-based withdrawal strategy that layers five mechanisms on a Guyton-Klinger guardrail base: (i) phased capital-preservation guardrails that tighten early and relax late in retirement; (ii) a sequence-of-returns awareness signal built on a withdrawal-adjusted expected-wealth ledger that does not mislabel a healthy but drawn-down portfolio as falling behind; (iii) a non-monotone dynamic floor that scales the enforced spending floor with the asset level; (iv) inter-annual smoothing; and (v) a maximum annual reduction cap. We evaluate ARAWS on a dual engine (historical rolling backtests over U.S. data, 1928–2025, and Monte-Carlo simulation) across 30/40/50/60-year horizons, using a minimum-required-principal metric under a binding essential-expense floor calibrated to a Taiwanese retiree (TWD 360,000/year, real). Across both engines ARAWS sits at the efficiency frontier: under the Monte-Carlo engine it posts the lowest minimum-principal point estimate among real strategies at every horizon—though within seed-level uncertainty of the simplest dynamic rules—saving 21–24% of required principal versus constant-real spending. We deliberately resist over-claiming, however. The margin over a trivial one-line rolling-average rule is slim (approximately 0–1.3 percentage points) and narrows to a near tie in point estimates in historical backtests—capital efficiency, it turns out, is largely captured by any reasonable dynamic rule. An immediate-drop-to-floor counterfactual sharpens the point: much of every dynamic rule's headline saving is purchased by the retiree's willingness to spend less, not by strategy skill. ARAWS is also not the smoothest strategy: its phased capital-preservation rule front-loads spending cuts, so a simpler ceiling-and-floor rule (Vanguard) delivers steadier income at the cost of approximately 10% more principal. What ARAWS offers is a particular path through the trade-off between principal, cut speed, income volatility, and floor exposure: frontier efficiency combined with a floor-enforced worst case and the highest typical-path minimum income among the efficient rules, weakly dominating a naive constant-percentage rule on the principal, cut-depth, and typical-path minimum axes (though not on lifetime consumption). We frame retirement decumulation as an explicit efficiency–stability frontier on which no single strategy dominates, position ARAWS at its efficient-and-floor-protected corner, contribute a localized empirical setting (Taiwanese essential floor, 30–60-year FIRE horizons) absent from a U.S.-centric literature, and specify the strategy completely enough for independent reimplementation, with a paper-specific verification package available from the author on request (Section 8). Rankings survive alternative return calibrations and an unhedged-TWD currency stress test; parameter-sensitivity and overfitting concerns are discussed candidly.

title: Stochastic Modelling of Italian Electricity Prices Across Volatility Regimes: GBM, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck, ARIMA-GARCH, and Markov-Switching GARCH

detail.title: Stochastic Modelling of Italian Electricity Prices Across Volatility Regimes: GBM, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck, ARIMA-GARCH, and Markov-Switching GARCH
detail.abstract: Italian wholesale electricity prices have experienced pronounced structural instability over the past two decades, driven by fuel-market shocks, rising renewable penetration, regulatory reform, and the extreme turbulence of the COVID-19 and 2021-2022 European gas crises. This paper evaluates four stochastic representations of the monthly Single National Price (PUN) over April 2004-July 2026: Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM), drift-corrected GBM via an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) mean-reverting mechanism, ARIMA-GARCH, and a two-state Markov-switching GARCH (MS-GARCH). The contribution is strictly econometric. Endogenous multiple-break detection places the instability of Italian power prices in the variance. A Quandt-Andrews test finds no significant break in the mean, the evidence for conditional heteroskedasticity is strong, and the unconditional volatility roughly triples between calm and crisis periods. That constant-variance failure sinks GBM. An OU correction picks up the shift in the long-run level but leaves the volatility dynamics unmodelled, and the conditional variance becomes adequate only under an ARIMA-GARCH(1,1) with Student-t innovations. MS-GARCH then recovers two states endogenously (calm, at ≈ 40% annualised volatility, and turbulent, at ≈ 79%) together with interpretable transition dynamics. On that classification the 2026 Iran-conflict months are calm-state noise, and the 2022 crisis regime does not reappear. Out of sample, no model beats a random walk with drift on point forecasts, which are statistically indistinguishable across models, while GARCH-type conditional variances improve density forecasts, but only during volatile regimes. The calibrated parameters are a necessary input for downstream valuation, risk-management, and hedging applications, which lie outside the present scope.

detail.abstract: Hyper-globalization, driven by the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia's war in Ukraine, which disrupted global supply chains, has given way to confrontational globalization: Global supply chains have begun to be rerouted through friendshoring, nearshoring, and inshoring, which also includes reshoring. For President Donald Trump, who aims to revive the American economy, friendshoring and nearshoring are unacceptable: MAGAnomics is based solely on inshoring, where not only do previously departed manufacturing companies return to the country (reshoring), but other companies in this sector of the economy must also give preference to operating in the United States. The primary instrument for increasing the share of manufacturing in the US economy is the imposition of high tariffs: Prioritizing manufacturing bears a superficial resemblance to Karl Marx’s economic theory. However, the far more obvious parallel is with the economic views of the mercantilists, which were thoroughly criticized by Adam Smith as early as the 18th century.

detail.abstract: On April 26–27, 2026, Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd. (NSE: SUNPHARMA) signed a definitive agreement to acquire Organon & Co. (NYSE: OGN) in an all-cash transaction valued at $14.00 per share, implying an enterprise value of $11.75 billion — the largest overseas acquisition ever undertaken by an Indian pharmaceutical company and the largest global biopharmaceutical transaction announced in 2026. This paper examines the deal as a case study in leverage-funded strategic M&A, integrating valuation analysis, capital structure implications, deal-structure mechanics, and regulatory considerations into a single framework. The analysis finds that Sun Pharma is acquiring Organon at a substantial discount to both sector trading comparables and its own valuation multiple: the transaction implies an EV/EBITDA multiple of approximately 6.2x against Organon's FY2025 adjusted EBITDA of ~$1.9 billion, versus Sun Pharma's own trading multiple of roughly 25x and typical large-cap pharma comparables of 10–15x+. This gap forms the core of the paper's central argument — that the deal is best understood not as a growth acquisition but as a balance-sheet arbitrage: a conservatively levered acquirer (Sun Pharma) absorbing a structurally over-levered but operationally sound target (Organon, carrying $8.6 billion in debt and a depressed ~3% net margin despite a healthy ~31% EBITDA margin) and financing the purchase through a $12 billion committed bridge facility that will push Sun Pharma's net leverage to 2.3x — its highest ever. The paper further examines the deal's regulatory dimension, including multi-jurisdictional antitrust clearance across the roughly 150 countries in which the combined entity will operate, and evaluates the principal execution risks: synergy realization (a guided $350 million in annual cost synergies), permanent debt refinancing, and integration risk given Sun Pharma has never absorbed a target of this scale. The paper concludes that the transaction's ultimate success will be determined less by the pricing discipline evident at signing — which appears favorable to Sun Pharma on every standard valuation metric — and more by execution over the 2026–2028 integration window, positioning the deal as either a landmark value-creating transaction or a cautionary case of leverage-driven overreach in emerging-market outbound pharmaceutical M&A.

title: The Open-Source Chinese AI Shock: Fear, Volatility, and the Repricing of Tech Giants
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: The Open-Source Chinese AI Shock: Fear, Volatility, and the Repricing of Tech Giants
detail.abstract: This study examines how a series of open-source artificial intelligence releases from Chinese laboratories shook financial markets between January 2025 and July 2026. We use event study methods and daily panel regressions to measure how high-tech and software stocks reacted to each announcement. Unlike past financial crises, where fear spread broadly across the entire market, the AI shock was highly concentrated. The ratio of tech volatility to broad market volatility (VXN/VIX) surged past 1.70, a level higher than during the 2008 Financial Crisis or the COVID-19 crash. This shows that investors were specifically worried about open-source AI disrupting proprietary software businesses, not about a general economic collapse. Options traders rushed to buy put options on tech stocks to hedge against further declines. Over the ten days following major model releases, incumbent software companies experienced cumulative abnormal returns of-4.20% (p < 0.01), confirming that markets view the open-weight Chinese AI models as a major threat to industry profits and future cash flows.

title: Smartphones and Children’s Mental Health

detail.title: Smartphones and Children’s Mental Health
detail.abstract: Children's mental health has deteriorated across high-income countries since the early 2010s, coinciding with the mass adoption of smartphones among young people. I provide the first quasi-experimental evidence on delaying children's smartphone ownership through a community-led policy. Since 2024 the Smartphone Free Childhood movement has coordinated families across the United Kingdom through a "Parent Pact" to delay giving children a smartphone until age 14. Using a matched difference in differences design, I compare changes in children's mental-health needs in English schools where a large share of parents signed with changes in similar schools where very few did. Where at least one fifth of families signed, school-recorded social, emotional and mental health need falls by around 8 percent of the counterfactual. At the same time, child psychiatric disability claims, determined independently by the Department for Work and Pensions, also fall by about 6 percent in the same communities. The effects are larger among younger children who are less likely to already have a phone and in neighborhoods where more parents sign the pledge. The findings support coordinated ownership delay as a near-zero-cost complement to school phone bans and statutory age limits, and they give parents causal evidence for delaying a child's first smartphone through the primary-school years.

title: The Digital Footprint Paradox of Artificial Intelligence: Environmental Costs, Comparative Context, and Public Health Value

detail.title: The Digital Footprint Paradox of Artificial Intelligence: Environmental Costs, Comparative Context, and Public Health Value

declarations.funderStatement: This work received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or nonprofit sectors.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being adopted across public health research, education, surveillance, and practice, and its environmental costs such as electricity, water, carbon, and data-center infrastructure have become a reason some professionals hesitate to use it. It is also, in daily practice, applied selectively once the same infrastructure serves video streaming, video conferencing, cloud storage, and social media, activities that are rarely questioned in professional settings. We compared the energy use, carbon emissions, and water consumption of AI queries with those of common digital activities, using a structured narrative synthesis of provider disclosures, agency reports, and peer-reviewed measurements. Estimates were harmonized to grams of CO₂-equivalent per functional unit and per day of assumed use, with system boundaries, accounting methods, and uncertainty ranges reported for every value. By recent measured estimates, a median AI text prompt consumes 0.24-0.34 Wh and emits well under a gram of CO₂e; twenty such prompts emit roughly 0.6-2.5 g CO₂e per day, against 70-110 g for two hours of video streaming and 150-1,000 g for an hour of video conferencing. Reasoningintensive queries, image generation, and full life-cycle accounting raise AI's per-task footprint by one to three orders of magnitude, and aggregate AI demand is the main driver of projected datacenter growth, with documented air-pollution health burdens and water stress concentrated in host communities, including in the southwestern United States. For public health, the marginal footprint of routine text-based AI use is small; the serious environmental questions concern infrastructure siting, grid mix, disclosure, and equity. We pose a call for mandatory, standardized reporting of training and inference energy use, water consumption, carbon emissions, hardware requirements, and facility-level impacts to enable credible comparison, public health assessment, and accountable governance.

title: The Loaded Wheel: Why First AI Crisis Will Be Governed by Finance, and What That Does to AI Governance

detail.title: The Loaded Wheel: Why First AI Crisis Will Be Governed by Finance, and What That Does to AI Governance

publicationDetails.detailsText: DISSENSUS WORKING PAPER SERIES DAI-2609 | July 2026

detail.abstract: The argument that only a crisis will break the deadlock in AI governance treats the crisis itself as a roulette wheel: exogenous in kind, unknowable in advance. I argue the wheel is loadednot in its timing, which is genuinely beyond reach, but in its governor. Focusing-event theory already privileges three properties on which a candidate crisis either opens a policy window or does not: legibility of harm (the framing contest of Boin, 't Hart, and McConnell), speed of attribution (the window decay of Kingdon), and maturity of the receiving regulator (Birkland's receiving community, Baumgartner and Jones's venue capture). Scored on these axes, a financial cascade does not dominate-autonomous-weapons and physical-harm events are at least as legible and as fast to attribute-but finance wins the combination, decisively on the third axis: it is the one domain that pairs a legible, quickly-attributable failure with a regulator holding exercised emergency powers over a continuously operating, un-groundable, internationally networked system, and whose window opens in public rather than inside classification. So whatever domain the first legible AIinvolved systemic event originates in, the modal outcome-and the claim is modal throughout: a plausibility ranking over governors strong enough to reallocate preparation portfolios, not a point forecast over domains-is that it routes to financial regulators, who produce governance faster than any other receiver could. I stress-test the ranking against out-of-domain history and against the objection that finance's own control layer contains the cascade; its sharpest near-term test is the cyber-finance hybrid, arguably the most probable first event of all, where the framework predicts financial regulators absorbing an AI-enabled security failure and answering it with market-structure rules that miss the mechanism. Because jurisdiction follows the corpse, the response will be fast and mis-scoped: sectoral, keyed to the legible failure, and structurally unable to reach the model layer the AI-governance community wants governed-financial mandates stop at regulated entities, and where they now reach the technology providers behind them, they reach them as providers of services, never as builders of models-and a financial crisis is structurally unlikely to reopen the question of who should govern the model as a model, because extending a tool a regulator already holds is fast where reaching for a mandate it lacks is not. It will import the documented pathology of crisis-born financial regulation-compliance ratchets that concentrate the industry, perimeters that push activity into the dark, assurance regimes that get gamed. I derive design principles for the pre-crisis shelf (general charters on sectoral vehicles, exposure measurement over rules, migrationproof monitoring) and price four borrowings from financial regulatory machinery against their own pathologies. The one failure mode the whole argument cannot reach is the one that never becomes legible: slow correlated drift that opens no window and routes nowhere.

title: Drawing the Line: The Spatial Non-Neutrality of Land Value Taxation

detail.title: Drawing the Line: The Spatial Non-Neutrality of Land Value Taxation
detail.abstract: Land value taxes (LVTs) tax land values, exempting buildings. Arnott and Stiglitz (1979) show that a 100% LVT can finance local public goods without distortion. This result fails once assessed land values capitalize neighboring spillovers, which enter the base only when they cross property lines. An LVT then favors merging parcels under positive spillovers and splitting under negative ones, and subsidizes externalities that depress neighbors' assessed land, functioning as an inverse Pigouvian subsidy. Difference-indifferences estimates from Cook County splits and mergers (2001-2023) confirm the required mechanism: assessed land values move in opposite directions, reversing between nuisance and positive-spillover exposures.

title: AI for Sustainability and Ecological Resilience in Urban Planning: Deploying Sociotechnical Data-driven Monitoring Systems

detail.title: AI for Sustainability and Ecological Resilience in Urban Planning: Deploying Sociotechnical Data-driven Monitoring Systems

detail.abstract: Given their extensive environmental footprints, resource demands, growing populations, and increasing vulnerability to climate hazards, cities and urban centers find themselves at the center of contemporary sustainability shifts and broader socio-ecological transitions. These conditions create a persistent need for monitoring and responding to various environmental risks and related public health concerns that are byproducts of these rapid transformations underway in urban areas. Existing urban planning scholarship has largely focused on infrastructure-based adaptation strategies, with comparatively less attention to integrating real-time data monitoring systems into urban decision-making frameworks. This reveals a critical gap in data-driven approaches needed to support rapidly growing cities. In addressing a vital aspect of this gap, this paper examines how AI-enabled sociotechnical monitoring systems can support environmental sustainability and ecological resilience in urban areas. The research draws on case studies that apply forms of geospatial and sociotechnical applications to assess ecological risk in major North American cities and recycling facility deployment in Costa Rica's urban centers. The aim is to evaluate the contributions of those technologies in addressing the socialenvironmental problems being faced in those urban areas, and their potential to optimize the decision-making accuracy, speed, and effectiveness of city officials, scientists, and urban planners in pursuing respective sustainability targets and resilience-building mandates. The findings show that as artificial intelligence reshapes decision-making across sectors, its growing capacity to process and interpret complex environmental data is creating new opportunities for sustainable and resilient urban planning. AI technology is contributing to positive social impacts. However, there is a shared challenge across municipalities in distinct regions. That is, AI-enabled sociotechnical data-driven monitoring systems produce actionable information and intelligence that municipalities often struggle to deploy or operationalize. This happens for various reasons, but primarily due to institutional and distribution capacity constraints. I synthesize these findings along with evidence from the broader literature to evaluate the resulting sociotechnical gap between algorithmic outputs and urban planning practice, and propose targeted governance interventions.

title: When a Machine Errs - Civil Liability in Australia

detail.title: When a Machine Errs - Civil Liability in Australia

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence now operates warehouse robots, autonomous vehicles, medical devices and industrial machinery capable of causing serious physical harm, yet Australian law has no single, purpose-built statute governing liability when an AI system malfunctions and injures a person. This article maps the patchwork of doctrines that currently apply; namely-negligence at common law, the statutory product liability and consumer guarantee regime under the Australian Consumer Law, work health and safety duties, sector-specific safety regimes for rail and road transport, and the Therapeutic Goods Administration's framework for AI-enabled medical devices. The article asks: who bears responsibility when these systems fail, and what pre-deployment testing, certification and risk management each regime demands.

detail.title: Sample-Size Phase Transition Ends the Hard-versus-Soft Clustering Debate

detail.abstract: For two decades, the clustering community has debated whether hard or soft partitioning yields better downstream results, with contradictory published conclusions. Here we show that a universal sample-size phase transition resolves this debate: hard pre-clustering dominates at small n, end-to-end soft clustering dominates at large n. Across 33 TCGA cancer types, this transition is signicant (Spearman r = 0.827, p = 3.0 × 10-9), with within-cancer resampling (r = 0.793) and single-cell replication (r = 0.820) conrming sample size, not biology, as the governing variable. The transition generalizes across six dataset typesfour positive modalities (cancer transcriptomics, MNIST images, R 2 = 0.977; PBMC single-cell; 20 Newsgroups text) and two negative controls (CIFAR-10 and synthetic null data, at ∆ ≈ 0, conrming cluster structure as prerequisite). The scaling law n crit = 6.3 × d 0.90 (R 2 = 0.985) explains why the debate has never been resolved empirically: all published benchmarks fall in the large-n soft-clustering regime, systematically missing the small-n regime where hard clustering dominates and most biomedical discovery occurs.

detail.abstract: Motivation: Differentiable causal discovery methods such as NOTEARS fail sharply on transcriptomic data where gene count d far exceeds sample size n. Beyond d ≈ 150 edges collapse to zero, yet no approach exploits the cluster structure inherent in gene expression to stabilize inference. Results: We introduce CAGate, which embeds adaptive clustering into NOTEARS optimization. A MAD-aware gate weights per-sample contributions so homogeneous subpopulations drive edge discovery. Across 33 TCGA cancer types (68 configurations), CAGate universally outperforms NOTEARS (mean ∆ = +158 edges). At d = 200, CAGate recovers 550+ edges where NOTEARS finds zero. The advantage is strongest in small-sample cancers (n < 323, ∆ = +213). External validation against CTD, ClinGen, and STRING confirms clinical relevance of discovered edges.

title: Interstate Inequalities in Maternal Health Service Utilization in India: Evidence from a Composite Performance Index Based on NFHS-6

detail.title: Interstate Inequalities in Maternal Health Service Utilization in India: Evidence from a Composite Performance Index Based on NFHS-6

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract:
Background: India continues to show wide interstate disparities in maternal health service utilization, which constrain progress toward the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3·1 target of a maternal mortality ratio (MMR) below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030. This study aimed to construct and validate a composite Maternal Health Performance Index (MHPI) using National Family Health Survey-6 (NFHS-6, 2023–24) data, and to identify state-specific priorities for achieving the SDG target.

Methods: Six maternal health service utilization indicators were equally weighted and averaged to derive the MHPI (range 0–100) for 35 States/Union Territories. States were classified as High, Medium or Low performers using mean ± 0·5 SD cut-offs. Inter-indicator and indicator–MHPI associations were examined by Pearson correlation; the MHPI–MMR relationship was assessed by linear regression against Sample Registration System (SRS) data for 19 States. Internal consistency, construct, criterion and discriminant validity, and robustness to alternative (principal component analysis-derived) weighting were evaluated.

Findings: The MHPI ranged from 7·38 (Nagaland) to 92·21 (Kerala) (mean 64·53, SD 21·80). Fifteen States/UTs (43%) were High performers, 12 (34%) Medium and eight (23%) Low. South and West zones recorded the highest mean MHPI (84·97 and 83·35, respectively); the Northeast recorded the lowest (39·84) with marked within-zone heterogeneity. All six indicators correlated significantly with the MHPI (r = 0·714–0·944); iron-folic acid (IFA) consumption for ≥180 days showed the weakest inter-indicator correlations (r = 0·345–0·601). MHPI correlated negatively with MMR (r = −0·647, p = 0·003; R² = 0·419). An MHPI of ≥74·91 was identified as the threshold associated with attainment of the SDG 3·1 target; six States met both criteria, while Bihar, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh and Assam showed the largest deficits and were classified Critical Priority.

Interpretation: The MHPI is a valid, reproducible composite measure that captures substantial interstate heterogeneity in maternal health service utilization and predicts state-level MMR. It offers a practical tool for ranking States, tracking programme performance, and prioritizing resource allocation toward Critical Priority States as India approaches the 2030 SDG deadline.Funding This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

title: The Legal Framework for the Clinical Management of People with Differences of Sex Development across the World: Practical and Ethical Implications

detail.title: The Legal Framework for the Clinical Management of People with Differences of Sex Development across the World: Practical and Ethical Implications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding.

detail.abstract:
Background: Differences of Sex Development (DSD) management has undergone major worldwide changes, shifting from early surgical/hormonal interventions towards models centered on individual autonomy driven by legal frameworks. This study aimed to assess how legal frameworks shape clinical practice and their broader medical and societal implications.

Methods: We conducted a multidisciplinary comparative study across 30 countries/states combining (1) legal analysis of enacted laws, draft bills, precedents and regulatory documents issued by heath authorities; (2) a physician-based survey on real-world clinical practice; (3) an ethical analysis integrating medical, legal, and social science expertise. Data were systematically examined regarding the scope of DSD definitions determining legal coverage, treatment decision-making processes and their actors, individual consent, medical necessity thresholds and parental authority.

Findings: Individual consent is the center of treatment decision-making across all texts. Implementation varies widely, ranging from prohibition of early procedures to court-based decisions, or MDTs processes organized at local, regional or national levels. Medical necessity thresholds differ between countries, from consideration of future urinary and sexual function to restriction to short-term risks or life-threatening conditions. In 70% of texts, parental views are not mentioned or are considered insufficient to initiate treatment. Age of autonomous decision-making is most often not specified, with reference instead to notions of maturity and comprehension. Posterior hypospadias is variably classified as outside the DSD framework or included within it, especially when associated with hormonal or genetic abnormalities.

Interpretation: Beside bringing the undisputable advantage of the homogenization and centralization of care in reference centers, this evolving legal framework redefines pediatric decision-making by prioritizing individual autonomy, reshaping parental authority, and introducing tensions between medical indication, consent, and functional outcomes. Beyond DSD, these changes raise broader questions regarding the boundaries of medicine, age of autonomy, and potential societal implications of non-binary recognition. The findings highlight a complex and evolving interface between medicine, law, and society.

title: Who Bears the AI Shock? The Distributional and Fiscal Incidence in the UK

detail.title: Who Bears the AI Shock? The Distributional and Fiscal Incidence in the UK
detail.abstract: I examine how the simulated household and fiscal effects of an AI labour-market shock in the United Kingdom vary with its incidence. I link occupation-level AI exposure to workers in the 2024-25 Family Resources Survey and use PolicyEngine UK to simulate employment, wage and capital-income shocks. The design covers 66 shock-size combinations and five displacement-incidence families that hold aggregate displacement fixed. In the central 7 per cent displacement calibration, the 50-draw mean Exchequer cost is £17.7 billion and absolute before-housing-costs poverty, measured against a baseline-fixed threshold, rises by 1.87 percentage points. Across incidence families, the mean fiscal cost ranges from £13.9 billion under uniform incidence to £20.6 billion under expertise compression and £32.8 billion in an author-constructed top-loaded stress test; poverty varies less. The Gini rises in every displacement scenario examined. In an additional sensitivity, imposing occupation-level wage cuts instead of job losses produces a larger fiscal cost, little change in poverty and a small fall in the Gini. These simulations suggest that both incidence and the adjustment margin matter for household outcomes and the public finances.

detail.abstract:
Background: Thailand faces a rising burden of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), which drive morbidity, healthcare utilization, and economic costs. The Praboromarajchanok Institute (PBRI) 7-Color Model was introduced for population-level screening and risk stratification, but evidence on its effectiveness and economic value remains limited. This study evaluated changes in risk distribution and cost-effectiveness of the PBRI Model in Sing Buri province from 2022-2024, against a 2021 baseline.

Methods: Repeated cross-sectional analyses used patients’ most recent annual visit from six health centers and six hospitals. Risk was classified using the PBRI Model, with high-risk prevalence defined as Dark Green to Black. Percentage-point (pp) changes from baseline were estimated with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Regression-adjusted cost-effectiveness analyses in hospitals adjusted for age, sex, payment type, and hospital fixed effects, from societal and payer perspectives. Sensitivity analyses tested alternative “high-risk” definitions.

Findings: The PBRI Model was associated with shifts toward lower-risk categories. In health centers, White increased (+5.33 pp) and Red remained elevated (+3.5 pp), while Yellow and Black categories declined. In hospitals, White (+4.13 pp) and Light Green (+2.61 pp) increased, while Dark Green declined (-4.08 pp). From the societal perspective, the intervention was cost-saving and more effective than baseline across all years. From the payer perspective, higher expenditures were associated with greater reductions in high-risk prevalence, with improving cost-effectiveness over time.

Interpretation: BRI Model implementation was associated with reduced high-risk hypertension and T2DM and improved cost-effectiveness over time, supporting broader implementation in high-burden settings.

title: Empowerment or Subordination? Gender Contradictions in Latin America's Conditional Cash Transfer Programmes

detail.title: Empowerment or Subordination? Gender Contradictions in Latin America's Conditional Cash Transfer Programmes
detail.abstract: Conditional Cash Transfers (CCTs) have become a widely adopted social protection programme aimed at poverty alleviation in Latin America. Despite their widespread implementation, the long-term effects of CCTs on welfare and poverty reduction remain unclear. This essay critically analyses gendered assessments of CCT programmes in Peru, Mexico, and Nicaragua, focusing on women's empowerment and inclusion. While CCTs were designed to empower women by channelling funds to them and encouraging investment in human capital, their implementation often reinforced traditional gender roles and responsibilities. Despite improvements in child health and education, women's social and economic status within households remained largely unchanged. In some cases, CCTs exacerbated gender inequalities by increasing women's unpaid labour and limiting their agency. By examining the contradictions in CCT outcomes, this essay highlights the tension between the theoretical goals of empowerment and the practical realities of programme implementation, questioning the inclusivity and effectiveness of these interventions.

title: Intertemporal Poverty Across Europe: Evidence From Before and After COVID-19
affiliations: and

detail.title: Intertemporal Poverty Across Europe: Evidence From Before and After COVID-19
detail.abstract: We study intertemporal poverty before and after the COVID-19 pandemic in several EU countries using the EU-SILC longitudinal panel survey. To this end, we conduct two complementary analyses: (i) a comparison of two four-year balanced panels (2016-19 vs. 2020-23) across 17 countries; and (ii) a single panel tracking the same individuals over 2019-22 across 20 countries, with German figures drawn from the SOEP rather than EU-SILC. We assess intertemporal poverty before and after the outbreak of COVID-19 using a two-parameter class of measures that allow different degrees of sensitivity to (i) fluctuations in poverty gaps over time within individuals (through a parameter α) and (ii) inequality in intertemporal poverty between individuals (through β). Contrary to early predictions, intertemporal poverty fell in most countries after the outbreak, with the largest declines in countries with higher baseline levels (Bulgaria, Romania, Spain, Lithuania) and concentrated in the chronic rather than transient component. This decline is even more apparent under an anchored poverty line, mitigating concerns about mechanical effects from a decreasing median due to the pandemic. However, both the direction and magnitude depend on the value judgements embedded in the measure. Weighting cross-individual inequality more heavily (β > α) amplifies the declines yielding reductions in all 20 single-panel countries. In contrast, weighting within-person volatility more heavily (α > β) produces a markedly more mixed picture.

title: Are ML Classifiers Transferable? An Empirical Study of False Positive Detection for MISRA-C Violations in Automotive Software

detail.title: Are ML Classifiers Transferable? An Empirical Study of False Positive Detection for MISRA-C Violations in Automotive Software
detail.abstract: The adoption of machine learning (ML) techniques to streamline static analysis compliance has gained traction in automotive software development, particularly for managing the high volume of MISRA-C violations in legacy codebases. However, a critical assumption underlying these approaches remains underexplored: whether ML classifiers trained to detect false positives in one context can be transferred effectively to another. This study presents an empirical investigation of classifier transferability for false positive detection in MISRA-C violations within automotive software. Using a dataset of static analysis findings from multiple automotive codebases, we evaluate the performance of classifiers trained on one project when applied to different codebases, development teams, and violation patterns. Our results reveal that while classifiers demonstrate strong performance within their training domain, transferability is significantly limited by differences in coding practices, violation distributions, and project-specific deviation patterns. We identify key factors affecting transferability and propose guidelines for practitioners seeking to leverage ML-assisted false positive detection across projects. These findings have implications for the deployment of AI-based static analysis tools in safety-critical automotive development, where ISO 26262 compliance demands predictable and validated tool behavior.

detail.abstract:
Bharat faces a paradox of civilisational depth. It is the custodian of the world’s most sophisticated ancient frameworks for understanding human wellbeing — frameworks that were not merely philosophical but empirically generative, practically applicable, and epistemologically ahead of what the modern West has only recently begun to approach. Yet it measures, governs, and reports the wellbeing of its 1.4 billion citizens and 500 million-person workforce using instruments borrowed almost entirely from traditions that lack this depth. The Bharat Wellbeing Index (BWI) is an act of civilisational recovery: the systematic retrieval, operationalisation, and institutional deployment of the Panchakosha model from the Taittiriya Upanishad as the foundational architecture for India’s national wellbeing measurement and governance system.

This paper presents BWI Version 3.0 — a substantially revised, expanded, and deepened edition that advances six original contributions. First, it establishes the Panchakosha as not merely a cultural heritage artefact but a scientifically valid, epistemologically superior, and practically deployable framework for multidimensional wellbeing measurement — drawing on neuroscience, psychophysiology, positive psychology, and systems biology to demonstrate the empirical convergence of modern wellbeing science toward the model that the Vedic tradition articulated 2,500 years ago. Second, it positions BWI explicitly as an instrument of national sovereignty in the wellbeing science domain: India measuring its own people by its own knowledge, rather than by borrowed frameworks calibrated to different civilisational assumptions. Third, it deepens the BWI’s Vedic and Dharmik architecture — integrating insights from the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, the Arthashastra of Kautilya, the Charaka Samhita, and the Bhagavad Gita’s Karma and Dharma frameworks — into specific dimension indicators and scoring rationales.

Fourth, Version 3.0 produces a complete, deployable regulatory compliance architecture linking each BWI dimension to BRSR NGRBC Principles, ISO 45003, the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, the POSH Act 2013, and five SDGs, with specific disclosure output formats. Fifth, it introduces a disaggregated demographic wellbeing architecture for women in the workforce, mid-level managers, senior professionals navigating the experience-obsolescence paradox, and CXO/legal executives — the populations most differentially at risk and most inadequately served by existing instruments. Sixth and most practically significant, it presents three detailed, deployable Pilot Recommendations — for a State Government, an educational Campus, and a Public Sector Undertaking (PSU) — structured as reference implementation blueprints for researchers, policymakers, and institutional leaders.

The paper concludes with a formal recommendation that the Government of India consider the BWI as the foundational instrument for India’s national preventive health governance architecture, and positions the paper as a foundation document for a sustained Applied Indic Wisdom research programme of global significance.

title: Anatomy of a Null Result: A Pre-registered, Adversarially Audited Case Study of Retail Systematic Trading in Crypto Perpetuals (2018-2026)

detail.title: Anatomy of a Null Result: A Pre-registered, Adversarially Audited Case Study of Retail Systematic Trading in Crypto Perpetuals (2018-2026)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no funding for this work. The live-trading experiment was conducted with the author's own account (~296 USDT), as disclosed in the paper.

detail.abstract:
This is a pre-registered, adversarially audited case study of what a technically competent retail trader can actually extract from crypto perpetual futures. Over 18 experiment families I evaluated a strategy space of 20,891,648 configurations × 31 presets (~6.5×10⁸ evaluations per symbol-pass on GPU), on Binance USDT-margined perpetuals (top-45 by liquidity), 2018-2026, at taker costs, including ten weeks of real-money execution with certified simulation-tolive fidelity. Two results. (1) Out-of-sample transfer of past-performance selection is approximately null: the correlation between past and forward performance is +0.598 [0.451, 0.713] when measured on the same data that produced the selection, and-0.054 [-0.305, +0.389] on independent data. The apparent edge of the optimized system (profit factor 3.317 in-sample) collapses to 0.917-below breakeven-when parameters are fixed a priori. (2) The genuine signals detected never cleared an honest bar: their magnitude is below retail costs (liquidation-cascade survival gap ≈ +1 bp gross per trade; hourly seasonality < 10 bps) or below a trivial benchmark (market-neutral momentum Sharpe 0.541 vs. 1.443 for an equal-weighted buy-and-hold; funding-carry long leg ≈ market beta). These findings replicate the established literature on backtest overfitting and retail trading losses; the contribution is the mechanistic anatomy from inside one operation, with open artifacts. Limitations-survivorship as an explicit ceiling, ~3 effective evidence clusters rather than 18 independent ones, a bounded domain, cryptographically verifiable pre-registration for only 3 of 18 families-are stated up front.
