The author directed all research decisions and takes full responsibility for all claims. Full statement: Section 4 of the paper and AI_ASSISTANCE.md in the repository.

title: Beyond the PhD: Scaling California's Quantum Workforce for Commercialization
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Beyond the PhD: Scaling California's Quantum Workforce for Commercialization
detail.abstract:
California’s quantum research strength creates a commercialization opportunity that now depends on broader workforce infrastructure. PhD-trained scientists will remain essential, but commercialization will also require technician-level and technician-adjacent workers who can support hardware, fabrication, testing, operation, maintenance, cryogenics, optics, electronics, controls, mechatronics, and systems integration.

This memorandum examines barriers preventing broader domestic participation in California’s quantum workforce, drawing on public-source research, job-market evidence, role-profile studies, semiconductor workforce comparisons, and stakeholder interviews across industry, education, national laboratories, workforce intermediaries, and policy organizations. The analysis finds that California’s quantum ecosystem has substantial adjacent talent in community colleges, universities, apprenticeship programs, incumbent technical workers, and fields such as mechatronics, photonics, semiconductors, software, controls, and advanced manufacturing. However, much of that talent remains under-recognized and under-connected because employer needs, educational pathways, credential signals, hands-on training access, and stakeholder coordination remain fragmented.

The memorandum recommends three linked models: a California Quantum Skills Compact and Certification Pathway, a Quantum Technician Earn-and-Learn Pathway, and Shared Quantum Training Infrastructure and Retention Anchor. These models would help define and update quantum-relevant skills, connect paid training to employment, expand hands-on access, and link workforce development to company retention. Since quantum technology remains early-stage, unevenly commercialized, and fragmented across hardware platforms, these models should be treated as adaptive frameworks rather than fixed implementation plans. Current demand appears real but modest in absolute scale, making the appropriate response targeted, measurable, and expandable. The central policy opportunity is to align workforce development, regional access, affordability, shared infrastructure, and company retention as part of one stronger commercialization strategy for California’s quantum ecosystem.

title: Rethinking Job Analysis in Dynamic Work Environments: Implications for Training Alignment, Transfer of Training, and Employee Performance

detail.title: Rethinking Job Analysis in Dynamic Work Environments: Implications for Training Alignment, Transfer of Training, and Employee Performance
detail.abstract: Job analysis serves as the foundation of personnel selection, training, performance management, and workforce planning by identifying the knowledge, skills, abilities, and other characteristics required for effective job performance. However, traditional job analysis approaches were developed under assumptions of relatively stable work structures and clearly defined job boundaries. Contemporary organizations increasingly operate within dynamic environments characterized by technological disruption, hybrid work arrangements, evolving skill requirements, and greater task variability. These changes raise important questions regarding the continued effectiveness of conventional job analysis methods in supporting organizational decision-making. This conceptual review examines contemporary developments in job analysis and evaluates their implications for training alignment, transfer of training, and employee performance outcomes. Drawing upon personnel psychology, work analysis theory, and training effectiveness literature, the review synthesizes evidence from foundational and contemporary scholarship published between 1978 and 2026. The analysis identifies a growing disconnect between traditional task-based job analysis frameworks and the increasingly adaptive nature of modern work. Existing research suggests that inaccurate or outdated job analyses may contribute to misaligned training investments, reduced transfer of learning, and suboptimal performance outcomes. Conversely, adaptive and context-sensitive approaches appear better positioned to capture evolving job requirements and support workforce agility. A conceptual framework is proposed linking adaptive job analysis practices to training alignment, transfer of training, and job performance. Directions for future empirical research are presented, including the examination of mediating and moderating mechanisms that may influence these relationships. Implications for organizational practice include improving workforce planning, enhancing employee development initiatives, and strengthening evidence-based human resource decision-making in rapidly changing work environments.

title: Trust Transfer: How Credibility Moves Through Networks, Brands, and Machines
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Trust Transfer: How Credibility Moves Through Networks, Brands, and Machines
detail.abstract:
This manuscript presents a comprehensive framework for understanding how credibility and trust transfer through social, commercial, and technological systems. Across fourteen chapters, the author develops and tests a core model applicable to a critical gap in the emerging answer engine optimization (AEO) field: understanding why organizations appear—or fail to appear—in AI-generated answers, and why adoption of AI systems by users significantly outpaces trust (66% use, 46% trust).

The framework, articulated as Source → Relationship → Target → Transfer, explains credibility movement across diverse domains: personal recommendations, celebrity endorsements, brand positioning, platform algorithms, influencer marketing, and artificial intelligence systems.

Using case studies and behavioral evidence, the work identifies:
- Five pathways through which trust transfers to new objects (applicable to AI system recommendations)
- Two speeds at which trust forms (borrowed signals vs. earned confidence)
- Mistrust contagion: how failures travel backward through trust networks and erode confidence
- The AI gap: structural reasons why 66% of people use AI systems but only 46% trust them
- Signal design: how organizations can deliberately build trustworthy relationships in algorithmic contexts

The analysis reveals that modern trust environments are simultaneously more efficient (credibility moves faster through networks) and more fragile (failures cascade quickly). The framework applies across geographies, sectors, and technologies—offering theoretical coherence to how credibility transfer works in the age of AI-generated answers.

This research provides foundational understanding for the emerging field of answer engine optimization, where organizations must understand not just technical visibility but the trust mechanisms that determine whether AI systems recommend them. Implications span organizational behavior, consumer psychology, digital platform design, AI transparency, and the practical strategy required for organizational positioning in AI-mediated discovery systems.

title: Measuring Subnational Welfare Across Sub-saharan Africa: Reproducible Relative-wealth Estimates from Open Satellite Data
affiliations: and RMIT University

detail.title: Measuring Subnational Welfare Across Sub-saharan Africa: Reproducible Relative-wealth Estimates from Open Satellite Data
detail.abstract:
Can openly licensed satellite and geospatial data alone produce a wealth map accurate and fine-
grained enough to guide policy where household data are scarce? This paper constructs relative
wealth estimates for 23 African countries from openly licensed data alone, without proprietary
inputs or daytime-imagery deep learning, anchored on the Demographic and Health Survey
(DHS) asset wealth index and built with gradient-boosted and interpretable sparse-linear
estimators. Fit on each country's survey, the estimates explain 69 percent of the variation in
cluster-level wealth (rank correlation 0.84); under leave-one-country-out transfer they explain 62
percent (0.76). Validated against two survey programmes withheld from training, they recover an
independent asset reference almost in full and three-quarters of an attainable asset-to-
consumption reference, each carrying a calibrated prediction interval. Targeting capture of the poorest improves with resolution, and the estimates are released as an annual series for 2017 to
2025, a public instrument a government can rebuild and a researcher can audit.

title: National Security-Related Foreign Investment Screening Laws and Investment Efficiency
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: National Security-Related Foreign Investment Screening Laws and Investment Efficiency
detail.abstract: This study investigates the effect of national security-related foreign investment screening laws on managers' investment choices. These laws weaken takeover markets by granting regulators broad new powers to revise or reject foreign takeovers of firms in national security-related industries. I identify exogenous variation in national security-related foreign investment screening laws using the enactment of a U.S. national security-related foreign investment screening law known as the Foreign Investment and National Security Act (FINSA). Consistent with managerial entrenchment theory, I document that, following the enactment of FINSA, national security firms' inefficient investment increases. Eventtime tests corroborate and cross-sectional tests demonstrate that results strengthen with treatment strength. Results generalize to seven alternative investment efficiency measures. Stacked panel tests exploiting regulators' staggered enforcement of FINSA across 66 industries over time between 2008 and 2021 further corroborate. Overall, this study documents the unintended consequences of national security-related foreign investment screening laws on managers' investment choices.

title: Job Design, Leadership Practices, and Employee Motivation in Military Organizations: A Quantitative Examination of Motivational Predictors Among Active-Duty Personnel

detail.title: Job Design, Leadership Practices, and Employee Motivation in Military Organizations: A Quantitative Examination of Motivational Predictors Among Active-Duty Personnel
detail.abstract: Employee motivation is a critical determinant of organizational effectiveness, performance, engagement, and operational readiness, particularly within military organizations characterized by hierarchical structures, demanding work conditions, and mission-oriented objectives. Although extensive organizational psychology research has examined the influence of job design and leadership practices on employee motivation in civilian settings, limited empirical evidence exists regarding these relationships within military environments. The purpose of this quantitative cross-sectional correlational study is to examine the extent to which job design characteristics and leadership practices predict employee motivation among active-duty military personnel and whether leadership practices moderate the relationship between job design and motivation. Grounded in the Job Characteristics Model, Self-Determination Theory, and Transformational Leadership Theory, the study examines three job design characteristics, autonomy, task significance, and feedback, and their relationships with employee motivation. Leadership practices are examined as both independent predictors and potential moderators. A purposive stratified sample of approximately 250 active-duty military personnel will be recruited across operational, administrative, technical, and supervisory units. Data will be collected using the Job Diagnostic Survey (JDS), the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire (MLQ-5X Short), and the Work Extrinsic and Intrinsic Motivation Scale (WEIMS). Data analysis will include descriptive statistics, reliability analyses, confirmatory factor analyses, hierarchical multiple regression, and moderation analyses using the PROCESS macro. The findings are expected to contribute to the organizational psychology literature by extending motivation research into military contexts and providing evidence regarding the applicability of established motivation theories within highly structured work environments. Practically, the study may inform leadership development initiatives, personnel management strategies, and organizational interventions designed to enhance employee motivation, engagement, well-being, and operational effectiveness within military institutions.

title: Beyond DEI Programs: Workforce Service Management as the Operational Infrastructure for Sustainable Gatebreaking in STEMM Ecosystems

detail.title: Beyond DEI Programs: Workforce Service Management as the Operational Infrastructure for Sustainable Gatebreaking in STEMM Ecosystems
detail.abstract: Organizations across science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and medicine (STEMM) are operating in an environment in which equity-related commitments are increasingly exposed to political scrutiny, legal uncertainty, technological disruption, and changing workforce expectations. Although diversity, equity, inclusion, and belonging (DEIB) programs have expanded participation and improved organizational awareness, many remain vulnerable because they are organized as episodic interventions rather than institutionalized management systems. This article identifies a theoretical and operational gap in Gatebreaking scholarship: the absence of a coherent architecture for governing the workforce services through which opportunity, inclusion, capability, and organizational resilience are produced. To address this gap, the article introduces Workforce Service Management (WSM) as a conceptual framework that integrates workforce governance, human resource management, diversity and inclusion, artificial intelligence governance, service management, risk management, and international standards into a unified theory of organizational capability. Diversity & Inclusion Service Management (DISM) is presented as the first operational domain of WSM, translating ISO 30415 from guidance into auditable management practice. The article further develops an ISO Standards Crosswalk connecting ISO 30415, ISO 30201, ISO 30414, ISO 30403, ISO/IEC 42001, ISO 37301, ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 20000, ISO 45001, and ISO 9001 as complementary contributors to workforce service maturity. The argument is conceptual rather than empirical: WSM is proposed as an emerging interdisciplinary field for studying how organizations institutionalize equitable workforce capability under sociopolitical pressure. The article concludes by outlining a research agenda focused on maturity models, measurement, AI-enabled implementation, benchmarking, workforce risk, and comparative institutional analysis.

title: Bridging Machine Learning & Economic Decision Theory A Unified Criterion for Feature Selection in Employee Turnover Prediction Models

detail.abstract: Machine learning models predict employee turnover with ever-increasing accuracy, but accuracy is not what firms pay for. A missed departure and a false alarm carry radically different price tags, yet virtually the entire turnover prediction literature evaluates models with statistical metrics (AUC, F1) that treat both errors alike. This paper is the first to apply Elkan's (2001) cost-sensitive classification framework to turnover prediction, developing an Expected Misclassification Cost (EMC) criterion for feature selection, calibrated with firm-specific cost parameters from the retail chain studied by Friebel, Heinz, and Zubanov (2022, Management Science). Using 237,859 employee-month observations across 248 stores, we show that the "best" feature set is not a property of the data alone, but of the cost model behind it. Under conventional one-time (stock) costs, three compensation-based features minimize EMC at €21.14 per employee-month. Correcting for the empirically documented temporary nature of retention interventions through a present-value (flow) adjustment raises the optimal classification threshold from 0.158 to 0.543 and selects three entirely different, tenure-based features cutting costs to €17.28. The mechanism is a counterintuitive population-level reversal: each missed leaver costs 5.3 times more than a false alarm, but because stayers outnumber leavers 20 to 1, a percentage point of false positives is 3.8 times more expensive than one of false negatives. Optimal feature sets also prove context-dependent, nesting from 9 features in low-turnover stores to 22 in high-turnover stores. For a 5,000-employee firm, the flow-corrected sparse model saves €380,000 annually, 27% over the full-feature benchmark a difference invisible to AUC and F1. Monte Carlo simulations confirm it is the most robust specification under joint uncertainty about replacement costs and intervention effectiveness.

title: Pathways To a Circular Economy in the Agriculture-food System: Actor-Based Analysis of Digital Capacity, Institutional Alignment, and Collaboration Dynamics using The Eddu-M Model
affiliations: Aydın Adnan Menderes University and Selçuk University

detail.title: Pathways To a Circular Economy in the Agriculture-food System: Actor-Based Analysis of Digital Capacity, Institutional Alignment, and Collaboration Dynamics using The Eddu-M Model
detail.abstract:
Aim: This study addresses the transition to a circular economy (CE) in agri-food supply chains,
focusing on how digitalization, institutional capacity, and collaboration shape CE practices. It high-
lights a research gap in existing literature, which often lacks multi-actor, multi-country perspectives.
The paper introduces the EDDU-M model to analyze these dynamics in Türkiye and Italy – two coun-
tries with different digital and institutional maturity levels.
Material and methods: A mixed-methods design was used, combining Structural Equation Modeling
(SEM) for hypothesis testing with fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) and thematic
analysis. Data were collected from 412 businesses across seven supply chain actors (e.g., producers,
processors, exporters) through surveys and interviews. The study measured digitalization, CE practices,
institutional capacity, and collaboration structures, with country context as a moderating variable.
Results: Digitalization significantly boosts CE performance in both countries, but its effect varies
across actors. In Türkiye, logistics and exporters benefit most, while in Italy, the impact is more
evenly distributed. Collaboration and institutional capacity also strongly influence CE outcomes.
fsQCA revealed that different combinations of digital tools and collaborative dynamics can lead to
high CE performance, depending on the national and actor context
Conclusions:The EDDU-M model provides a comprehensive framework for understanding CE tran-
sitions in agri-food systems. It shows that digital tools alone are not sufficient – contextual factors
like cooperation quality and institutional support are equally vital. These insights offer practical
guidance for policymakers aiming to promote sustainable transformation across diverse agricul-
tural ecosystems

title: Training Your Replacement: Employee-trained Agents, Trade Secrets, and the Retained Replica

detail.title: Training Your Replacement: Employee-trained Agents, Trade Secrets, and the Retained Replica
detail.abstract: Employers have begun to build internal agents trained on their own employees, systems that ingest a worker's messages, documents, and code in order to reproduce that worker's output. Meta describes deploying such a "second brain" across tens of thousands of staff; a lawsuit over its 2026 layoffs describes employee-trained agents built to replicate the output of the people being cut. This essay asks a narrow legal question the surrounding coverage skips: who owns the replica, and what, if anything, does the worker retain in a reusable model of their own judgment. The answer under existing doctrine is stark and one-directional. Work-made-for-hire rules, invention-assignment agreements, and the firm's control of the system place the artifact with the employer, and where copyright fails because an AI output has no human author, trade-secret law protects the same artifact without requiring one. Every route leaves ownership with the employer and the worker with no claim. None of them has a category for what the thing is: a durable, reusable replica of the worker's operative judgment that keeps producing after the worker is gone. It names that artifact the retained replica and the process that yields it self-extraction, and argues that employment law, built to govern labor rented during a term, has no concept for the employer's retention of a working copy of the worker after the term ends. The essay closes by mapping the design space a counterweight would occupy, consent at the point of capture, an extension of the digital-replica statutes to occupational judgment, a residual economic interest in the replica's output, and a limit modeled on the settled protection of a departing worker's general skill, and argues that the last is the cleanest: a replica fitted to an individual worker closely enough to substitute for them should be presumptively unenforceable against the person it was drawn from.

title: Feeding A Nation: State Procurement Efficiency and India's Food Security
affiliations: Gautam Buddha University, Gautam Buddha University and Gautam Buddha University

detail.title: Feeding A Nation: State Procurement Efficiency and India's Food Security
detail.abstract: Aim: This study examines how state-level procurement performance shapes India's food security outcomes by assessing the linkage between procurement efficiency, minimum support prices (MSPs), and Public Distribution System (PDS) offtake across major grain-producing states. Material and methods: Using a panel dataset spanning 2005-2023 for rice and wheat across Punjab, Haryana, and Uttar Pradesh, random-and fixed-effects panel regressions were estimated alongside diagnostic tests for heteroskedasticity, serial correlation, and multicollinearity. Procurement efficiency was quantified through the Procurement Efficiency Ratio (PER), Contribution Ratio (CR), and Gini coefficient to track inequality and concentration trends. Results: Punjab and Haryana demonstrate strong MSP responsiveness, high efficiency, and disproportionately large contributions to national grain stocks. In contrast, Uttar Pradesh under-contributes despite its production dominance, reflecting institutional bottlenecks. The Gini coefficient increased from 0.48 to 0.63, indicating rising concentration and systemic risk. Panel regression results also show that procurement significantly drives national PDS distribution, with lagged effects. Conclusions: Institutional capacity not production alone determines effective procurement. Strengthening procurement systems in lagging states, diversifying sourcing regions, and embedding efficiency monitoring mechanisms are critical for enhancing equity and resilience in India's food security architecture.

title: A Five-Zone Architecture for Radiation Shielding Performance Standards in Spacecraft and Off-Earth Infrastructure
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Five-Zone Architecture for Radiation Shielding Performance Standards in Spacecraft and Off-Earth Infrastructure
detail.abstract:
The international legal and technical architecture governing spacecraft contains no unified standard for radiation shielding performance. Liability allocation under the 1972 Liability Convention presumes a measurable standard of care that does not exist; in-orbit insurance is priced on aggregate mission risk because underwriters cannot differentiate shielding posture between operators; and procurement requirements vary incoherently across programs. Existing technical references (the European Cooperation for Space Standardization’s ECSS-E-ST-10-12C, the United States’ NASA-HDBK-4002B, and the component-level test standards of the Joint Electron Device Engineering Council (JEDEC) and the Department of War) provide rigorous calculation methods, design-margin policies, and test procedures, but none constitutes a unified, conformance-ready performance specification, and none extends coherently beyond the Earth-orbital environment.

This paper proposes a five-zone architecture for radiation shielding performance standards spanning the operational environments of the expanding off-Earth economy: Earth Orbital, Cislunar, Inner Solar, Jovian, and Outer Solar. For each zone, performance is specified across four parameter families (Total Ionising Dose (TID), Single-Event Effect (SEE) Linear Energy Transfer (LET) threshold, Displacement Damage Dose (DDD), and mission-duration cumulative exposure) with reference tiers drawn from the established radiation-environment literature and harmonized into a single conformance-ready reporting format. The architecture specifies performance rather than design: it defines what a system must achieve for a given zone, leaving suppliers free to compete on shielding solutions. Test methodologies reference established JEDEC and military-standard procedures. The framework’s reporting format is demonstrated through a worked example drawing on published flight results from International Space Station dosimetry and the Materials International Space Station Experiment (MISSE) program.

This paper sets out a pathway by which the architecture can be adopted as an industry standard (through professional standards bodies, insurance underwriting, procurement, and ultimately regulatory and soft-law reference) and describes the independent conformance-assessment institution required to administer it. We argue that the absence of such a standard is not a gap in data, which is abundant and well-characterized, but a gap in institutional structure; and that supplying the missing performance-and-conformance layer is both technically tractable and commercially and strategically significant as humanity builds infrastructure beyond Earth, in orbit first, then on the lunar and Martian surfaces. We conclude with an invitation to a multi-stakeholder consortium to develop and steward the standard.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that Nietzsche’s anti-egalitarianism depends on equivocation between conceptions of power as quantitative superiority and qualitative feeling (das Machtgefühl) and between associated conceptions of equality as similarity (die Ähnlichkeit) and opposition or resistance (der Widerstand). Nietzsche’s key arguments against equality fail when applied to the qualitative form of power, since the feeling of power does not directly correlate with quantitative ability and requires relatively equal or proportional resistance. Consequently, Nietzsche’s commitment to the promotion of humanity’s highest individuals does not entail the rejection of moral egalitarianism in every form and even supports a pluralistic egalitarianism that promotes equality understood not as similarity but as multiple, proportional resistances (die Veilheit, die Widerstände).

detail.abstract: Does matching loan repayments to expected cash flows raise take-up and the welfare impact of microcredit? We test this in a randomized controlled trial with Morocco's largest microfinance institution. The experiment introduces two individual-liability products: a loan with a five-month grace period and a tailored contract with instalments matched to expected revenues. Over 3,000 applicants are randomly offered one of the new contracts or the standard loan. The products attract distinct borrowers: agricultural households take the grace-period loan, while entrepreneurs operating smaller, more capital-constrained businesses choose the tailored schedule. The tailored loan raises sales and profits through non-agricultural business expansion and labour reallocation to self-employment; the grace-period loan shows similar but insignificant effects. Neither worsens repayment, and we find no effects on investment or consumption. A second-stage information campaign across 440 villages shifts stated preferences but not take-up, consistent with supply-side frictions.

detail.abstract: This conceptual paper develops a conditional, multi-theoretical framework examining how human capital development influences economic resilience in African developing economies integrating under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). Drawing on empirical findings from the author's doctoral study in Tanzania (n=353, six sectors) and comparative evidence from Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, Ethiopia, and Rwanda, the paper challenges the prevailing assumption that human capital accumulation automatically. The framework integrates multiple complementary theoretical perspectives to propose that human capital impacts resilience indirectly through labor market efficiency, with institutional quality acting as a moderating boundary condition. The paper introduces three novel theoretical contributions: the capability-deployment gap (the systematic failure of labor market institutions to convert educational capabilities into economic functionings) and the Labor Market Capability–Resilience Model (LMCRM), which repositions labor market alignment as the primary resilience determinant. Six theoretically derived propositions are advanced for empirical testing. The framework offers actionable recommendations for the African Union's Continental Education Strategy for Africa 2026–2035 and AfCFTA National Implementation Committees.

detail.abstract: Hierarchical portfolio allocation methods produce diversified portfolios while avoiding the instability of mean-variance optimisation. The framework depends on two separable choices: how assets are grouped and how capital is allocated across those groups. This thesis asks which of these choices matters more for out-of-sample portfolio performance. The empirical design crosses four linkage methods with four allocation kernels, evaluated on a multi-asset ETF universe from 2008 to 2026 across 3,200 resampled walk-forward paths. The results show that allocation kernels account for most differences in risk-adjusted performance, while the linkage method mainly affects turnover. Risk-aware kernels improve risk-adjusted performance and reduce downside risk relative to 1/N. Practitioners should treat the allocation rule as the primary modelling choice in hierarchical portfolio construction, with linkage choice used mainly to manage implementation stability.

detail.abstract:
We define mutual-fund stock-selection skill not as a human trait but as a measurable residual: the idiosyncratic component of performance that remains after the replicable exposures modeled in this decomposition — market, sector, subsector, and Fama–French size/value — are orthogonalized away, and that exhibits cross-sectional stability under out-of-sample testing. Using a point-in-time, holdings-based architecture, we reconstruct each fund's return from the securities it actually held and strip those exposures sequentially — a position-level identification that asks whether the stock-specific return a fund *generated* persists, not whether a historical return intercept does.

The isolated stock-selection residual exhibits statistically significant out-of-sample persistence: the forward top-minus-bottom-quintile spread is about **+2.3 percentage points**, with annual non-overlapping reliability of ***t* ≈ 3.4**. When the identical point-in-time machinery is applied to style- and sector-timing components as negative-control signals, their forward predictive content does not survive; stock selection does. The differential survival supports the interpretation that the result is specific to the stock-selection residual, not a generic consequence of the validation machinery. The practical consequence is for manager diligence: conventional tools — style classification, sector allocation, benchmark-relative attribution, and recent performance — describe what a fund owned but are weak evidence of *repeatable* skill, because the standard toolkit blends stock selection with style and sector exposure rather than isolating it. A longitudinal variance decomposition localizes the persistence entirely within the *between-fund* variance — a persistent between-fund level difference, not a transient timing signal. We read the result narrowly: a robust ranking signal within a chosen mandate, not unconditional evidence that active management outperforms net of fees.

detail.abstract: The Greek housing-affordability debate rests on an unposed measurement question: which rent? The harmonised index of contracted rents, which prices the tenancies households already hold, rose 13 percent between 2015 and 2025, while the Spitogatos index of asking rents, which prices the lettings a mover must sign, rose 82 percent. This paper documents that wedge and traces its consequences using the HICP, the Spitogatos Price Index, EU-SILC incomes, and Bank of Greece apartment prices over 2011-2026. Three results emerge. First, contracted and asking rents tell opposite affordability stories, and the gap is an insider-outsider wedge between sitting and mobile tenants that official indices miss. Second, the pressure is spatially concentrated: an asking rent for a 75-square-metre dwelling absorbs between 49 and 102 percent of household disposable income in southern Athens, depending on household type, against about a third of that in rural northern Greece. Third, a Shapley accounting shows that whether the rent-to-income ratio rose or fell depends jointly on the rent measure, the income concept, and the base year. The crisis is concentrated at the margin of mobility, so rental affordability cannot be monitored, nor support indexed, with a contracted-rent index alone.

detail.title: Can doctrine harness silicon law clerks?

detail.abstract: Large language models have arrived in the court room: not as decision-makers, but as decision-aids. Realistically, the human judge in the loop can only do so much. What can be done to prevent the AI clerk from surreptitiously introducing ideological bias, and from being manipulated by the parties? We investigate experimentally whether an institutional constraint that has a guiding effect on human judges also helps to discipline silicon law clerks. Specifically we study how strongly the obligation to reason in terms of established legal doctrine constrains AI outputs, on two channels: by directing attention to relevant precedents, and by imposing structure on the reasoning process. Six treatments are designed to isolate and reinforce these two channels through which legal doctrine operates. We emulate similarity-based reasoning with a Vector RAG and structural reasoning with a Graph RAG, and combine both interventions. We test seven LLMs, comparing both outcomes and a rich set of metrics for the quality of legal reasoning, using decisions by the European Court of Human Rights as ground truth. Even without RAG, frontier models produce impressive outputs. But RAG interventions align outcomes and explicit reasons significantly and substantially more with the human benchmarks.

detail.abstract: Using the Distributional Financial Accounts of the United States, we study the effects of monetary policy on the wealth distribution. The direction and persistence of these effects depend on the policy instrument. Interest rate cuts initially reduce wealth inequality but increase it in the medium-run. Asset purchases, instead, increase wealth inequality but only temporarily. Using household-level data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, we document a wealth reversal at the bottom of the distribution: lower interest rates raise housing wealth in the short run but lead to higher mortgage debt and lower net wealth over time, contributing to the medium-term rise in inequality.

detail.abstract: This paper develops an agent-based framework (DeTail) to assess the state-contingent tail effects of releasable macroprudential capital buffers. The model features heterogeneous firms, households, and banks, and a single central bank, all interacting in a fully integrated, stock-flow consistent framework which generates endogenous credit cycles. Using this approach, we evaluate how time-varying capital requirements affect the time-varying distributions of credit growth, firm and household default rates, and bank losses along the credit cycle. Policy experiments show that releasing capital buffers during economic downturns preserves credit supply by improving risky (lower-tail) credit outcomes, reduces both household and firm defaults, and supports macro-financial resilience by limiting tail bank losses. At the same time, capital buffer accumulation during upturns imposes minimal costs and does not significantly constrain lending. These findings support the active use of releasable buffers to mitigate systemic risk and smooth credit cycles without weakening the banking system.

detail.abstract: Those who conduct a superficial study of the West often fall into the delusion that Western civilization has become a completely secular society where religion no longer plays any role. This is a severe intellectual blind spot. To comprehend the true reality of the West, one must contrast its outward public behavior with its inward power structures. While the West transformed its historical and religious roots into an axis of power, the Muslim world embraced fabricated tales and traditions in the name of history, rendering itself intellectually paralyzed. This paper analyzes how the Jewish and Christian worlds leveraged religious framework adjustments to capture financial and cultural hegemony, contrasting this with the structural stagnation found in contemporary Muslim historiography. The Dual Face of the West: Hollow Secularism vs. Institutional Roots It is true that the general public in the Western world, particularly in Europe, has grown entirely weary of the church, biblical tales, and traditional religious morality. The younger generation there is captive to capitalism, material comforts, cutting-edge technology, and absolute personal freedom. Churches stand empty, converted into museums, libraries, and pubs. However, this is merely one facet of the West. Conversely, the political, legal, economic, and cultural architecture of the West is still born of and sustained by the Judeo-Christian Heritage.

detail.abstract: Although Japan's healthcare system for older adults employs income-based redistribution, the lifecycle-permanent income hypothesis implies that wealth may be an important indicator of older adults' economic capacity. Using recently accumulated panel data for those aged 65-77 years, this study examines the effects of household income and wealth on the use of medical care, while controlling for observable health status and individual fixed effects to avoid spurious correlations. My empirical analysis finds significantly positive effects of pension income and financial wealth on the utilization of medical care, and their elasticities to out-of-pocket medical expenditure are 0.016 and 0.008, respectively. title: Hayek Displaced: Can AI Solve the Socialist Calculation Problem?

detail.title: Hayek Displaced: Can AI Solve the Socialist Calculation Problem?
detail.abstract: The algorithmic capacity of contemporary artificial intelligence revives the socialist calculation controversy that Mises and Hayek were long thought to have closed. If algorithms can synthesize the dispersed information that Hayek identified as the irreducible obstacle to central economic planning, has the Hayekian argument been technically falsified? This article argues that the answer requires a structural reframing rather than a direct refutation: the Hayekian limit is not abolished by AI but displaced, deepened, and ultimately threatened. Four structural layers are identified: an epistemological layer, partially superseded by computational advance; an axiological layer (specification of the objective function), against which the Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback counter-argument fails on three structural grounds: the is/ought gap, axiological Goodhart, and irreducible plurality; a tacit layer, restated in dynamic rather than ontological form, where legibility degrades the substrate it purports to capture; and a reflexive layer, where Goodhart-type distortion couples with substrate atrophy to produce what is here termed a society of facades. Beyond these, a fifth and more radical horizon is identified: the dissolution of the Hayekian premise itself under large-scale algorithmic preference fabrication, where the framework loses its referent and "coordination" ceases to be a concept distinct from "manufacture." The Hayekian premise is thus shown to be conditional rather than universal, dependent on a degree of preference autonomy that the algorithmic age does not automatically preserve. The constitutional response is organized around a master commitment to polycentric institutional architecture, defended against the realist objection under the structural principle that monocentric systems maximize performance under parametric stability while polycentric systems maximize survival under structural change, with cognitive opacity and reflexive auditability as its corollaries. This constitutionalism is epistemic in character: it protects not a substantive outcome (the market) but the conditions under which decentralized coordination remains conceptually distinct from centralized fabrication-the ecology of judgments through which complex social orders coordinate.

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: A Bibliometric and Science-Mapping Analysis from an Institutional and Management Perspective
detail.abstract: This article maps the field of artificial intelligence in higher education (HEI-AI) from an institutional and management perspective. We draw on 52,270 peer-reviewed articles and reviews indexed in Web of Science and Scopus between 1959 and 2025. Using the bibliometrix package and its biblioshiny interface in R, we combine descriptive indicators with science-mapping techniques, including co-authorship and co-citation networks, keyword co-occurrence, thematic mapping and thematic evolution. The initial corpus of 94,845 records was cleaned by merging the two databases, removing duplicates and restricting the sample to full-length journal articles and reviews that explicitly address AI in higher education. The results show a long period of slow growth followed by an exponential expansion after 2023, closely aligned with the diffusion of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT. At the country level, China dominates in publication volume, while the United States leads in citation impact. Countries such as France contribute fewer but highly cited papers and function as additional intellectual hubs. Conceptual and thematic analyses indicate a gradual shift towards more technical and data-driven work, centred on artificial intelligence, teaching and learning in tertiary education, and learning analytics, prediction, classification and performance metrics. Interpreted through neo-institutional theory, these patterns point to legitimacy-oriented AI adoption, coercive and mimetic isomorphism, and the growing influence of bibliometric indicators on organisational fields. The paper argues that HEI-AI should be understood as a strategic management and governance issue rather than only a pedagogical innovation, and it outlines implications for institutional AI strategies, policy design and future research on organisational adaptation in higher education. AI is not just technology; it is a process that redefines the institutional structure.

title: Quantum Computing and the Accuracy of Stock and Cryptocurrency Price Prediction: A Critical Assessment

detail.title: Quantum Computing and the Accuracy of Stock and Cryptocurrency Price Prediction: A Critical Assessment
detail.abstract: In this paper, I consider how quantum computing affects the accuracy of predicting stock and cryptocurrency prices compared with classical statistical methods and machine learning algorithms. The limitations of traditional financial models based on historical data and interrelationships between variables were demonstrated during the failures of financial forecasts, particularly in 2008. Machine learning techniques like neural network models and long short-term memory algorithms have partly solved the problem of the limitation due to the increase in the amount of processed data. However, these techniques are still limited by classical computation and financial markets, which are influenced by geopolitical, psychological, and sentiment factors. Quantum computing provides a different way of working due to its ability to operate with superpositions and entanglement, enabling simultaneous evaluation of many variables and outcomes rather than sequential evaluation. Based on recent experiments in the industry (for instance, the HSBC and IBM quantum-enabled trading pilot of September 2025) and benchmark studies for hybrid quantum neural networks, according to the paper, quantum computing is able to increase prediction accuracy in specific applications by about 3.4 percent to 4.9. Current hardware constraints, cost and sensitivity to environmental noise, together with the irreducibly irrational component of market behaviour, mean these gains remain experimental rather than deployable at scale. In conclusion, the study shows that quantum computing should be seen more as an addition to, and not a substitute for, AI and statistics, and that the real applicability of quantum computing in price prediction would come after further developments in hardware and data.

detail.abstract:
A portfolio can look diversified yet be concentrated in exposures that move together because they answer to the same underlying driver. The world's largest sovereign fund has measured it, and found its own tools understating the exposure to one of these drivers by close to an order of magnitude. Diversification reduces portfolio risk only to the extent that the residual exposures left after factor and market risk are removed are genuinely uncorrelated. This paper shows, drawing on published climate-analytics disclosures, that for climate-exposed institutional capital that condition does not hold, and that the deployed tools of modern portfolio construction systematically book as diversifiable a residual that is in fact correlated and systematic. 

The failure is empirical rather than theoretical: portfolio theory has modelled the full covariance matrix since Markowitz (1952), but the covariance estimates that drive real allocation are backward-looking, while climate-exposed correlation is structural, forward-looking, and rising. The paper names this under-measured exposure Risk 0. Norges Bank Investment Management's own climate analysis, quoted in the epigraph, arrives at a roughly 19 per cent potential loss on its US equity holdings under a current-policies trajectory, against the roughly 2 per cent a standard Climate Value at Risk model returns, a gap NBIM attributes to the systemic macroeconomic effects such tools omit. In February 2026 MSCI, the provider of that very model, published a macroeconomic physical-risk model finding that systemic spillovers can raise losses by up to nine times the direct-damage estimate. A US$1 billion portfolio model, illustrative and heuristic, puts a number on the cumulative cost of unmeasured correlated drag at the level of a single fund; a four-channel, order-of-magnitude estimate, stated as a floor rather than a measurement, places the value at stake across the institutional system above one trillion US dollars within a decade. 

The paper engages the modern portfolio theory and climate-finance literatures on their own terms, and reads the failure in two registers: the statistical, and by analogy the commercial and human cases for the transition, long framed as competing when they are coupled. The implication for institutional capital allocation is material: the deployed tools systematically understate total exposure, and the gap is not a rounding error.

title: Simplifying the Tax Code is a Pro-growth Policy
affiliations: George Mason University - Mercatus Center

detail.title: Simplifying the Tax Code is a Pro-growth Policy
detail.abstract: This paper argues that tax simplification should be understood not merely as an administrative reform, but as a pro-growth policy with significant macroeconomic implications. A compelling alternative to the current income-based system is the consumption-based tax framework proposed by American economists Robert E. Hall and Alvin Rabushka in 1978. Their proposal replaces a narrow, distortion-laden tax base with a simpler structure that treats saving and investment neutrally—unlike the current income tax system, which often taxes income when it is earned and again when the returns to saving and investment are realized, while also requiring delayed cost recovery through depreciation rules that raise the effective tax burden on capital.

title: Global Pension Asset Allocations and Debt Markets
affiliations: , The University of Hong Kong, Bank for International Settlements (BIS) - Monetary and Economic Department and University of Pennsylvania - Finance Department

detail.title: Global Pension Asset Allocations and Debt Markets
detail.abstract:
The pension sector is an important investor group in global financial markets and a key holder of government and corporate debt. This article examines the evolution of pension fund asset allocations around the globe and documents two important structural changes. First, pension investors have shifted portfolio share allocations away from fixed income securities. This trend is robust across Defined Contribution (DC) and Defined Benefit (DB) programs as well as country groups. Second, pensions have instead shifted allocations into riskier investments within mutual funds as well as alternative investments. We hypothesize that a global decline in interest rates is one potential driver of this change. Using a global sample, we show that declining local currency government bond yields are associated with lower bond pension portfolio shares and higher holdings shares of mutual funds and foreign assets. We discuss the potential implications of these trends for borrowing costs. The declining holding share of pensions as a long-term investor group implies financing costs are less sensitive to new debt issues, but more sensitive to global uncertainty.

title: Who is Afraid of Eurobonds?
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University, Johns Hopkins University, University of Warwick and Sveriges Riksbank - Research Division

detail.title: Who is Afraid of Eurobonds?
detail.abstract:
The current euro area policy framework conflates short-run stabilization with long-run fiscal sustainability, exposing members to deflationary and inflationary tail risks. We employ an estimated euro area model to analyze an alternative framework that separates these objectives. A centralized Treasury issues Eurobonds to finance countercyclical stabilization, while national governments retain responsibility for long-term fiscal sustainability. The Treasury can coordinate with the monetary authority in case of a large recession, with no need to suspend fiscal rules at the national level. The arrangement functions as an automatic stabilizer, eliminating the tail risks of deflation and fiscal stagflation.

title: Energy-efficiency Investments and Consumption-Portfolio Choice
affiliations: , Tilburg University - Department of Econometrics & Operations Research and Maastricht University - School of Business and Economics

detail.title: Energy-efficiency Investments and Consumption-Portfolio Choice
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the optimal portfolio, consumption, and energy-efficiency investment decisions of a Dutch household facing energy price risk during retirement using a continuous-time life-cycle model. The household can reduce its exposure to energy price risk through energy-efficiency home renovations, modeled as an impulse-control problem in which the household chooses whether and when to upgrade its home's energy label. Energy prices follow a regime-switching jump-diffusion process calibrated to Dutch residential gas prices around the 2022 energy crisis. While a simple net present value calculation suggests label upgrades are beneficial for most households, our model shows that many households optimally delay or forgo renovation despite the positive NPV. We identify biometric risk and liquidity constraints as the main drivers of this reluctance. Our results show how energy price, house price, and biometric risk jointly shape household portfolio composition and energy-efficiency renovation timing, with implications for policy aimed at promoting residential energy efficiency.

title: The Environmental Costs of Sanctions: Flaring and Venting in Venezuela
affiliations: Bocconi University - Department of Economics, Bocconi University and University of Bristol, School of Economics

detail.title: The Environmental Costs of Sanctions: Flaring and Venting in Venezuela
detail.abstract:
Economic sanctions on oil-producing autocracies change not only the quantity of oil but also how it is produced. Combining field-level production data with satellite measurements of gas flaring and atmospheric methane across six Latin American countries from 2012 to 2024, we study the U.S. sanctions on Venezuela. Per-barrel gas flaring in Venezuela rose about two-and-a-half-fold even as production fell by two-thirds, a pattern no unsanctioned neighbor shows, so environmental damage under sanctions is about two and a half times what a proportional decline in output would predict. Three channels generate this gap: the exit of small, dirty fields (composition) is more than offset by surviving fields running their infrastructure past design capacity (strain) and cutting their operating budgets (maintenance). We identify strain from the response of satellite-measured methane to the world price of naphtha, the imported diluent Venezuela's extra-heavy crude requires, and maintenance from a November 2022 U.S. Treasury license that allowed only Chevron to resume operations at its Venezuelan fields. A similar pattern of rising per-barrel emissions despite falling output appears under the sanctions on Iran (after 2018).

title: Industry Distress Anomaly
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School, The University of Hong Kong - University of Hong Kong and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Finance

detail.title: Industry Distress Anomaly
detail.abstract:
We document a robust industry-level distress anomaly in which more distressed industries earn significantly lower expected equity returns. The anomaly is distinct from the firm-level distress anomaly (Campbell, Hilscher and Szilagyi, 2008). It remains significant after controlling for firm-level distress but disappears in placebo industries formed by randomly reshuffling firms across actual industries. Both theoretically and empirically, we show that competition-distress feedback amplifies the exposure of industry profit margins and equity returns to discount-rate shocks. Industries with greater idiosyncratic left-tail risk are more distressed but exhibit weaker competition-distress feedback. This effect reduces their exposure to discount-rate shocks and thus lowers their expected equity returns.

title: Self-Fulfilling Credit Scores
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: Self-Fulfilling Credit Scores
detail.abstract:
A decline in credit scores can worsen the borrower's financial position, making default a self-fulfilling prophecy. We estimate the causal effect of credit scores on default using a rule that counts multiple inquiries within 14 days as one, moving scores without changing credit reports. Regression discontinuity estimates around the 14-day cut-off show that an additional counted inquiry lowers scores by five points on average. Default does not respond among consumers with clean records, but rises by 3.2 percentage points over two years among those with prior derogatories. For these consumers, at least 13 percent of the relationship between scores and default is self-fulfilling. We show that scorers would want to limit self-fulfilling defaults if their objective is forecast accuracy, but not if it is separating defaulters from non-defaulters, because that objective rewards the score for the defaults it causes.

title: Information and Macroeconomic Expectations: Global Evidence
affiliations: Georgetown University and National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)

detail.title: Information and Macroeconomic Expectations: Global Evidence
detail.abstract:
Unique global data on 47,000 consumers across 47 countries representing 90% of world GDP reveal universal patterns in macroeconomic belief formation. Most consumers form beliefs based on local information sources (utility bills, shopping, and acquaintances) that provide signals not representative for the overall consumption bundle, so that seeking information leads to forming biased macroeconomic expectations. Distrust in governments and central banks, the producers of aggregate economic information, helps explain reliance on local sources and the lack of learning from aggregate realizations. Observed macroeconomic volatility fuels distrust. In the cross-section, we confirm that certain demographics correlate with expectation biases but mostly due to different sorting into information sources, rather than different processing of the same economic information. These globally established facts inform advances of theories of belief formation and the design of communication strategies as a macroeconomic policy tool.

title: Trading Off Openness: Economic Information and Immigration Policy Preferences
affiliations: CMCC - Centro Euro-Mediterraneo sui Cambiamenti Climatici, Università degli Studi di Milano, University of Bologna and

detail.title: Trading Off Openness: Economic Information and Immigration Policy Preferences
detail.abstract:
We conducted a survey experiment with over 8,000 participants in Germany, Hungary, and Italy to examine how information about the economic impact of immigration affects the support for more open immigration policies. Respondents who received projections showing higher future incomes under more open immigration policies reported greater support for these policies. The treatment also partly changed how prior attitudes affected policy preferences. Structural estimates suggest that majority support for immigration above current levels would require annual per-capita income gains of about 1.2% in Italy and 1.7% in Germany, and still larger or unattainable gains in Hungary. These increases are large relative to recent historical growth rates, suggesting that economic benefits alone are unlikely to generate vast support for more open immigration policies.

title: Investing in Mothers? The Long-Run Impact of a Universal Child Care Program on Maternal Work and Income
affiliations: University of Toronto, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics and University of British Columbia (UBC) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Investing in Mothers? The Long-Run Impact of a Universal Child Care Program on Maternal Work and Income
detail.abstract:
We provide new estimates of the effects of universal child care on the long-term labor outcomes of mothers, documenting the life-cycle impact of Quebec’s universal, subsidized child care program on maternal labor supply, earnings, social program benefit receipt and tax remittances. We find an enduring positive impact on mothers’ employment long after children have aged out of the preschool years. There is also a long-run impact on earnings which grows to be twice as large as the participation effect. This arises because of growth in the intensity of labor force participation and a rise in hourly wages over time, suggesting that initial investments in work have multiplier effects later in women’s careers. There is clear evidence of occupational upgrading but most of the growth is within occupation, including the impact of more labor market experience in the years after children are out of child care. We show that, as a result, tax remittances grow over the lifecycle, and social assistance and employment insurance receipts fall. Our estimate of the fiscal balance of these effects reveals that the net present value of the flow of fiscal benefits may recapture between 75 and 117 percent of the upfront costs of the program.

title: Beyond Price: Rights Trading in Strategic Factor Markets
affiliations: Syracuse University - Whitman School of Management and Tulane University

detail.title: Beyond Price: Rights Trading in Strategic Factor Markets
detail.abstract:
Research on strategic factor markets has largely treated the terms of exchange as price. We argue that many strategic transactions instead divide value through contractual bundles in which payment terms and control rights are interdependent. In university technology licensing, we theorize Rights Trading: contingent payment, future improvement claims, and commercialization scope operate as linked components of the contractual bundle through which surplus is allocated. Using 858 hand coded university–industry licenses, we find that contracts relying more heavily on royalty and milestone provisions grant licensees stronger future improvement claims and broader commercialization scope. The results persist across controls and fixed effects and are directionally consistent with complementary instrumental-variable, event-study, and selection-bound analyses. We further show that this relationship is stronger when university technology transfer offices have greater contracting experience, suggesting that contracting capability shapes value appropriation in strategic factor markets. More broadly, the study shows that value appropriation in strategic factor markets depends not only on what organizations pay for strategic resources, but also on how contracts allocate control over their future development and commercialization.

title: Equity as Tribute: The Market for Passive State Equity
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Equity as Tribute: The Market for Passive State Equity
detail.abstract:
Firms have begun granting passive equity stakes to the government that regulates them. The received reading is “skin in the game:” ownership moves profits onto the treasury's balance sheet, so policy softens. We show that once the price of the stake and the firm's policy exposure are determined in equilibrium, the owners' consent reveals nothing about whether they benefit. Sellers capitalise the induced policy improvement into the price, so an anticipated purchase can only occur at a discount; a government with bargaining power pays zero for a sufficiently exposed firm; and a government that can first raise exposure manufactures precisely enough of it to drive the negotiated price to its legal floor. Equity becomes tribute. Prohibition is nonetheless dominated: at fixed exposure, a passive stake corrects the political underweighting of shareholders. Welfare is maximised by priced permission—an ownership cap at the fixed-exposure optimum and a per-unit price floor equal to baseline no-stake value. The floor, unlike the cap, requires no knowledge of the government's political weights.

title: The Effects of U.S. Public R&D on Global Growth
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, Texas A&M University - Mays Business School, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, Harvard University and Stanford University

detail.title: The Effects of U.S. Public R&D on Global Growth
detail.abstract:
This paper provides the first causal estimates of the global social returns to U.S. public R&D. We use a narrative identification strategy to quantify the effects of exogenous shocks to U.S. R&D appropriations on the dynamic TFP response of 69 foreign economies from 1980–2019. A U.S. R&D appropriations shock equal to 1 percent of the federal R&D capital stock raises foreign TFP by approximately 1 percent after 12 years. This response is driven primarily by nondefense rather than defense R&D and is concentrated in non-OECD economies. These patterns are most consistent with diffusion occurring through openly accessible scientific content, capital-embodied trade, and technological leapfrogging by economies further from the global frontier. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that the global social returns to U.S. public nondefense R&D are roughly twice as large as the domestic returns, meaning the U.S. captures about half of these productivity benefits.

detail.title: Retail Betting Markets
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the rapid expansion and convergence of retail betting markets. We analyze market design elements, discuss economic utility, and highlight shared behavioral drivers of sports betting markets, prediction markets, and retail options trading. Our review underscores how technological innovation, behavioral biases, and regulatory arbitrage have shaped recent market evolution. We highlight important considerations for policy-makers facing a changing landscape and outline possibilities for further research.

title: The Price and Distributional Impact of Flood Risk Disclosure: Evidence from US Housing Platforms
affiliations: University of Colorado - Boulder, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School and Northeastern University

detail.title: The Price and Distributional Impact of Flood Risk Disclosure: Evidence from US Housing Platforms
detail.abstract:
How does information disclosure reshape the allocation of environmental risk in the housing market? We quantify the price and distributional impact of the nationwide disclosure of property-level flood risk from First Street on U.S. housing platforms. Using a difference-in-RD design that exploits discrete cutoffs in the disclosed risk categories, we find that homes labeled as "extreme'' flood risk experience a 3.3% price discount and stay on the market for a week longer, relative to those labeled as "severe'' risk. These effects are strongest for coastal properties and remain pervasive across different FEMA floodplain designations. Disclosure also generates significant household resorting: buyers of extreme-risk homes have 5.3% lower income, are more likely to use FHA financing, and are older. Through a discrete choice model, we find that the redistribution of risk to lower-income households is primarily driven by price changes rather than heterogeneous preferences for flood risk.

title: Counterproductive Sustainable Investing: The Impact Elasticity of Brown and Green Firms
affiliations: Boston College - Carroll School of Management and Yale School of Management

detail.title: Counterproductive Sustainable Investing: The Impact Elasticity of Brown and Green Firms
detail.abstract:
We develop a new measure of impact elasticity: the change in a firm's environmental impact due to a change in its cost of capital. We find that reducing green firms' financing costs leads to minimal impact changes, while increasing brown firms' financing costs causes significant negative impact changes. Thus, sustainable investing strategies that shift capital from brown to green firms contain a counterproductive channel that makes brown firms more brown without making green firms more green. A mistaken focus on percentage reductions in emissions rewards already-green firms for trivial reductions in emissions and gives brown firms weak incentives to improve.

title: Immigration and Macroeconomic Outcomes in OECD Countries
affiliations: Bank of Italy, University of California, Davis and University of California, Davis - Department of Economics

detail.title: Immigration and Macroeconomic Outcomes in OECD Countries
detail.abstract:
OECD countries experienced declining native population growth and rising net immigration over 1990-2024. We compile a new dataset of net immigration rates to OECD countries from all origins and show that most of the increase came from non-OECD countries and was predominantly high-skilled. Push factors, network effects, and policy indices explain little of the large cross-country heterogeneity in immigration dynamics; unexpected shocks and surges were common. Using local projections and several sources of identifying variation, we then estimate the relationship between immigration and growth in GDP per capita, labor productivity, capital investment, and total factor productivity (TFP). Immigration from non-OECD countries was a significant predictor of GDP per worker growth, primarily through higher investment. High-skilled immigration, in particular, was associated with stronger human capital accumulation, faster TFP growth, and greater capital deepening. Native population growth, by contrast, had no or weakly negative effects on GDP per capita and productivity. These results are consistent with a large literature documenting the positive productivity and growth effects of immigration, especially high-skilled immigration.

title: The Welfare Effects of Conditioning the Potential Duration of UI Benefits on Prior Work History
affiliations: University of Calgary and University of Southern California

detail.title: The Welfare Effects of Conditioning the Potential Duration of UI Benefits on Prior Work History
detail.abstract:
Most unemployment insurance (UI) systems condition the potential duration of benefits on claimants' work history, yet little evidence exists on whether doing so is socially optimal. We study this question using 25 regression discontinuities in Canada's UI system, where benefit duration increases discretely when prior hours worked crosses various thresholds. Using administrative records covering the universe of UI claims from 1997 to 2018, we estimate the fiscal effects of extending potential duration across the work-history distribution. On average, an additional week lengthens unemployment by 0.30 weeks and costs the government $96. However, this average effect masks significant heterogeneity: the mechanical cost falls steeply with prior hours, while the behavioral cost increases modestly. Consequently, the fiscal externality of extending UI rises with labor market attachment. Embedding these estimates in a sufficient statistics framework, we find that the fiscal externality of a uniform extension is 76% larger than that of an extension targeted at claimants with short histories. Moreover, aggregate welfare can be raised at zero fiscal cost by redistributing benefits from high to low hour claimants.

title: Evidence of How Electronic Reporting and Automated Auditing Affects Regulatory Compliance and Environmental Performance
affiliations: Clark University - Department of Economics, San Diego State University and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency - National Center for Environmental Economics

detail.title: Evidence of How Electronic Reporting and Automated Auditing Affects Regulatory Compliance and Environmental Performance
detail.abstract:
We investigate whether, by providing better and more timely information, the first mandatory online reporting and auditing program for wastewater discharge releases in the U.S. improved facility compliance and environmental performance, while also allowing state regulators to more effectively monitor and enforce regulations. Examining reporting programs with automated feedback features can also offer insights into the potential for artificial intelligence-based tools to improve compliance and environmental performance. Difference-in-difference results suggest that the program resulted in significant increases in the completeness of reporting and reductions in discharges but also greater reported violations. We find that effects are larger for minor dischargers and publicly owned facilities. We also find evidence consistent with the more efficient targeting of inspections by state authorities towards plants with a history of recent noncompliance, which could be a potential mechanism driving these results.

title: Profits and Social Impacts: Complements vs. Tradeoffs for Lenders in Three Countries
affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business, Stanford University, Northwestern University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and Dartmouth College

detail.title: Profits and Social Impacts: Complements vs. Tradeoffs for Lenders in Three Countries
detail.abstract:
The canonical approach to corporate governance posits a tradeoff between maximizing shareholder profits and maximizing other aspects of shareholder welfare such as social impact. Advances in machine learning that enhance the firm's ability to target specific customers may exacerbate or ameliorate this tradeoff. We estimate these tradeoffs using data from randomized microcredit approvals in South Africa, the Philippines, and Bosnia. We examine social impact on two dimensions: credit access (i.e., reaching disadvantaged groups that typically have less access to financial markets) and impact (i.e., treatment effects on household income). Two of the three lenders could have increased average loan profit margin by 7–9 percentage points through machine learning-based targeting. However, such targeting pushes against social impact goals vis-à-vis credit access; specifically, women and lower-income households would have been more excluded (the implied impact on borrowers' income, also central to the dual goal of social impact, is too imprecisely estimated to draw an inference). To gauge the magnitude of the first tradeoff, we examine how profits would change if the lenders altered whom they lent to within each quintile of baseline borrower income, thus holding the distribution broadly similar but fine-tuning the targeting within income bands. Such a constraint would lower the profit gains of targeting by about half. These findings highlight the importance of quantifying tradeoffs and complementarities when deciding what to maximize.

title: Spillover Effects in Complementary Markets: A Study of the Indian Cell Phone and Wireless Service Markets
affiliations: University of Sussex Business School, University of Sussex Business School, University of Michigan and University of Massachusetts, Amherst

detail.title: Spillover Effects in Complementary Markets: A Study of the Indian Cell Phone and Wireless Service Markets
detail.abstract:
This paper studies how spillovers across complementary markets shape product variety and firm entry. We examine the Indian cell phone and wireless service markets during the 4G rollout and estimate a structural model of demand, pricing, carrier network expansion, and phone product choice. The estimation results support the economic forces through which complementarity generates spillovers. Counterfactual simulations show that banning budget Chinese phones slows 4G deployment by roughly five quarters and lowers consumer welfare without raising domestic firms' profits. Similarly, an unrestricted subsidy outperforms a domestic-only subsidy in expanding network coverage, increasing consumer welfare, and raising domestic firms' profits.
