title: The Opportunity Cost of Corruption in Public Resource Allocation: Evidence from India's Education Sector, 2016-2022
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Opportunity Cost of Corruption in Public Resource Allocation: Evidence from India's Education Sector, 2016-2022
detail.abstract: India allocates close to 3 percent of GDP annually to education, yet foundational learning deficits remain widespread: the 2022 ASER survey found 42.8 percent of rural Class 5 students could not read a Class 2-level text. This paper asks whether state-level prosecutorial impunity under the Prevention of Corruption Act explains part of that gap, using a panel of 15 major Indian states over 2016-2022. Impunity is defined as one minus the ratio of PCA convictions to registered cases, from NCRB Crime in India reports. Two-way fixed effects regressions, controlling for per capita income and pupil-teacher ratio, associate a one-unit increase in impunity with 6.3 additional points of reading deficiency (p = 0.107), with directionally consistent results for enrolment. An opportunity cost exercise using verified UDISE+ enrollment figures implies over 1 million students across three high-impunity states could reach grade-level literacy at Kerala's accountability level. Identification is not causal; weak significance reflects the conservative design with a small panel and a single corruption proxy.

title: Graph-Based Hybrid Neural Network Approaches for Early Rumor and Misinformation Detection in Social Media: A Systematic Literature Review
affiliations: Modibbo Adama University of Technology, Modibbo Adama University of Technology and Modibbo Adama University of Technology Yola

detail.title: Graph-Based Hybrid Neural Network Approaches for Early Rumor and Misinformation Detection in Social Media: A Systematic Literature Review
detail.abstract: One of the most urgent issues facing modern information ecosystems is the spread of rumors and false information through the social media platforms. A popular paradigm for simulating the intricate relational and temporal dynamics of social media propagation graphs is Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), especially hybrid designs that include Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and Graph Attention Networks (GATs). However, there has not been a thorough synthesis of this study strand's trajectory and constraints in the most recent literature. In compliance with the PRISMA 2020, this systematic literature review (SLR) finds, evaluates, and summarizes 104 peer-reviewed and pre-publication studies from 2024 to 2026 that deal with GNN-based rumor and misinformation detection in social media contexts. Freestanding GCN designs, freestanding GAT architectures, hybrid GCN-GAT models, multimodal graph methods, temporal and dynamic graph networks, and survey contributions are the six main methodological categories identified by thematic analysis. According to quantitative bibliometric research, publication production increased significantly in 2025 (n = 49), with temporal and hybrid techniques together making up 33% of the corpus. Ten important research needs are found, covering early detection thresholds, cross-platform generalizability, adversarial robustness, explainability, and ethical deployment, despite significant performance improvements on benchmark datasets such as Twitter15, Twitter16, Weibo, and PHEME. These results offer a solid body of evidence to direct the development of next-generation hybrid GCN-GAT systems for reliable, scalable, and temporally aware misinformation detection.

title: Litigation Risk in Energy Technologies: Evidence from U.S. Patents
affiliations: University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee - Department of Economics, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee and University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee

detail.title: Litigation Risk in Energy Technologies: Evidence from U.S. Patents
detail.abstract: We study patent disputes in the energy sector using litigation data in the U.S. from 2001 to 2016. The estimations of a dynamic fixed-effect Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood innovation model show the characteristics of applicants and patents with an elevated risk of litigation. Specifically, patents frequently cited, those invented by small firms, and patents with a faster review process face a higher risk of litigation. These results provide an overview of patent disputes in the energy sector.

title: From Field to Firm: College Sports and Early-Stage Career Choice
affiliations: Harvard Business School - Finance Unit, Harvard University - Department of Economics, Duke University and

detail.title: From Field to Firm: College Sports and Early-Stage Career Choice
detail.abstract:
This paper examines how networks formed through college athletics influence the early-career trajectories of Ivy League graduates. Tracking professional histories of 120,306 Ivy League graduates, we compare each graduate's actual first job against other potential jobs that the graduate could reasonably have taken. Athletics-based networks, especially team-based connections, materially influence initial job choice. Employing one additional alum from a specific Ivy League collegiate sports team increases the probability that a same-team athlete joins the firm by 193.70% relative to the baseline match probability. Likewise, employing one more Ivy League alum who played a specific Varsity sport increases the probability that any Ivy League athlete who plays the same sport joins the firm by 16.40%, while employing one more alum who played any sport at a specific Ivy League university raises the probability that any Ivy League athlete from the same university joins the firm by 4.60%. For team-based connections, these effects persist whether the alum and the college athlete were direct peers whose college years overlapped or older “network” affiliates whose college years were completely disjoint. Our results demonstrate that college athletics-based social networks materially influence initial job placement and early-career trajectories for top college graduates. More generally, they clarify how non-academic social capital shapes the job searching and matching process within labor markets.

detail.abstract: Conventional frameworks treat the timing of the energy transition as policy-dependent, and therefore contestable and easy to defer. This paper dates it from economic logic instead. Where a technology follows Wright's Law, unit cost falling by a consistent percentage with each doubling of cumulative production, the relative cost of clean and fossil energy is a mathematical regularity, not a scenario: clean technologies have learned at roughly 15 to 35 per cent per doubling, depending on the technology, for decades, while fossil energy learns at approximately zero and coal's delivered cost escalates with depletion. Applying this asymmetry across seventeen Asian economies, the energy systems underlying the Asian portion of the series' twenty-one-exchange universe (WP-01; Appendix G), dates the merit order crossover: the cost event at which new firm clean supply undercuts the marginal operating cost of existing coal. Merit order death is the capital event that follows, as the plant's dispatch collapses until it strands. Imported gas has already crossed; coal crosses for most economies in the early-to-mid 2030s, within a band from the late 2020s for the best-resource economies to the mid-2030s for the geothermal-dependent, and distributed within each economy by delivered cost. Because the dating rests on documented learning rates rather than on forecasts of policy or sentiment, it is robust to ordinary political volatility, if not to discontinuities. Finance and Wright's Law address roughly three-quarters of Asia emissions on cost. Of the rest, aviation awaits a technology the cost curve has not yet reached, and the balance moves on governance, not gigawatts. The consequence is a transition readiness risk the market has not priced: exposure carried in portfolios before the dates arrive. The advantage lies not in knowing that Wright’s Law exists, which is public, but in knowing when it bites. That the dates fall inside the investment horizon.

We study how temperature fluctuations affect U.S. state-level economic conditions using high frequency, weekly data from 1987 to 2024. detail.abstract: Evidence-based governance depends on fiscal indicators, rankings, audit findings, and econometric analysis, but these tools do not directly measure the internal structural balance of a policy system. This study develops Arithmetic Power Geometry (APG) as an interpretable structural intelligence layer for public policy. Using a machine-readable dataset of Indian State Finances for 28 states over 2013–14 to 2022–23, derived from Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) state-finance material, the study transforms six fiscal variables into APG weights, entropy, concentration, diversity, and effective-dimension indicators. The selected variables are revenue receipts, revenue expenditure, capital expenditure, committed expenditure, outstanding debt, and outstanding guarantees. Results show that APG identifies balanced, moderately balanced, watch-list, and debt-dominated fiscal structures without replacing conventional public finance analysis. In 2022–23, Sikkim, Nagaland, Manipur, Meghalaya, Chhattisgarh, and Uttar Pradesh appear as the most structurally balanced cases, whereas Tamil Nadu, Haryana, West Bengal, and Punjab appear as debt-dominated risk cases under the defined APG thresholds. Robustness checks across alternative power normalizations show that the squared APG specification gives stronger dominance separation while preserving high rank association with nearby power choices. The central contribution is not another fiscal ranking; it is a reproducible policy-MRI framework that reveals how fiscal components jointly form a governance structure. APG is proposed as a transparent, complementary, and data-driven layer for fiscal resilience monitoring, comparative state-level governance analysis, and student-oriented public policy research.

Using mandatory Outlook reports from Chinese mutual funds, we decompose each fund’s equity-market beliefs into macro fundamentals, government policy, and residual sentiment. Policy beliefs, rather than macro beliefs, predict subsequent market returns and help explain the positive alphas observed in China’s mutual fund industry. Using maturing wealth management products as an instrument for future aggregate fund flows, we show that funds strategically position their stated beliefs to cater to investors. detail.abstract: Background: Cancer control in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) is constrained by a critical shortage of skilled healthcare professionals across the oncology continuum. With the cancer burden rapidly increasing in low-and middleincome countries (LMICs), scalable and innovative workforce development models are urgently needed. Methods: We implemented a multi-component oncology capacity-building program in Kenya between 2017 and 2019, incorporating long-term formal training, short-course preceptorships, research mentorship, and multidisciplinary virtual tumor boards. The program targeted multiple healthcare cadres, including physicians, nurses, pharmacists, and research personnel. Outcomes included workforce expansion, training participation, research productivity, and implementation of digital oncology platforms. Results: A total of 32 healthcare professionals were supported for long-term oncology training across 10 institutions. Additionally, 98 participants received short-term training through continuing medical education, 2 workshops, and conferences. The program supported 33 scientific abstracts and presentations at international conferences. Virtual multidisciplinary tumor boards connected eight satellite centers, facilitating collaborative case discussions and expanding access to specialist oncology expertise. Conclusion: This program demonstrates the feasibility of a scalable, hybrid model for accelerating oncology workforce capacity in SSA. Multisectoral partnerships, mentorship, and digital health platforms are critical enablers of sustainable cancer control in LMICs. Increased investment in such models is essential to address persistent disparities in global cancer outcomes.

detail.abstract: Tolerance-Based Exact Matching requires exact overlap on categorical variables and applies a prespecified percentage band to continuous variables, extending Coarsened Exact Matching (Iacus, King and Porro, 2012) into a hybrid procedure introduced in earlier work (Borluk, 2026a). That study, and the treatment-effect application that followed it (Borluk, 2026b), fixed the tolerance width at a single value, 7.5 percent, without separately justifying the choice. This paper closes that gap by proposing a data-driven tolerance selection criterion that jointly considers standardized mean difference (SMD) balance and the retained matched-sample share. The criterion is tested against fixed tolerance values (5, 7.5, and 10 percent) on a synthetic firm-level panel of 6,000 observations. The findings show that the data-driven criterion can reach a balance that some of the fixed values fail to achieve, without shrinking the sample as much as the tightest fixed tolerance does. The study aims to give impact-evaluation practitioners, and researchers early in their careers, a reproducible tool that removes tolerance-width selection from the realm of arbitrary judgment.

detail.abstract: Credit scoring is one of the key tasks of bank risk management. Traditional models based on logistic regression are limited by linear dependencies and are inferior in accuracy to modern machine learning methods. The article examines the main ML algorithms used in credit scoring tasks-gradient boosting, random forests, and neural networks-analyzes the experience of their implementation in the US, EU, and China, and identifies key regulatory constraints and the problem of interpretability. Models based on XGBoost achieve an AUC-ROC of up to 0.99 versus 0.94 for logistic regression; in stress testing, the gap widens to 0.83 versus 0.68. The use of explainable AI tools (SHAP, LIME) makes it possible to combine predictive accuracy with decision transparency. A comparative analysis of three jurisdictions shows that regulatory approaches differ substantially, yet ML scoring is universally moving into the stage of an industry standard.

detail.abstract: Do entry fees clean up interconnection queues? No jurisdiction had repriced queue entry while under observation, so the question has been argued through models. The most prominent model, a structural analysis of PJM by Johnston, Liu, and Yang, first answered yes. Its revised 2026 version finds that fees barely move completed capacity, because the projects that congest the queue most are also the most valuable. Japan has now run the missing experiment, twice in one winter, and this paper pre-registers its evaluation. Cumulative battery-storage connection-study applications in Japan reached 113 GW by March 2025, on the order of national peak demand, while grid-connected utility-scale storage stood at 0.23 GW. From January 2026, new applications must document land-use rights. From April 2026, gridscale batteries face a doubled security deposit, forfeited on voluntary withdrawal. We assemble the first research panel from the grid coordinator's disclosures, 2018-2025, and document the run-up in application counts. Battery study applications grew 16-fold in two years and reached 86% of study applications by late 2025. They spiked in December 2025, the last month before the first reform, a timing consistent with deadline-driven filing that the phased rules made individually rational. Congestion pools in the Tokyo demand center, not in the renewable-rich north. The battery series has an explosive pre-trend, so we specify an interrupted time-series design with counterfactual bracketing, not difference-indifferences. Outcomes, specifications, and detection thresholds (a 42-77% collapse) are fixed here, before the first post-reform data release. We also state in advance which outcomes would remain inconclusive.

detail.title: Kinship Networks and the Adoption of New Technology: Western Medicine in China, 1835-1935
detail.abstract: Whether traditional kinship institutions impede or facilitate the adoption of new technology is contested. We study the diffusion of Western medicine as a new technology in China, 1835-1935. Using newly digitized prefecture-level data on Western-style hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, and physicians, we find that after Christian missionary arrival, prefectures with stronger pre-1835 kinship organizations built 43.5 percent more indigenously founded hospitals. Exploiting epidemics as exogenous shocks, we show that hospital construction responded more prominently in strong-clan prefectures; physician sorting confirms a supply-rather than demand-side channel. The clan effect vanishes under the 1949-1978 planned economy and re-emerges after the market reforms. Kinship institutions can accelerate, not obstruct, modern technology diffusion.

detail.title: More Good is Better
detail.abstract: One consequence of depopulation is so quiet that it would be easy to skip past it without noticing. Many billions of lives that could be excellent and full of wellbeing and joy would never be lived. Would that silence be a peace to welcome or a loss to mourn? Questions about values-questions beyond the graphs and numbers-surface whenever someone asks about the long-term future of the human population. In this chapter we ask these questions, and invite the reader to consider the ethics of depopulation. We present arguments that the chance to live a good life counts for something. To affirm this benefit is to say that depopulation matters beyond what it means for the trajectory of the economy, for balancing a government's budget, or for geopolitical power. The solvency of public pension programs is not the only thing at stake. Population is people.

title: Managing the Transition to an Economy of Freely Chosen Activity under Pervasive General-Purpose Robotic Automation: A Mathematical and Agent-Based Policy Model with a Critical Review of the Literature

detail.title: Managing the Transition to an Economy of Freely Chosen Activity under Pervasive General-Purpose Robotic Automation: A Mathematical and Agent-Based Policy Model with a Critical Review of the Literature
detail.abstract: We develop a federal-level decision-support framework for managing a long-run transition to an economy in which artificial intelligence and inexpensive general-purpose robots can perform a substantial share of cognitive and physical tasks. The framework does not forecast the technology's arrival: 2041, 2046, and 2051 serve as conditional midpoint scenarios, and one policy package must perform acceptably across all of them. A discrete-time mathematical system is coupled with an agent-based simulation of heterogeneous citizens, six sectors, and a dedicated public transition account. The policy vector combines a tax on automation rents, statutory public participation in robotic capital, a social dividend, lifelong-learning capacity, a public fund, and staged work-time reduction. An operational index measures the capacity for free activity: voluntarily usable time conditional on material security, skills, motivation, and trust. In the illustrative central experiment, the managed package reduces the below-threshold income share from 23.3% to 7.9% and the income Gini from 0.383 to 0.183, at the cost of 6.4% lower output per capita in 2061; a cash-dividend-only policy improves distribution but barely moves free-activity capacity. No numerical level is an estimate for any real economy: the experiment compares mechanisms within one illustrative parameterization. We provide a pre-specified calibration protocol (method of simulated moments, backtesting, ensemble re-optimization), a staged roadmap with monitoring indicators and stopping rules, and a critical review of six literature strands. Code, random seeds, tables, and figures are fully reproducible.

title: What a Positive Out-of-Sample R 2 Identifies - Relative Forecast Performance, Regime Comparisons, and Economic Attribution
affiliations: Simon Fraser University (SFU)

detail.title: What a Positive Out-of-Sample R 2 Identifies - Relative Forecast Performance, Regime Comparisons, and Economic Attribution
detail.abstract: An out-of-sample R 2 ranks a complete forecasting rule against a benchmark; claims about predictor content, regimes, mechanisms, and investor value concern different empirical objects. Forecast tests evaluate rules, not economic interpretations; we formalize the resulting identification problem and specify the comparison each broader claim requires. Our framework separates unrestricted performance from restriction effects, pooled-history state comparisons from state-local predictability, aggregate performance from economic-channel attribution, and forecast accuracy from investor value. We derive exact channel and regime decompositions, characterize Shapley attribution conditional on representation, prove that observed forecast paths do not identify a unique representation, and obtain sharp bounds on signal attribution. Across our applications, alternative defensible comparisons yield opposing signs and rankings. Because the out-of-sample R 2 does not select among them, economic interpretation is underdetermined. Our reporting standard resolves this indeterminacy by linking each economic claim ex ante to the comparison and uncertainty assessment it requires.

detail.title: Algorithmic Pricing for Efficient Electricity Grid Performance: A Calibrated Counterfactual of Residential and Industrial Demand Response
detail.abstract: Most U.S. retail electricity tariffs remain flat or rely on simple time-of-use blocks, even though wholesale electricity costs can vary sharply across hours. This creates a central regulatory question: when should retail prices become more responsive to system conditions, and how complex should those prices be? We compare a transparent, periodically recalibrated timeof-use tariff with a more complex algorithmic tariff. We develop a Stackelberg model in which a distribution utility sets prices for two customer classes, heterogeneous households and manufacturers, and customers adjust demand in response. The model is calibrated using public data on household electricity use, demographics, industrial facilities, tariff-trial responses, and ISO New England 2024 day-ahead wholesale prices. Simulating one year of hourly operation on a feeder with 10,000 households and 30 manufacturers, we find that the algorithmic tariff reduces system peak demand by 5.9 percent and operating cost by 2.8 percent relative to flat pricing. Fixed calendar TOU and critical-peak pricing lower costs but shift some demand to adjacent hours. A recalibrated TOU tariff, whose peak window is periodically updated using realized peak patterns, captures most of the peak reduction, lowering peak demand by 4.9 percent while remaining simpler and more transparent than algorithmic pricing. However, algorithmic pricing roughly doubles monthly bill volatility and concentrates savings among higher-income homeowners. A revenue-neutral, demographic-conditioned fixed-charge adjustment of about $25 per year largely equalizes savings across customer groups. The findings are robust to alternative assumptions about industrial load shares, renewable penetration, demand elasticities, and wholesale price volatility. We conclude with five regulatory design choices for commissions considering retail demand-response tariffs under FERC Order 2222.

detail.abstract: Synthetic drugs including fentanyl and methamphetamine are produced from precursor chemicals that flow through legitimate international trade. These chemicals are traceable in customs records, but they are rarely analyzed systematically by researchers. The infrastructure needed to do so is either locked behind proprietary platforms or reconstructed from scratch for each individual study, leaving the field fragmented and findings non-reproducible. This paper introduces ChemFlow, an open-source platform that applies three explainable analytical methods to UN Comtrade data: mirror-gap analysis, spike detection, and substitution detection. The platform covers 15 verified HS codes drawn from the INCB Red List, spanning 602,290 trade observations from 2015 through 2024. The substitution detection method operationalizes the scheduling-response behavior described qualitatively in INCB monitoring literature as a computable signal in trade data; to our knowledge it has not previously been formalized in the drug policy literature. Applying the platform to the primary documented fentanyl precursor trafficking route, we find that China reported zero exports to Mexico and Canada under the dedicated ANPP and NPP subheadings (HS 293336 and 293337) introduced by the 2022 WCO revision. At the same time, flows in the pre-existing basket code (HS 293339) spiked 39 percent to Mexico and 96 percent to Canada in the same implementation year before returning to historical baselines. Three years on, the 2022 WCO reclassification does not appear to have achieved its intended monitoring objective on the routes the US government identifies as the primary fentanyl precursor supply chain. The full dataset is released under CC-BY 4.0 and all code is open-source, enabling independent replication and extension.

detail.abstract: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio (Bailey and López de Prado, 2014) corrects an observed Sharpe ratio for the number of trials N behind it, separating genuine skill from the selection bias of a large backtest search. Its practical weakness is structural: N is supplied by the same researcher whose result it constrains. A search over a thousand configurations, reported as a single trial, satisfies the formula while defeating its purpose. The correction is sound; its input is self-reported. We present a construction that removes the researcher's discretion over that input. The trial set is committed to a Merkle tree before evaluation; the trial count N is the leaf count of the tree, not a reported scalar; and the winning strategy is bound, inside a zero-knowledge proof (a STARK), to be the maximum over the committed leaves. The deflation is then recomputed in-circuit on Merkle-pinned prices, net of a cost model the credential discloses, so the figure an allocator reads is derived by the circuit rather than asserted by the manager. The output is a credential, checkable by anyone, in seconds, without disclosure of the strategy, whose anti-overfitting correction cannot be understated within the committed search. We give the commitment scheme and its in-circuit binding; state precisely the manipulation it eliminates (understating N, cherry-picking a non-maximal winner, softening the cost model) and the residual trust it does not (off-ledger trials, closed only by forward pre-registration); and report a live implementation that additionally computes, in-circuit, the Probability of Backtest Overfitting over all C(16,8) = 12,870 combinatorially-symmetric splits (via recursive proof composition), together with the Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio and Hansen's Superior Predictive Ability. We demonstrate the system on its own flagship strategy, which it rules not significant (DSR 0.68, below the 0.95 bar), and publish that failure as the reference credential.

title: Enterprise Behaviour Intelligence: A Variational Decision Functional Integrating Spectral Graph Theory, Persistent Topology, Decision Memory and Quantum-Inspired Optimization

detail.title: Enterprise Behaviour Intelligence: A Variational Decision Functional Integrating Spectral Graph Theory, Persistent Topology, Decision Memory and Quantum-Inspired Optimization
detail.abstract: Contemporary enterprise AI systems-large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, and agentic workflow automation-compute decisions as isolated predictions of the form Decision = f(Data). This paper proposes an alternative hypothesis: enterprise decisions are better modeled as trajectories of an evolving graph state. We define an Enterprise Behaviour Action Functional over admissible trajectories of a dynamic enterprise graph G(t), aggregating six terms: spectral connectivity derived from the graph Laplacian; persistence-weighted topological features; a decision-memory continuity penalty; a constrained QUBO decision-energy term solvable by classical, quantum-inspired, or QAOA-based methods; interventional causal estimates computed with the do-operator; and a noisesuppression term weighted by a pairwise structural coupling score. The optimal intervention is characterized as a stationary point of the functional, δS/δG = 0, giving an Euler-Lagrange-type interpretation of enterprise decision-making. We describe the computational pipeline, propose a validation statistic (Structural Coupling Divergence) separating structural from semantic similarity, and specify an experimental protocol on synthetic supply-chain, portfolio-contagion, and constructionlending datasets. We are explicit about scope: the framework is quantum-inspired, physics-analogical in motivation, and requires no quantum hardware; empirical results reported here are limited to the stated synthetic settings.

detail.title: The Early Career and the Sources of Lifetime Inequality
detail.abstract: We study the first years after labor-market entry as a formative period for lifetime inequality. We estimate a life-cycle model with endogenous labor supply, human-capital accumulation, frictional labor markets, and endogenous savings using profiles anchored at labor-market entry. The model captures the rapid skill accumulation, employment transitions, and job mobility that characterize the early career. We show that beginning the analysis several years after entry reclassifies outcomes generated by early-career shocks, labor-supply choices, skill accumulation, and job mobility as initial heterogeneity. Initial conditions account for only 26 percent of lifetime earnings inequality when measured at entry, but their importance rises to 46 percent when measured five years later. We show that the rise in wage inequality during these years is driven primarily by sorting between human capital and match quality: workers with greater human capital increasingly obtain better matches. This sorting arises because human capital raises job-finding rates, lowers separation risk, and raises the quality of job offers.

title: The Paradigm Shift: How Artificial Intelligence Impacts Modern Educational Environments

detail.title: The Paradigm Shift: How Artificial Intelligence Impacts Modern Educational Environments
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed the educational landscape, shifting traditional pedagogical frameworks toward dynamic, personalized, and agent-driven learning ecologies. This paper presents a comprehensive examination of AI's current impacts on modern educational environments. By reviewing literature on social-physical sensing, large language models (LLMs), and adaptive tutoring systems, we outline the evolution from passive recommendation algorithms to autonomous, tool-calling AI agents in the classroom. Through an analysis of emerging paradigms-such as the integration of crowdsourced human-machine intelligence and the normative boundaries of AI behavior-this study identifies key benefits, including enhanced personalization and administrative efficiency, as well as critical challenges related to ethics, student agency, and academic integrity. Two tables are provided to contrast traditional and AI-enhanced learning models and to summarize key applications. We conclude that while AI offers unprecedented opportunities for educational advancement, successful integration requires robust pedagogical frameworks and ethical oversight.

detail.abstract: Waiting lists are commonly read as measures of unmet need. Using the complete administrative record of 1.52 million placement requests to São Paulo's municipal childcare system, we show that during a large expansion the demand side adjusted mainly through when families joined the queue. Across the 2010-2016 birth cohorts, registration before the first birthday rose from 11 to 50 percent and median age at first application fell from 36 to 12 months; among children registered by 24 months, the share registered before 12 months rose from 0.33 to 0.71. The shift appears within families-later-born children are registered 7.2 months earlier than their older siblings, net of family fixed effects and cohort trends-and is not explained by broader registration alone, by reservation of future places, or by a discrete administrative reform. Over the same period the service improved: treating aging out of eligibility as a competing risk, the one-year probability of referral rose from 0.56 to 0.88, and the gain grows once cohorts are standardized to a common applicant composition. Across all applicants, an accounting decomposition of age at administrative resolution attributes almost the entire decline to earlier application rather than to a shorter interval to resolution. The municipality's recurring public indicators summarize the stock of registered demand, with only a coarse duration split, but do not report the age-at-registration distribution or the flows that generate the stock. Because the timing of entry is itself a choice, the published stock of a registered waiting list is an equilibrium object rather than a direct measure of unmet need.

detail.abstract:
International students have become indispensable to Japan’s service sector. Beyond formal regulations and individual qualifications, their employment outcomes are heavily driven by the specific networks through which they discover vacancies. This paper examines how job-search channels affect hourly wages for Chinese international students in Japan, contrasting formal Japanese-language channels (such as university boards and local platforms) with co-ethnic networks (such as WeChat and Xiaohongshu). We conceptualize this phenomenon as an "information tax"—a hidden wage penalty stemming from reliance on low-friction, native-language networks. Though these networks ease the job search for newly arrived or less proficient students, they trade off long-term earnings by narrowing the scope of available wage offers.

Using a cross-sectional survey of Chinese international students in Japan, this paper estimates the wage impact of using Japanese versus Chinese-language job-search channels. Because channel selection is likely endogenous, we introduce a geographical instrument: travel time to the nearest Chinese community area or supermarket. While proximity to these hubs drives exposure to native-language job openings, it should not directly influence wages after accounting for urban centrality, prefecture, Japanese proficiency, and gender. Given the inherent challenges of spatial instruments, the design adopts a conservative approach, embedding multiple pre-specified robustness checks to validate this exclusion restriction.

The empirical analysis scales through five specifications—ranging from a simple bivariate model and successive layers of individual and geographic controls, to a 2SLS instrumental variable model and a final mechanism check adding commuting and job types. This approach bridges classical information economics and network theory with micro-level data, clarifying the dynamics of ethnic networks and labor-market segmentation.

detail.abstract: Financial systems record visible events with increasing precision: payments posted, trades executed, accounts opened, disclosures acknowledged, orders submitted, and defaults triggered. Behavioral economics and behavioral finance have likewise produced rich accounts of observed choices, defaults, attention, present bias, loss avoidance, and investor behavior. This article argues that finance also requires a disciplined theory of meaningful absence. Behavioral economics explains many reasons why people do not act, but it offers less unified guidance on when a recorded non-occurrence should count as behavioral evidence rather than missingness, ordinary delay, or deliberate no-action. The article introduces revealed omission as a measurement construct for those cases. A revealed omission is the non-occurrence of a pre-specified financial signal when the signal was expected ex ante, the actor or process had a reasonable opportunity to produce it, the observation channel was functioning, the relevant time window had closed, and salient exclusions or confounders had been considered. Dynamic Omission Vectors summarize multiple qualified non-events while preserving the basis for expectation and the conditions of observation. The contribution is not a new behavioral bias, credit score, anomaly detector, or intervention system. It is a theory-building and measurement contribution that connects qualified non-events to limited attention, procrastination, status quo bias, rational inattention, non-take-up, and investor attention while making no empirical performance claim for DOVs themselves.

title: Beyond Location: Origin-Conditional Valuation of Premium Residential Markets -A Framework and a 25-City Pilot

detail.title: Beyond Location: Origin-Conditional Valuation of Premium Residential Markets -A Framework and a 25-City Pilot
detail.abstract: Purpose-To develop and pilot a valuation framework in which a city's effective premium-residential proposition is conditioned on the resident's origin, rather than assumed origin-independent as in existing city instruments. Design/methodology/approach-Fourteen classifiers across three time horizons (structural, jurisdictional, operational; weighted 50/30/20) produce a composite score for 25 anchor cities; a calibrated Posture matrix then conditions the composite on the resident's civilizational origin (multiplier range 0.55-1.35). A frozen-input back-test scores 2019 vintages of four candidate declining markets against the framework's confirmation rule. Findings-Origin reorders city rankings. London's effective proposition differs by 30.4% between Western-and Gulf-origin residents-a gap that is base-independent, reflecting the posture ratio itself. Bucharest inverts between Orthodox-and Western-origin families. The structural classifier layer flagged Hong Kong's and San Francisco's residential deterioration before price indices registered it. Research limitations/implications-Origin multipliers are author-calibrated pending expertpanel validation; the twelve-zone civilizational grid is deliberately coarse; within-city reception of specific groups is outside the framework's scope by construction. Practical implications-The Posture multiplier functions as an origin-conditional discount or premium; contested-horizon flags translate into holding-period constraints; the Fallen Star confirmation rule operates as a structural stop-loss-parameters directly usable by cross-border buyers, wealth advisors and family offices. Originality/value-To the author's knowledge, this is the first residential valuation framework that makes the observer's origin an explicit pricing variable.

detail.abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, remote primary care services were rolled out in England at unprecedented rates; this systematic change was met with public concerns, especially around healthcare quality and equity in access. To understand the policy rationales for using remote services and the standards for such services through an equity lens, we conducted a review of policies and guidelines. In policies and guidelines, remote services were portrayed as an opportunity to improve and restore services after the pandemic. Remote services should adhere to the same standards as face-to-face services, while local surgeries (clinics) and general practitioners (GPs) had flexibility to decide the best approach given circumstances. While there was acknowledgement of inequity in digital access, policies and guidelines overlooked complexities of delivering services to a heterogenous population. Future policies would benefit from clearer definitions and roles of different healthcare modalities and clearer evaluation plans to constantly improve primary care services.

detail.abstract: U.S. government agencies use estimates of the value of a statistical life (VSL) to monetize mortality risk impacts of government policies. A recent meta-analysis by the OECD has reviewed VSL studies based on stated preference methods and revealed preference evidence from the labor market and consumer decisions. This article examines the U.S. studies considered in the OECD meta-analysis as well as those from prior VSL meta-analyses, including Viscusi and Masterman (2017a) and OECD (2012). After excluding studies of the VSL for the military, the average VSL estimates are similar to those used by U.S. government agencies. title: Beyond the Pitch: Cybersecurity, National Security, and Logistical Challenges of the FIFA World Cup Through the Case Study of Iran's Participation

detail.title: Beyond the Pitch: Cybersecurity, National Security, and Logistical Challenges of the FIFA World Cup Through the Case Study of Iran's Participation
detail.abstract: The FIFA World Cup represents one of the largest international gatherings in the world, combining sports, diplomacy, technology, commerce, and global media attention. Although traditionally viewed as an athletic competition, modern World Cups have evolved into complex security operations requiring coordination between governments, private corporations, intelligence organizations, and international institutions. The participation of the Iranian national soccer team provides a significant case study for examining the relationship between cybersecurity, national security, and logistical challenges associated with major sporting events. Iran's geopolitical position, history of cyber operations, and involvement in international disputes create additional security considerations for host nations responsible for protecting athletes, spectators, infrastructure, and information systems. This paper examines how Iran's participation in the FIFA World Cup affects cybersecurity planning and national security decision-making. It analyzes potential cyber threats including state-sponsored cyber operations, ransomware, distributed denial-of-service attacks, espionage, and information warfare. Additionally, the paper evaluates broader security concerns involving counterterrorism, intelligence collection, diplomatic protection, and civil unrest. Finally, it explores logistical challenges associated with transportation, communication systems, accommodation security, and international coordination. This research argues that the presence of Iran at a FIFA World Cup does not inherently represent a direct security threat; rather, it increases the complexity of the security environment because of existing geopolitical tensions. Effective protection of global sporting events requires an integrated approach combining cybersecurity, intelligence sharing, critical infrastructure protection, and traditional security operations.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is moving from specialist technology teams into ordinary organizational decisions, including
procurement, employment, customer service, investigations, fraud detection, cybersecurity and document analysis.
The governance challenge is therefore not merely whether an AI model performs well. It is whether the organization
can identify where AI is used, assign accountability, classify risk, maintain proportionate controls, detect change
and provide decision-useful assurance. This paper presents a practical framework for internal auditors who need to
assess AI governance without becoming data scientists or relying on a single universal checklist. It explains how to
connect board oversight, executive ownership, risk classification and lifecycle controls; how to evaluate data,
model, privacy, security, third-party and human-oversight risks; and how to design a focused AI governance audit
using suitable criteria and defensible evidence. The central objective is informed confidence. Organizations should
be able to use AI deliberately while demonstrating that material risks are understood, controlled, monitored and
escalated. Internal audit contributes by testing both control design and operating effectiveness, translating technical
complexity into business consequences, and reporting the decisions that management and governing bodies need to
make.

title: Who Bears the Burden? Real Wage and Employment Adjustment to Upstream Inflation Shocks Across Monetary Policy Regimes Singapore and the United Kingdom

detail.abstract: This paper examines how the instrument of monetary tightening determines the distributional burden of inflation adjustment across workers. Using Singapore (exchange-rate targeting, S$NEER framework) and the United Kingdom (interest-rate targeting, Bank of England) as the comparison pair, we test whether the 2021 to 2023 tightening episode produced different real wage and employment outcomes across frameworks. Three hypotheses are evaluated. First, real wages fell further and recovered more slowly in the UK than Singapore during tightening (H1). Second, the real wage gap closed faster in Singapore (H2). Third, exchange-rate tightening preserved employment better than interest-rate tightening (H3). Results support H1 and H2 but not H3. Singapore real wages remained positive throughout the episode, while UK real wages turned negative in 2022 (-3.0%) and 2023 (-0.2%) before recovering. Cumulative real wage growth during tightening was +7.7% in Singapore versus +2.0% in the UK. Employment outcomes were statistically indistinguishable across frameworks: the DiD coefficient on unemployment is near zero (0.034pp, p = 0.844), and synthetic control analysis using New Zealand and Denmark as donor countries confirms a near-zero average treatment effect (+0.22pp). Sectoral decomposition reveals that Singapore manufacturing and food services-the sectors most exposed to dollar-invoiced imports-experienced the lowest nominal wage acceleration, consistent with the S$NEER absorbing the import cost shock at the border before it reached domestic labour markets. The instrument of tightening does not determine who loses their job. It determines who loses their purchasing power.

title: The Quantum Clock Is Ticking: Financial Stability and the Regulation of Quantum-Vulnerable Digital Assets
affiliations: Duke University School of Law

detail.title: The Quantum Clock Is Ticking: Financial Stability and the Regulation of Quantum-Vulnerable Digital Assets
detail.abstract: In March 2026, researchers at Google Quantum AI published resource estimates showing that the elliptic-curve cryptography used by Bitcoin, Ethereum, and many other major blockchains could be broken with far fewer quantum-computing resources than previously believed. The authors validated their estimates through a zero-knowledge proof while withholding the underlying circuits. Within two months, an independent researcher reproduced the circuits and a public challenge improved on them. The quantum threat to digital assets has moved from a remote theoretical concern to a concrete migration problem. At the same time, U.S. policymakers are integrating quantum-vulnerable blockchain infrastructure into the financial system through federally regulated stablecoins, chartered crypto institutions, exchange-traded products, and tokenized securities. This Article examines the collision between those policy trajectories. It argues that financial stability should govern the response and that the federal objective should be containment of transmission from a failing legacy network into regulated finance. Congress should create a quantum-resilience perimeter under which covered intermediaries, stablecoin issuers, investment products, and market infrastructures may, after a defined transition, operate only through networks and digitalasset arrangements certified as quantum-resilient. Qualification should require protection of every material cryptographic function and a credible plan to prevent mass unauthorized monetization of assets controlled by deprecated credentials. Protocol communities would retain authority to choose the technical method, including migration, quarantine, recovery, rate limits, issuer-led reissuance, or permanent unspendability. Nonqualified networks could continue through self-custody and peer-to-peer use, but they would remain outside regulated custody, collateral, derivatives, tokenized markets, and U.S.-regulated dollar channels. The proposal thus protects financial stability without directing consensus rules or prohibiting private ownership.

detail.abstract: The natural rate of interest (r*) plays a central role in monetary policy analysis, but its estimation is inherently model dependent. This paper studies how alternative econometric specifications affect the estimates of r* in the euro-area. We propose a Hybrid Common Trend Vector Autoregression that incorporates a large information set, stochastic volatility, and fat-tailed innovations. Using euro-area data spanning the last 25 years, we find that these features materially improve inference, reducing the width of 95\% credible intervals for r* by as much as 100 basis points relative to conventional specifications. Our results point to a persistent decline in the natural rate between 2000 and 2020, followed by a moderate post-pandemic recovery. The decomposition of r* identifies the trend of labor productivity growth as the dominant driver of its long-run movements. The findings suggest that uncertainty surrounding r* is partly econometric in nature and can be reduced through richer empirical specifications.

detail.abstract: We study state restrictions on the ability of local governments to suspend the drivers' licenses of residents for unpaid traffic tickets as a natural experiment in expanded access to legal driving. Using a staggered event study design, we examine how these reforms affected countylevel labor market outcomes in Core Based Statistical Areas. Collectively, the results indicate that the state reforms produced efficiency gains through greater mobility of residents. We find that reforms reduced the unemployment rate among residents of suburban and urban counties by 0.49 and 0.28 percentage points, respectively, and increased employment levels at establishments located in suburban counties. There is corroborating evidence that the mechanism is enhanced mobility, as the reforms also induced a larger share of workers driving to work, and foot traffic data show increases in mobility in suburban counties, particularly at gas stations.

title: The Validation Bottleneck: Alpha Discovery When Hypotheses Are Free

detail.title: The Validation Bottleneck: Alpha Discovery When Hypotheses Are Free
detail.abstract: Large language models have made investment hypotheses effectively free, moving the binding constraint on alpha discovery from generation to validation. Restricting a model's data feed does not restrict its knowledge: it has read the anomaly literature, so its training cutoff is the only valid out-of-sample boundary. Put the two facts together and the strategies tested multiply without limit while the evidence that can judge them accrues at one year per year. Three consequences follow. The smallest alpha an allocator can certify rises with the logarithm of the number of strategies the industry tests, because the luckiest fluke among them looks better the more are tried. Alpha that decays faster than the evidence accrues cannot be certified within its own lifetime. And firms drawing hypotheses from the same model correlate their discoveries, on that model's most celebrated ideas, before either holds a position. Two pre-registered experiments then measure the contamination and the bind. Told to propose predictors not yet in the literature as of a past date, five models across three lineages return that literature anyway: 26-55% of their "novel" proposals match predictors already in the library. Convergent rediscovery could explain that; it cannot explain the sign. The predictors they propose most often are those that performed worse afterward (combined z =-3.88). They reproduce fame, not future returns. Evaluated strictly after verified cutoffs, none of the roughly 900 evaluable strategies clears false-discovery control, and no model's best pick beats the best of an equal number of random draws from the same restricted language; two of the three do worse. The models' own stated predictions about their mechanisms held 39% of the time, against 70% for mechanisms already documented as true put through the same tests-and 46% against 86% on the one window long enough to test structure. By the second consequence, no window available today could certify a true strategy either: the nulls measure the window's width, not the models' quality. Hypotheses are free, and worth what they cost until validated.

title: Examining the Impact of Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism on Southeast Asian Countries: Evidence from India, China, and Japan

detail.title: Examining the Impact of Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism on Southeast Asian Countries: Evidence from India, China, and Japan
detail.abstract: This paper quantifies the trade and production-network implications of the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) for three major Asian manufacturing economies-India, China, and Japan-across the carbon-intensive sectors most directly affected by the regulation: steel, aluminium, and cement. The analysis proceeds in four linked stages. A carbon cost accounting framework first translates sector-level embedded emissions into ad valorem trade cost equivalents at prevailing EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) prices. A structural gravity specification then maps these cost shocks into bilateral export-volume responses, using a calibrated trade-cost semi-elasticity drawn from the empirical trade literature. A scenario analysis evaluates the extent to which domestic carbon pricing aligned with EU ETS levels can mitigate exposure under the CBAM equivalency principle. An input-output extension based on OECD Inter-Country Input-Output (ICIO) tables traces direct and indirect supply-chain spillovers, with particular focus on India. Three findings emerge. First, ad valorem CBAM cost exposure varies widely across countries and sectors, ranging from 6 percent for Japanese steel to 72 percent for Indian cement, with crosscountry differences driven primarily by emissions intensity. Aluminium emerges as the most exposed sector across all three economies. Second, gravity-based simulations indicate that CBAM-induced export contractions to the EU are substantial for emissions-intensive sectors and only partially offset by reallocation to non-EU destinations, leaving meaningful net export losses. Third, full domestic carbon pricing alignment with the EU ETS reduces exposure by 59 to 94 percent across countries and sectors, but the residual gap is largest where emissions intensity is highest, indicating that pricing alignment is necessary but not sufficient. Input-output analysis for India further shows that 38 percent of the steel sector's exposure propagates through indirect supply-chain linkages, with non-CBAM sectors such as machinery, equipment, and construction absorbing material spillovers. The findings carry implications for the design of domestic carbon pricing instruments, industrial decarbonisation strategies, and trade policy adjustment in increasingly carbon-constrained global markets.

title: From National Resource to Workplace Risk: How China's Family Planning Policies Reframe Women's Reproductive Capacity and Shape Gender Discrimination in Urban Labor Markets

detail.abstract: This thesis examines how China’s evolving family planning policies have reshaped gender inequality in the urban labor market. Over the past four decades, China has transitioned from restrictive population control under the One-Child Policy to an explicitly pronatalist framework under the Three-Child Policy. While these shifts aim to address demographic decline and labor shortages, they have also transformed how women’s reproductive capacity is perceived within employment contexts. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with legal experts, scholars, and human resource professionals, this study analyzes how demographic governance interacts with labor market institutions, cultural norms, and employer decision-making. It argues that pronatalist policies do not operate in isolation but reinforce existing structural inequalities by intensifying employers’ perceptions of women, particularly those of childbearing age, as potential reproductive risk bearers. The findings show that workplace discrimination functions through cumulative and anticipatory mechanisms across the employment life cycle. At the hiring stage, employers engage in statistical discrimination by factoring in expected maternity costs. During employment, women face slower promotion, exclusion from high-value tasks, and career interruptions associated with pregnancy and caregiving. These disadvantages are further compounded by institutional factors such as weak enforcement of anti-discrimination laws, unequal distribution of care responsibilities, and earlier retirement policies for women. By integrating perspectives from biopolitics, sociological theories of gender norms, and labor market discrimination, this thesis demonstrates that gender inequality in China is structurally produced through the interaction of policy, culture, and market incentives. It concludes that without redistributing the costs of reproduction—through stronger legal enforcement, expanded childcare support, and greater male participation in caregiving—pronatalist policies may inadvertently exacerbate workplace inequality while failing to achieve their demographic goals.

title: The Risk of Search: Why High Worker Wage Premia are Linked to Lower Job Separation Rates

detail.title: The Risk of Search: Why High Worker Wage Premia are Linked to Lower Job Separation Rates
detail.abstract: This thesis studies the relationship between worker wage premia and job mobility. Using matched administrative data from Veneto, Italy, I document a novel empirical pattern: workers with higher worker and firm wage premia are significantly less likely to change employers. While the negative association between firm wage premia and separations is consistent with the existing literature, the negative relationship for worker wage premia contradicts standard interpretations. To rationalize this finding, I develop a model of on-the-job search with endogenous search intensity, CRRA utility, and a log-additive wage structure. When workers' risk aversion exceeds log-utility (ρ = 1), higher-premium workers optimally reduce search effort, resulting in lower job separation rates. I derive a local approximation of the model-implied hazard and estimate it using a complementary log-log specification. The results imply economically meaningful effects on job separation rates and expected match duration. I use these estimates to calibrate the "search cost elasticity" and document additional heterogeneity in these effects by gender and occupation.

Under the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) ETF purchase program, the individual stocks that accumulate at asset management companies are lent out to the stock lending market and affect stock price formation as a supplyside factor (an increase in short selling). This paper empirically evaluates the effects of the ETF purchase program while explicitly taking the financial functions of the stock lending market into account. detail.abstract: The legal regulation of technology, including artificial intelligence and other autonomous systems, has been a priority for policymakers worldwide over the past decade. Simultaneously, much of the regulatory burden is delegated to private entities, such as standardisation organisations and tech platforms, which establish their own systems of governance, creating hybrid regimes where formal law intersects with technical standards and informal norms. Ultimately, implementing these regulations – whether legislation or private rule-making – falls on the tech community, especially software developers and engineers expected to build compliant systems. Our paper employs the concept of legal consciousness as a lens through to analyse this problem. While scholarship shows that legal meaning is relational and multi-sited, circulating across institutional and digital spaces, we know little about how developers encounter and interpret norms in everyday work. Do they rely on compliance teams, peer networks, social norms or fragmented online resources? How do these pathways influence compliance, avoidance or resistance? This paper establishes a foundation for future research by providing a conceptual and an analytical framework, including levels of analysis and structured steps for empirical investigation.

title: When Do Accountants Matter? Evidence from Random Allocation of Tax Experts

detail.title: When Do Accountants Matter? Evidence from Random Allocation of Tax Experts
detail.abstract: Do firms respond to foreign regulatory scrutiny by recruiting expertise from abroad? Following the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA), U.S. public firms' domestic effective tax rates fell below their foreign rates by up to three percentage points by 2022, which coincided with increased rates of foreign tax audits. Using proprietary individual-level data on H1-B visa lottery outcomes obtained through a FOIA request, we find that firms with greater foreign tax authority exposure are more likely to seek foreign tax experts. Among the firms that apply for foreign tax experts, we find that firms whose H-1B petitions are randomly selected in the lottery subsequently achieve more favorable tax audit outcomes, consistent with a causal effect of access to foreign expertise. Our results concentrate among firms that recruit experts for their past experience with foreign tax authorities, among experts that demand a wage premium over the prevailing wage, and among firms with less access to Big 4 auditor-provided tax services. Importantly, we find no evidence that firms respond to foreign tax authority scrutiny by expanding their domestic or foreign tax departments more broadly, suggesting that the H-1B channel reflects targeted demand for specialized local expertise rather than a general scaling-up of tax resources. Overall, our findings suggest that U.S. firms respond to increased foreign regulatory scrutiny by hiring experts with local institutionalized (i.e., "soft") knowledge, and that access to such human capital mitigates firm-level regulatory burden.

detail.abstract: Cryptoassets are increasingly entangled with the traditional financial system, and how this activity integrates into national economies and behaves under stress bears on financial stability and the design of public digital money. However, blockchain pseudonymity and the lack of geographic identifiers force existing work to rely on indirect proxies to infer and locate market participants. Here we use a regulatory registry that directly identifies the on-chain addresses of all crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) registered in Austria, reconstructing their on-chain transaction activity across Bitcoin, Ether, USDC, and USDT through May 2025, and separating retail-like from institutionally mediated flows. We find that Austrian CASPs intermediate roughly $30 billion with external counterparties and are integrated globally rather than domestically. In value, this activity is dominated by a few institutional counterparties; in number, by retail-like ones. Around three major shocks, the Terra-Luna collapse, the FTX bankruptcy, and the Silicon Valley Bank failure, the two groups respond through different mechanisms, and stablecoins do not act as a uniform safe haven. The clearest case is SVB, where retail-like deposits and institutional withdrawals are consistent with USDC's two-tiered redemption mechanism. These patterns are invisible in aggregate data. Registry-based, transaction-level measurement thus offers a reproducible, cross-jurisdictional basis for monitoring how cryptoasset markets transmit risk.

detail.title: Automation, Augmentation, and the Productivity Translation Lag: An Economic Framework for Generative AI
detail.abstract: Generative AI has expanded the technological frontier across a broad range of cognitive tasks, yet its effects on aggregate productivity remain elusive. This paper develops the Productivity Translation Framework (PTF), a conceptual architecture that explains this gap by tracing how AI capability is translated into economic outcomes through seven causally linked stages: frontier expansion and socioeconomic adoption, the dual mechanisms of automation and augmentation, their asymmetric productivity multipliers, market elasticity as demand-side moderator, marginal cost structure as supply-side moderator, competitive normalization and market restructuring, and the augmentation-to-automation transition. The framework integrates task-based automation theory, endogenous growth economics, and innovation management to show that automation and augmentation are structurally different production mechanisms with different scaling properties: automation multipliers are potentially unbounded while augmentation is constrained by human cognitive bandwidth. Market elasticity and marginal cost jointly determine whether AI creates new economic activity or restructures existing activity, yielding four archetypal scenarios. Three novel concepts are introduced. The augmentation trap describes how firms scaling through augmentation in elastic markets build workforces vulnerable to subsequent automation. Competitive normalization explains why augmentation advantages erode rapidly into baseline expectations. The productivity translation lag reframes the Solow paradox as a structural consequence of the organizational redesign required to transition from augmented to automated production. Nine testable propositions are developed.

An Outsider's Critique of a Self-Diagnosed, Recurring Blind Spot in Macroeconomic Instruments for General-Purpose Technologies
detail.abstract: This paper argues that mainstream macroeconomic instruments-aggregate output, productivity, and total factor productivity (TFP) statistics-are structurally built to register the diffusion of a general-purpose technology, not the phase transition that precedes diffusion. It traces a single methodological blind spot across four independent instances spanning nearly four decades: Robert Solow's 1987 observation that the computer age was invisible in the productivity statistics; Paul David's 1990 historical account of the electrification lag that explained why; Paul Krugman's 1998 forecast that the internet's economic impact would not exceed the fax machine's; and the current (2024-2026) generation of AI-productivity forecasts by Christopher Pissarides and Daron Acemoglu, each of which again finds no aggregate signal. The recurrence of the same instrument-diffusion mismatch across four laureates and four decades-three of the individuals laureates for work unrelated to this specific question-is treated as evidence of a discipline-level pattern rather than of any individual's error. The paper further shows, using Acemoglu's own disclosed exclusion of the R&D/idea-production channel and Lawrence Summers's public critique of that exclusion, that the blind spot is in at least one prominent instance a known and acknowledged modeling choice rather than an oversight. A working counterexample the Korea Development Institute's sectoral "Canary Dashboard," announced July 9, 2026-is presented as evidence that the gap is instrumentally fixable. Consistent with the outsider standing declared in Section I, the paper explicitly does not propose how the discipline should fix it; that diagnosis is offered from outside the guild, and the repair is left to those inside it.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the macroeconomic effects of defense spending shocks in emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs), with a focus on Asia and the Pacific over 1990– 2023. Using large cyclically adjusted defense shocks identified through local projections, we find that defense spending generates modest but persistent positive output responses in EMDEs, while effects in advanced economies are weak or negative. Within EMDEs, multipliers are strongest in South Asia and weaker in East Asia, reflecting differences in labor intensity and capital intensity of procurement. Functional decompositions show that core military outlays and defense-related research and development drive the positive effects. State dependence is central: fiscal space, revenue capacity, financial development, institutional quality, and—critically— conflict exposure shape both the size and persistence of multipliers, with much stronger effects in high conflict environments. Regional spillovers are weak, short-lived, and turn negative at longer horizons. Extensive robustness checks confirm the stability of these findings.

detail.abstract: The proliferation of economic uncertainty indicators —ranging from text-based indices like the Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) index to market-based measures such as the VIX and the ECB’s Country-Level Index of Financial Stress (CLIFS)— has enriched the analytical toolkit of economists and policymakers. Yet these indicators often diverge, sending conflicting signals about the state of uncertainty in the economy. This paper argues that such divergence is not a flaw but a feature: each indicator captures a distinct dimension of uncertainty. Using topic modeling techniques applied to national news corpora, we construct a taxonomy of uncertainty narratives across five European countries and classify episodes of divergence between the EPU and CLIFS indicators. Our findings reveal systematic patterns: EPU peaks are predominantly driven by political and institutional developments, CLIFS peaks by financial market stress and joint peaks by systemic crises. These results underscore the multidimensional nature of uncertainty and highlight the need for structured interpretative frameworks. By linking narrative content to indicator behavior, our approach offers a novel lens for understanding uncertainty dynamics and provides practical tools for researchers and policymakers navigating an increasingly complex informational environment.

detail.abstract:
Key points

– On 11 November 2025, the Grand Chamber of the Court of Justice of the European Union largely upheld the Directive on Adequate Minimum Wages. This represented a substantial rejection of both the Danish request for annulment of the Directive and the very broad reading of the competence exclusion advanced by Advocate General Emiliou.

– The Court’s conclusions are underpinned by a reworking of the direct interference test inherited from its previous case law on the competence exclusion in the field of pay, adapted to the specific circumstances of the annulment action at issue, which concerns a measure that has a direct connection with the issue of pay.

– In examining the Directive, the Court finds that most provisions do not directly interfere with Member States’ determination of pay. The only exceptions are Article 5(2), which requires four mandatory criteria for setting and updating statutory minimum wages, and Article 5(3), which prohibits automatic indexation where it would reduce those wages; these provisions were annulled, while the rest of the Directive was upheld.

– The Court’s judgment allows for a more optimistic outlook on the future of European social policy, dispelling the clouds that had gathered as a result of the pending action for annulment of the Directive.

– However, it also highlights even more clearly that the achievement of its core objectives is largely dependent on the willingness and ambition of Member States in transposition and implementation.

detail.abstract: Fragmented medical record-keeping and an untracked over-the-counter (OTC) pharmaceutical economy represent two persistent and related barriers to health-system efficiency in emerging markets. This paper examines these barriers through a case study analysis situated within a broader research question: how national identification (ID) infrastructure can be leveraged to achieve health data interoperability in resource-constrained settings. Findings suggest that National ID-based interoperability can meaningfully reduce transaction friction between clinics, pharmacies, and insurers, but that exclusion risk, standardization cost, and regulatory lag remain material constraints. title: A Papal Blueprint for AI Governance: Subsidiarity, Solidarity, and The Common Good From Magnifica Humanitas

detail.title: A Papal Blueprint for AI Governance: Subsidiarity, Solidarity, and The Common Good From Magnifica Humanitas
detail.abstract:
American AI governance is a normative vacuum. There is no federal AI statute, no Section 5 framework for non-economic AI harms, no antitrust doctrine for epistemic monoculture, and no settled foundation for AI fiduciary duty. This Article argues that Pope Leo XIV's encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, signed on May 15, 2026, on the 135th anniversary of Rerum Novarum, can fill that vacuum as canonical soft law, shaping American AI law without binding it, just as Rerum Novarum shaped American labor law a century earlier. Rerum Novarum's vocabulary of dignity, the right to organize, and subsidiarity had no positive law equivalent in 1891. Forty-four years later, Senate debate over the National Labor Relations Act drew directly on it. The conditions favoring a similar migration into positive law are stronger today for AI governance than they were in 1891 for labor governance. The Vatican maintains diplomatic relations with 184 states, and Anthropic's co-founder stood beside the Pope at the encyclical's presentation to publicly acknowledge that AI governance cannot be left to industry alone.
This Article extracts three operative principles from the encyclical (subsidiarity, solidarity, and the common good as the criterion for evaluating legitimate private power) and applies them to FTC unfairness doctrine, Sherman Act monopolization analysis, and the emerging law of AI fiduciary duty. It confronts the Establishment Clause objection directly, showing that treating a papal document as a normative resource raises no constitutional difficulty, and answers further objections concerning the encyclical's religious source, its selection over other traditions, and doubts about its practical effect. In doing so, the Article offers a pragmatic framework for courts and regulators navigating AI governance in the absence of statutory guidance.

title: Regional Economic Resilience and Coordinated Development in China: Adaptive Capacity, Structural Transformation, and Institutional Foundations

detail.title: Regional Economic Resilience and Coordinated Development in China: Adaptive Capacity, Structural Transformation, and Institutional Foundations
detail.abstract: Regional economies are increasingly exposed to external shocks-from financial crises and trade disruptions to technological shifts and environmental stresses. The capacity of regions to withstand, adapt to, and recover from such shocks, termed regional economic resilience, has emerged as a crucial determinant of long-term spatial equity. This paper develops a conceptual framework linking regional economic resilience to China's coordinated development agenda. Drawing on evolutionary economic geography and resilience theory, the analysis identifies four core mechanisms through which resilience shapes regional convergence: adaptive capacity through diversified industrial structures, institutional agility and learning, social capital and networked governance, and the ability to transform existing assets into new growth paths. The paper argues that resilience is not merely about returning to a pre-shock equilibrium but about reconfiguring regional economies towards more sustainable and inclusive trajectories. The spatial heterogeneity of resilience in China, with coastal regions generally exhibiting stronger adaptive capabilities than inland areas, risks widening regional disparities unless addressed through deliberate policy. The paper discusses China's experience with regional resilience, highlighting cases of successful adaptation in old industrial bases and the role of state-led initiatives in building local capacity. It proposes policy pathways for strengthening resilience in less-developed regions, including fostering economic diversification, supporting local innovation ecosystems, enhancing social safety nets, and promoting cross-regional cooperation. The study concludes that embedding resilience thinking into regional coordinated development represents a paradigm shift from vulnerability reduction to proactive capacity building, essential for achieving spatial justice in an era of heightened uncertainty.

detail.title: Proving the Board Decision: Evidentiary Battles in Brazil's Dividend Tax Transition
detail.abstract: Brazil's Law No. 15,270/2025 ended a thirty-year exemption on distributed profits and, in doing so, made the survival of that exemption for pre-2025 earnings conditional on a dated corporate act: the distribution had to be approved by a shareholders' or quotaholders' resolution before a statutory cliff date, and later paid in the form originally set out in that act. This paper argues that the drafters thereby converted a question of intertemporal law into an essentially evidentiary one, turning the existence, date, content, and regularity of the corporate resolution, together with the fidelity of future payments to the original act, into the decisive battleground of the coming litigation. Written from the standpoint of the legal practitioner who must build, contest, or adjudicate that proof, the paper analyzes the evidence and counter-evidence of backdating, proposes the notion of an accounting evidentiary asymmetry grounded in IAS 10, distinguishes two very different disputes generated by the same rule (genuine resolutions adopted in haste versus resolutions fabricated afterwards), and offers a seven-step decision framework that allocates the burden of proof at each stage. Although the statute is Brazilian, the underlying problem of cliffdate deliberations is universal, and the December 2025 surge of last-minute distributions offers an unusually clean natural experiment for empirical study.
