detail.title: A Demand-Side Alternative to Renewable Curtailment: Natural Field Experimental Evidence from Two Countries
detail.abstract:
As renewable generation plays a growing role in the energy system, periods of negative wholesale electricity prices are becoming increasingly common and are expected to grow dramatically over the next ten years. Traditionally, system operators respond by paying generators, especially renewables, to curtail production, or mandating that they do so without compensation. In this study, we propose and test a novel alternative: exposing consumers to free and negative prices to stimulate demand when supply is abundant. We implemented large-scale nationwide natural field experiments simultaneously in Great Britain and Spain, with roughly 60,000 residential customers in each country randomized to receive varying financial incentives to “turn up” their electricity. We found that demand increased substantially as prices fell to zero, but paying customers to consume beyond zero price yielded little additional response. Households with electric vehicles and rooftop solar had a larger elasticity than households without such technologies, suggesting demand turn-up becomes more effective as households adopt low-carbon technologies. In Great Britain, consumption was largely shifted from adjacent hours, while in Spain the increase appeared to represent net new demand. We develop a welfare framework showing conditions under which demand turn-up improves on curtailment; we find that by inducing additional consumption in periods and locations where the marginal cost of supply is low, demand turn-up generates welfare gains that curtailment leaves uncaptured.

The business models identified in this study demonstrate that climate action can be embedded in viable and profitable farming strategies across all farm types. Whether through local, quality-based production, cooperative and vertically integrated models, or high-tech precision systems, farms can simultaneously improve resilience, strengthen income, and reduce emissions. Crucially, these pathways are not theoretical. They reflect real practices already emerging across Poland and were co-developed through a participatory research process involving farmers and sector experts.

At the same time, the transition will not happen automatically. The core barrier is not a lack of solutions, but a lack of enabling conditions. For most farms, especially small and medium ones, engaging in environmental action requires first building economic stability and resilience. Where income is uncertain, risk-taking is low. Climate action will therefore only scale if it aligns with farmers’ economic logic and is supported by policies, markets, and financial instruments that reduce transition risk.

Farmers must be at the center of this process. Their experience, knowledge, and trust networks are essential for shaping credible and scalable solutions. As this study shows, adoption is driven less by abstract environmental goals and more by demonstrated economic and agronomic benefits. Strengthening peer learning, advisory systems, and farmer-led innovation will be critical to accelerating change.

Ultimately, the transition of Polish agriculture is not about choosing between farm types or development models. It is about enabling multiple pathways to coexist and contribute to a shared objective: a sector that is economically viable, resilient to climate risks, and capable of delivering meaningful environmental outcomes. There is both space and need for all farms to take part in this transformation, provided the conditions are in place to make it possible.

detail.abstract: Decentralized exchanges (DEXs) facilitate the trustless trading of digital assets via Automated Market Makers (AMMs), replacing traditional intermediaries with deterministic smart contracts. This paper introduces a continuous-time presentvalue framework to evaluate equilibrium liquidity provision in AMMs, reconciling trading fee revenues with structural economic costs. Our framework addresses a gap between macro-tokenomics and market microstructure by introducing the token's latent convenience yield into the liquidity provider's hurdle rate-a pricing factor widely recognized in tokenomics but absent from existing AMM literature. We mathematically decompose the total economic friction into this foregone nonpecuniary utility and a microstructural adverse selection cost. We show that as transaction fees vanish, this adverse selection cost asymptotically converges to a continuous flow cost that generalizes standard Loss-Versus-Rebalancing (LVR) by explicitly penalizing the passive portfolio for forfeited directional drift and systematic tail risk. When calibrated to high-frequency ETH-USDT transaction data from Uniswap and Binance, our dynamic extension endogenously replicates the sticky, low-frequency nature of empirical mint and burn events through a statedependent no-adjustment band. Finally, we invert the equilibrium condition using our flow-form approximation to provide an empirical methodology for extracting a token's latent convenience yield directly from the net returns of active AMM pools.

title: LLMs and Systematic Measurement Error
affiliations: , , University of Oklahoma- Division of Finance and

detail.title: LLMs and Systematic Measurement Error
detail.abstract: Measures derived from Large Language Models (LLMs) are pervasive while researchers commonly treat such measures as observed data rather than generated regressors. For S&P 500 firms from 2005-2024, we show that LLM-derived measures contain non-classical measurement error driven by two distortions: omission and injection. Due to these distortions, LLM measures neglect meaningful terminology, shift meaning and reshape tone. Using the predictive content of omission and injection rates, we develop and apply a measurement error diagnostic to three settings: Item 1A risk disclosures, earnings calls, and direct-prompt measures. Measurement error is most severe for construct-style ratings of long disclosures, milder for the same constructs on shorter earnings-call texts, and substantially attenuated for direct-prompt measures, though the diagnostic reveals measurement-related contamination across all three designs.

title: The Winner's Blessing in Asset Sales
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin and University of Texas at Austin - Department of Finance

detail.title: The Winner's Blessing in Asset Sales
detail.abstract: We study the sale of operating assets when the seller retains a financial stake and privately observes how valuable the asset will be under different buyers, developing a first-price scoring auction in which allocation depends on both bids and buyer suitability. Seller discretion in allocating the asset creates two opposing bidding incentives: downward bid shading and a novel "winner's blessing," under which winning reveals favorable information about a bidder's own fit. Discretion always improves allocative efficiency but typically lowers seller payoff when bidders are few while increasing it with rising competition. Finally, disclosure eliminates the winner's blessing, weakens bidding, and therefore reduces seller payoff.

title: The Long-Term Impact of Extended Military Service on Women's Employment, Education, and Fertility

detail.title: The Long-Term Impact of Extended Military Service on Women's Employment, Education, and Fertility
detail.abstract: Military service has been found to have significant consequences for conscripts' employment, education, and other life outcomes, as it affects young people in a crucial phase of their lives. Previous research has extensively examined the impact of military service on men. However, we know little about how it may affect women. Exploiting an exogenous change in the length of women's mandatory service in Israel as a natural experiment, I estimate the long-term effect of extended military service on women's education, fertility, and labor market outcomes. At the time of the policy change, women were excluded from combat duty and fulfilled roles that resembled employment in the civilian labor market. In addition, the service required women to temporarily delay education and motherhood, focusing solely on their professional duties while serving. Thus, studying the implications of mandatory service for women offers insights into a policy that provides a full-time employment-like experience at a young age. Based on data from the 1962 and 1971 censuses, I find that each additional year of service leads to a persistent and positive impact on women's labor force participation, increasing it by 18% at age 27 and 12% at age 38. Furthermore, serving longer increases women's probability of attending higher education in the short run, but this effect vanishes over time. Finally, longer service induces women to postpone motherhood without altering their total fertility.

title: Cash Welfare Generosity, Take-Up, and Targeting: Evidence from TANF Reforms
affiliations: University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics and Korea Institute for International Economic Policy

detail.title: Cash Welfare Generosity, Take-Up, and Targeting: Evidence from TANF Reforms
detail.abstract: Many states in the U.S. have recently increased the generosity of cash welfare benefits provided through the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program. Taking advantage of the staggered implementation of benefit adjustments across states and rich administrative data, this paper studies the effects of cash welfare generosity on program applications, approval rates, caseloads, and recipient characteristics. We find that a $100 increase in maximum TANF benefits has little effect on TANF application volumes and only modest effects on application approval rates. However, it increases caseloads by 15.5% at a 12-month horizon, which an accounting exercise attributes predominantly to reduced exits from the program. Consistent with these results, we find that the observable characteristics of TANF participants are largely stable following benefit changes. Our findings suggest that higher TANF benefit generosity does not substantially undermine the program's targeting efficiency.

title: Limiting The President's Power Under The Antiquities Act Of 1906: A Monumental Endeavor

detail.title: Limiting The President's Power Under The Antiquities Act Of 1906: A Monumental Endeavor
detail.abstract: This Article examines the scope of presidential authority under the Antiquities Act of 1906, using President Clinton's 1996 designation of the 1.7-million-acre Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument as a lens for a broader historical inquiry. Tracing the Act's legislative origins and its application by presidents from Theodore Roosevelt through Clinton, the Article argues that judicial deference and congressional inaction have combined to make the President's power to unilaterally designate national monuments virtually unchecked. Courts, from <u>Cameron v. United States</u> through <u>Wyoming v. Frank</u><u>e</u>, have consistently declined to second-guess presidential determinations of what constitutes an "object of historic or scientific interest," while Congress—despite repeated efforts, including the 1997 "National Monument Fairness Act"—has been unable to enact meaningful limits on the Act's broad delegation of authority. The Article concludes that, notwithstanding significant controversy surrounding large-scale withdrawals such as Grand Staircase-Escalante and President Carter's 1978 Alaska designations, congressional correction remains the only effective check on the President's exercise of this power—a check history suggests Congress is unlikely to use.

detail.abstract: This study explores the critical intersection of environmental change and micro-level socioeconomic vulnerability by examining how climate variability, specifically relative humidity that influences household food insecurity. Focused on two climate-sensitive Indonesian provinces, Aceh and West Nusa Tenggara (NTB), the research addresses the growing phenomenon of food insecurity exacerbated by changing environmental conditions. By isolating relative humidity as a specific climate driver, this paper contributes novel empirical evidence on its micro-level impacts, filling a gap in the literature regarding how these specific climate variables affect diverse demographic segments on a massive household scale. To conduct this analysis, the study utilizes pooled microdata from the 2018 and 2024 National Socioeconomic Survey (SUSENAS), encompassing 294,919 households in Aceh and 13,424 in NTB. This extensive dataset is merged with district-level climate indicators. The researchers employ logistic regression and clustered robust regression to measure both the primary and heterogeneous effects of climate variables, rigorously controlling for a range of socio-demographic and economic factors. The empirical results consistently demonstrate that higher relative humidity significantly increases food insecurity across both provinces. Furthermore, clustered robust regression estimates reveal that this adverse effect is substantially stronger for households already experiencing high levels of food insecurity, highlighting a pronounced vulnerability. Subgroup analyses indicate that rural and male-headed households bear the brunt of these climate-induced shocks. Conversely, higher household expenditure remains the strongest predictor of food security, while education and access to basic infrastructure, such as electricity and clean water, serve as crucial mitigating factors that protect against these environmental impacts. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that rising relative humidity acts as a significant shock to household food security, disproportionately affecting already vulnerable populations. The findings underscore the urgent need for policymakers to design and implement climate-resilient rural development policies. By integrating targeted climate adaptation strategies with poverty reduction initiatives, educational access, and infrastructure improvements, policymakers can effectively bolster household resilience against future climate shocks.

title: Buying a Job, Renting a Job, No Job: The Franchise Contract from the Taxi Plate to the Robotaxi
affiliations: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney

detail.title: Buying a Job, Renting a Job, No Job: The Franchise Contract from the Taxi Plate to the Robotaxi
detail.abstract: Riders in San Francisco pay a premium to travel with no driver, and within two years the robotaxi passed the second-ranked human network. This paper reads that event, and a century of the market for rides, through one linear contract whose unobservable effort is search for the next fare and whose observable is Krueger's capacity-utilisation measure. A single threshold in risk cost per unit of matching quality determines whether the optimiser sells a majority claim for a fee or hires a minority claimant. The industry's fixed daily lease is the contract's first-best form-the operator keeps the full meter, all extraction sits in the fee-so the medallion era's distortions were the entry quota and the dispatch technology, never the contract, which survives across much of Europe. Uber is the new medallion owner, leasing the meter by the minute: perfect flexibility, priced at a royalty near one halfthe revenue peak once the legal corner welds the fixed payment to zero, the classification boundary itself, and the split at which the Australian bailment settled a century earlier. Free entry makes utilisation, not earnings, the equilibrating variable, explaining Cramer and Krueger's invariant fifty percent; the royalty passes through to outlet workers, explaining Krueger's company-owned wage premium. The robotaxi ends the story: a central planner of search that cannot shirk or park, returning the industry to company ownership and pricing the departed monopsony rent in the gap between the human take and the robot take.

title: Housing + Health + Wealth: The Community Capital Flywheel

detail.title: Housing + Health + Wealth: The Community Capital Flywheel

detail.abstract: This paper argues that the dominant model of institutional real estate development-in which capital is deployed into communities, returns are extracted by distant investors, and residents remain perpetual renters-is both economically inefficient and socially corrosive over long time horizons. We present an alternative framework: the Community Capital Flywheel, operationalized through a Build-to-Rent-to-Own (B2R2O) development model, in which the deliberate architecture of mission-aligned capital creates measurable, compounding returns across three interlocked dimensions: housing stability, population health outcomes, and household wealth formation. The flywheel is powered by a stacked capital structure that pairs institutional investment with patient, below-market sources-philanthropic program-related investments, public credit enhancements, civic land dispositions, and mission-driven subordinate debt-each matched to its appropriate return expectation and aligned to the delivery of community benefit rather than its extraction. We argue that cities, community lenders, foundations, and mission investors already possess the tools to build this architecture. What has been missing is the policy and structural framework to deploy them in concert. We conclude with a framework for how these institutions can co-design capital and policy structures that accelerate asset transfer to residents, reduce long-term public service burden, and create durable, place-based belonging in the communities most in need of stabilization.

title: Comparing Fertilizer, Biofuel, and Transportation Channels in Energy-to-Cereal Price Transmission: Evidence from Time-Varying Connectedness and Partial Wavelet Coherence

detail.title: Comparing Fertilizer, Biofuel, and Transportation Channels in Energy-to-Cereal Price Transmission: Evidence from Time-Varying Connectedness and Partial Wavelet Coherence
detail.abstract: This study examines how energy-price movements are transmitted to cereal prices through fertilizer, biofuel, and transportation channels. Using monthly data on crude oil, natural gas, ethanol, urea, the Baltic Dry Index, and cereal prices, we combine TVP-VAR frequency connectedness analysis with partial wavelet coherence analysis. The principal contribution is to make the three channels directly comparable within a unified econometric framework in terms of their time-varying transmission strength, direction, persistence, and frequency structure. The results show that the energy–food price nexus is not a simple one-way process from energy to food markets. In the broader system, crude oil and cereal prices are the main net transmitters of shocks, whereas urea and ethanol prices are primarily net receivers. Although natural gas prices transmit shocks to urea prices, stronger feedback from cereal prices to urea prices indicates that the fertilizer channel does not follow a simple NatGas → Urea → Cereals sequence. The biofuel channel is characterized by strong oil–ethanol and ethanol–cereal linkages, while the transportation channel, represented by the Baltic Dry Index, is weaker and more episodic. Partial wavelet coherence results show that fertilizer and biofuel linkages are more pronounced over medium- to long-term horizons, suggesting delayed and persistent adjustment. These findings support integrated monitoring of energy, fertilizer, biofuel, transportation, and cereal markets when designing food-price stabilization policies.

title: Hierarchical Risk Parity Variants for Cryptocurrency Portfolios: Denoising, Detoning, Tail Dependence, Embeddings, and Statistical Inference, 2020–2026
affiliations: , Universidad del CEMA and UCEMA

detail.title: Hierarchical Risk Parity Variants for Cryptocurrency Portfolios: Denoising, Detoning, Tail Dependence, Embeddings, and Statistical Inference, 2020–2026

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose. This research received no external funding and was conducted as part of the authors' academic work at Universidad del CEMA.

detail.abstract:
We extend the 2025 conference study on Hierarchical Risk Parity (HRP) by addressing its two stated methodological follow-ups (Marchenko-Pastur denoising and spectral detoning) and by evaluating a broader cross-section of portfolio construction choices on a survivorship-bias-corrected, point-in-time Binance universe (146 ever-included symbols, 2020-2026). The comparison includes 27 constructed strategies spanning HRP-family variants, risk-based allocators, nested-clustering optimisers, momentum rules, and signal-aware extensions.

Across 76 monthly rebalances, the HRP-family variants remain tightly clustered in risk-adjusted performance (annualised Sharpe 0.69-0.75), and this result persists under a 547-cell hyperparameter sweep (combined Hansen Superior Predictive Ability (SPA) consistent p-value of 0.91). Strategies that alter the allocation step produce larger dispersion (notably the Minimum Variance Portfolio (MVP), the Correlation-Regularised Iterative Shrinkage Portfolio (CRISP), the Nested Clustered Optimization with CRISP allocation (NCO-CRISP), and Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO)), with CRISP and NCO-CRISP significant in pairwise Ledoit-Wolf tests versus baseline HRP in both full and post-COVID windows. However, after accounting for multiple comparisons, the headline SPA does not reject (consistent p-value of 0.51), and the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) is directionally consistent with that conclusion.

Post-COVID results indicate strong regime sensitivity: diversified HRP variants lose 51-64% of capital while Bitcoin (BTC) and BTC-concentrating allocators hold up better. We also revise an earlier interpretation on cluster stability: over the full panel, Pearson-based clustering is more stable than lower-tail dependence at monthly frequency. Overall, the evidence supports a cautious interpretation: within this universe, horizon, and search space, allocation choices are more strongly associated with performance differences than clustering perturbations, but those edges remain statistically fragile under search-adjusted inference.

title: Does What Goes Up Come Back Down? Pass-Through of Fuel-Tax Cuts and Increases in Korea​
affiliations: Korea Energy Economics Institute,  and Korea Energy Economics Institute

detail.title: Does What Goes Up Come Back Down? Pass-Through of Fuel-Tax Cuts and Increases in Korea​
detail.abstract: Temporary fuel-tax cuts are meant to cushion oil-price spikes, but their reversals determine whether relief creates a firm-favorable ratchet. We study Korea, where registered stations post tax-exempt prices for the same gasoline and diesel sold to certified agricultural and fishery users. In the full OPINET price-disclosure panel, these exempt prices provide a contemporaneous within-product control for common cost shocks; exact within-station matches provide a stricter validation sample concentrated in rural, less competitive markets. Across two cuts and two restorations directly estimated from 2018 to 2021, impact pass-through is incomplete, about 0.55 on the value-added-tax-inclusive posted-price benchmark, and rises over subsequent weeks. Nationally, cuts and increases pass through at comparable rates, clean-event comparisons are consumer-favorable, and sensitivity analysis rules out a firm-favorable asymmetry as large as those documented for value-added tax changes. Market structure affects the level, not the direction, of pass-through: thinner markets pass through less, but the competition gradient is similar for cuts and restorations. Applying preferred full-sample estimates to the 2018-2022 value-added-tax-inclusive fiscal base implies that about 39% of KRW 9.74 trillion did not reach consumers; the share rises to about 47% in the exact matched low-competition scenario. Temporary fuel-tax cycles therefore do not create a large hidden ratchet to firms, but tax cuts remain materially and spatially leaky relative to targeted transfers.

title: The Cornerstone of Law: Diagnosis and Treatment of the Sports Domain

detail.title: The Cornerstone of Law: Diagnosis and Treatment of the Sports Domain
detail.abstract:
This article applies the spirit of law – the conviction that substantive justice is the source and telos of all institutional life, while procedural justice is its instrument – to the domain of sport. The central thesis is that the spirit of law is the professional spirit that guides legal procedure to evolve continuously with dynamic, complex reality; this is the total basis of all legal regulation. It is also the necessity by which law maintains human society from collapse: procedural justice must always follow substantive justice, continuously changing its own boundaries of capability and cognition to adapt to complex reality.

When the governance framework of sport fails to evolve, the result is alienation: the institutional shell persists, but its substance has departed. Drawing on three foundational legal-theoretic principles – the isomorphic evolution thesis, the distinction between legitimacy and validity, and the Radbruch formula – the article diagnoses short track speed skating in granular detail, prescribes a graded penal code and a Care Rule requiring offenders to personally attend the rehabilitation of those they have injured, then extends the diagnosis to all sports. The argument holds that only through this legal-spirit-driven institutional evolution can sport truly maintain its spirit, protect athletic honour, and safeguard every athlete's physical and mental health – otherwise sport becomes something that looks beautiful on the surface but has no reason to exist.

title: Valuing Residential Power Outages in Selected Regions of China: Evidence on Willingness to Pay and the Value of Lost Load
affiliations: Dongbei University of Finance and Economics, University of Oulu - Department of Economics, Accounting and Finance and Dongbei University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Valuing Residential Power Outages in Selected Regions of China: Evidence on Willingness to Pay and the Value of Lost Load
detail.abstract: Power outages impose non-market welfare losses on households, including reduced comfort, disruptions to daily activities, and interruptions to information and communication services. These effects are not adequately captured by using output losses or direct costs alone. Using residential choice experiment data from selected regions of China, this study estimates willingness to pay (WTP) through conditional Logit, mixed Logit, and mixed Logit models with socio-economic interactions, and converts the resulting  estimates into the value of lost load (VOLL) using the corresponding energy not supplied (ENS) denominator. Under the preferred mixed Logit specification with socio-economic interactions and a fixed price coefficient, the marginal WTP for reducing an outage by one minute at durations of 20, 60, 240, and 540 minutes in the peak/weekday/non-summer benchmark scenario is 0.2001, 0.0667, 0.0167, and 0.0074 CNY, respectively. The corresponding region-weighted marginal VOLL estimates are 37.02, 12.34, 3.08, and 1.37 CNY/kWh, indicating a declining pattern as outage duration increases. Both marginal and duration-reduction  estimates show that the unit value of shortening an outage depends on  the welfare change and the associated ENS denominator. Individual-level WTP distributions and latent class results reveal substantial preference heterogeneity within the sample. Residential VOLL varies across outage scenarios,  WTP measures, and the ENS denominator. The results provide  scenario-specific evidence for households represented in the survey rather than a single national VOLL parameter. These findings can inform reliability regulation, evaluation of outage-duration improvements, and investment decisions in electricity distribution networks.

title: Identifying Promising Global Solidarity Levies for Financing the Low-Carbon Transition
affiliations: University of Tokyo, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Università Bocconi, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Bruegel

detail.title: Identifying Promising Global Solidarity Levies for Financing the Low-Carbon Transition
detail.abstract: The growing climate-finance gap has renewed interest in Global Solidarity Levies (GSLs) as potential sources of international climate finance. While numerous levy proposals have emerged, comparatively little attention has been devoted to how candidate levies should be identified and compared. This paper develops a framework for identifying promising Global Solidarity Levies based on two characteristics of their underlying tax bases: international production and international mobility. Applying the framework to a broad universe of proposed levies highlights international aviation and maritime shipping taxes as particularly promising candidates for further investigation. The paper then evaluates these candidates through an assessment of their institutional context, implementation pathways, and revenue potential. To support coalition-based climate finance, it introduces a revenue simulator designed to estimate revenues under alternative tax rates, behavioural assumptions, and participation scenarios. Designed for active use by policymakers and negotiators, the simulator is conceived as a negotiation and coalition-building instrument that allows policymakers to explore the implications of alternative levy designs and coalition structures. Simulation results suggest that levies on international aviation and maritime shipping could generate substantial revenues under a wide range of assumptions, with coalition-based arrangements capable of mobilizing significant resources even without universal participation. By providing both an identification framework and an evaluation tool, the paper contributes to ongoing discussions on innovative climate finance, climate clubs, and coalition-based approaches to international cooperation.

title: Prediction Without Priors: Kolmogorov's Urn
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and

detail.title: Prediction Without Priors: Kolmogorov's Urn
detail.abstract: Dreassi et al. (2026) warn against two confusions: mistaking a rule for assigning conditional laws for the data generating mechanism (M1), and over-reading asymptotic exchangeability (M2). Both confusions are real. Both are artifacts of insisting on a prior. We give a purely predictive account, in Kolmogorov's combinatorial spirit, in which no prior appears and neither confusion can be stated. Finite exchangeability is exactly a two-part code: name the type, then index within the type class. The Heath-Sudderth kernel is the uniform distribution on that class, so the urn whose composition is drawn before the sampling begins is also the model set of a Kolmogorov two-part description-the sense in which the urn is Kolmogorov's. Cover's structure function draws this for a Bernoulli sequence and for the Mona Lisa: the model is the painting, the index is the varnish, and one does not ask whether a description of the Mona Lisa is the Mona Lisa. The chain rule turns the law of a sequence into the accumulated logloss of its one-step predictives, and the Shannon-McMillan-Breiman theorem-applied to an exchangeable source, which is stationary but not ergodic-shows that this accumulated loss converges almost surely to the entropy of the directing measure. The de Finetti parameter is therefore an observable: a tail-measurable functional of the loss trajectory, not a posited object. M1 dissolves. At second order the prior reappears, but as a code: equalizing regret forces the Jeffreys weighting, which for a Bernoulli source is the arcsine law Be(1 2 , 1 2)-the Krichevsky-Trofimov add-one-half rule, and the shrinkage profile of the horseshoe. We then reinterpret all eight of the authors' examples. Their flagship Example 7 admits a one-line diagnosis: the covariance (n + i)/(n + j) depends on a ratio, not a lag, so the sequence is stationary in log n and not in n. It is an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process on the wrong clock. All four pathologies the authors list follow, and Xn ⇒ N (0, 2 3).

detail.abstract: Purpose: Differentiable causal discovery methods ignore curated domain regulatory knowledge and underperform in high-dimensional, small-sample transcriptomic data. This Methodology paper proposes a universal prior-regularized computational framework that injects pairwise domain priors into gradient-based DAG learning for stable graph recovery in data-limited regimes. Methods: Prior-regularized causal discovery augments the NOTEARS objective with a penalty λ p ∥W-W prior ∥ 2 F , where W prior encodes pairwise interactions from TRRUST and STRING (combined score > 900). The framework supports three backbones (NOTEARS, DAGMA, GOLEM). Validation includes DepMap CRISPR co-essentiality screening (1,208 genes × 18,531 cell lines) and GO enrichment (7,992 cancer-associated genes). Results: On synthetic Erdős-Rényi DAGs across six dimensions (d ∈ {30, 50, 80, 100, 150, 200}) with partial prior coverage (α ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7}), prior-regularized NOTEARS improves F1 in 15 of 24 configurations, with 98% relative gain at d = 30 (F1: 0.046 → 0.090) and a mean ∆F1 of 0.014 across all dimensions. The STRING prior achieves 100% coverage of TCGA cancer gene sets (mean 138 entries per d = 200 set, vs 21% for TRRUST). Consensus STRING analysis identifies TP53 (282 partners) and ribosomal ubiquitin proteins as dominant hubs anchoring prior-guided discovery. Conclusions: The framework enables causal discovery to leverage existing biological knowledge rather than rediscovering it, yielding the largest improvements where baseline performance is weakest. The methodology is database-agnostic, backbone-agnostic, fully reproducible, and applicable to any domain with curated pairwise knowledge.

title: To What Extent Has the French Government’s Implementation of Price Caps on Energy Been Effective in Reducing Inflation in France Since 2020?

detail.title: To What Extent Has the French Government’s Implementation of Price Caps on Energy Been Effective in Reducing Inflation in France Since 2020?

detail.abstract: The sharp increase in energy prices following the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russia–Ukraine conflict contributed significantly to inflation across Europe, prompting governments to adopt a range of policy interventions. France responded by implementing the Bouclier Tarifaire (Tariff Shield), a package of energy price caps and subsidies designed to protect households and businesses from escalating electricity and natural gas costs. This paper evaluates the effectiveness of these measures in reducing inflation in France since 2020. Using secondary data from government publications, the Banque de France, the OECD, the International Monetary Fund, and other reputable sources, the study analyzes inflation trends, energy prices, and macroeconomic indicators. The analysis applies the theories of cost-push inflation, demand-pull inflation, and the Quantity Theory of Money to examine the relationship between energy prices and overall price levels. The findings indicate that the French government's energy price caps were effective in moderating short-term inflationary pressures, protecting household purchasing power, and limiting the rise in the Consumer Price Index relative to several other European economies. However, the policy also imposed substantial fiscal costs and may create long-term challenges, including market distortions, reduced incentives for energy producers, and increased public expenditure. Overall, the paper concludes that France's energy price caps were an effective short-term inflation mitigation measure but are unlikely to constitute a sustainable long-term solution to inflation driven by structural energy market shocks.

title: International Capital Mobility and Covid-Era Capital Shocks
affiliations: Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies

detail.title: International Capital Mobility and Covid-Era Capital Shocks
detail.abstract: Theoretically, countries with greater international capital mobility should be more likely to experience a capital shock, especially following a major crisis such as Covid-19, and in this essay I empirically investigate the relationship between international capital mobility and sudden stops and surges in portfolio flows. In general, I find that the primary effect of capital mobility reduces the probability of a stop in portfolio debt flows and a surge in equities. However, this effect is offset by a country's risk premium, as proxied by the difference between a country's central bank policy interest rate and the U.S. federal funds rate. These empirical results imply that a capital management policy designed to minimize the probability of a sudden stop or surge in portfolio flows while maintaining access to international markets should focus on reducing the country's risk premium rather than imposing additional capital controls.

detail.abstract: This paper backtests three Value-at-Risk (VaR) models-Historical Simulation, Parametric (Normal), and Student-t-hold up when tested against S&P 500 daily returns covering January 2018 through December 2024. That seven-year run features four distinct market backdrops: the tail end of pre-COVID growth, the 2020 COVID-19 plunge and quick recovery, the bear market sparked by Fed rate hikes in 2022, and the rebound of 2023-2024. Lots of classic backtesting work just calibrates a VaR model once over a fixed period and then checks how it did, but that's not the approach here. Instead, this study uses a walk-forward design. Each model is recalibrated every day with the previous 250 trading days-and then checked against the next day's actual return. That gives us 1,509 out-of-sample forecast days between January 2019 and December 2024. To judge the models, three big backtesting tests get used: Kupiec's Proportion of Failures test (1995), Christoffersen's Conditional Coverage test (1998), and the Basel Committee Traffic Light test. All these fits under the SR 11-7 model-risk-management framework, which was the rule of the land until the Fed's April 2026 switch to SR 26-2. The results aren't just a clear "winner" vs "loser"-things are more nuanced. At the tough 99% confidence level, all three models formally miss unconditional coverage, but the gap is wide across them. The Parametric Normal model is the worst offender by far (44 violations, LR = 36.92, p < 0.0001), while Historical Simulation (26 violations; LR = 6.55) and Student-t (28 violations; LR = 8.91) get much closer to what you'd want. But it doesn't stop there-violation clustering seems everywhere. All models fail the Christoffersen independence test at 95%, and only Student-t barely manages independence at 99% (p = 0.107). Its conditional-coverage test still rejects, though, thanks to coverage shortfall. Breaking down subperiods, the grinding 2022 rate-hiking regime shakes up violation clustering more than the sharper COVID shock did, implying these gradual shifts are harder for fixed-window estimators to follow than abrupt ones. On the final 250 days, none make it into Basel's Green zone anymore. The takeaway? Clustering during regime shifts is baked into fixed-window VaR estimation-it's not something you fix just by ditching the Normal distribution. This matters for SR 11-7 model validation, and, after SR 11-7's replacement with SR 26-2, for how the new rules put more emphasis on materiality in model supervision.

detail.abstract:
Background: Diabetes mellitus is rising rapidly across low- and middle-income countries, yet early detection in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) remains limited. Context-specific, non-laboratory risk-screening tools could support community case finding. We aimed to develop and validate simplified diabetes risk-prediction models for SSA, with some focus on Malawi and young adult populations.

Methods: We pooled WHO STEPwise (STEPS) survey data from nine African countries totalling 47,594 participants. After harmonisation though, complete-case analytic sample comprised 31,625 adults aged 18-69 years. Eighteen models ranging from logistic and penalised regression, discriminant analysis, tree-based methods, k-nearest neighbours, support-vector machines and a neural network were trained on a stratified 70/15/15 split with five-fold cross-validation. The primary metric was the area under the ROC curve (AUC).

Findings: Pooled diabetes prevalence was 11.0%. Gradient boosting achieved the best discrimination (test AUC = 0.701), seconded by logistic regression (0.698). Support-vector machines (0.518) and k-nearest neighbours (0.653) performed worst. Age and BMI were the dominant predictors, followed by diet, education and salt intake. Performance fell markedly in adults under 40 (best AUC ≈ 0.61). Adding waist circumference and hypertension raised the AUC by 0.11 on the subset with complete clinical data. For Malawi, logistic regression performed best (cross-validated AUC = 0.645).

Interpretation: Simplified, non-laboratory risk models can support diabetes screening in SSA, performing comparably to some established tools. Accuracy was modest especially in younger adults. Incorporating waist circumference, hypertension and family history, alongside external validation, could improve performance and enable integration into community and primary-care screening.

title: Hearsay in High Definition: Body-Worn Cameras and the Future of Intimate Partner Violence Prosecutions

detail.title: Hearsay in High Definition: Body-Worn Cameras and the Future of Intimate Partner Violence Prosecutions
detail.abstract: Technological advances in police responses to intimate partner violence (IPV) have outpaced evidentiary hearsay rules. Specifically, the rapid adoption of body-worn cameras (BWCs), fueled by racial justice and police reform advocates, has produced previously unavailable, vivid, and timely recordings of IPV victims' accounts of abuse. Unfortunately, state and federal rules governing hearsay often prevent juries from considering these out-of-court statements. Such restrictions carry particular force in IPV cases, where victims frequently recant or decline to testify at trial due to abuser manipulation or distrust of the criminal justice system. Courts and legislatures have eased some evidentiary restrictions in IPV cases in recognition of the persistent problem of victim nonparticipation. Nevertheless, existing doctrine has not fully addressed how hearsay rules should apply to victims' statements captured on BWCs in IPV investigations. This Article offers two proposals to close that gap. First, courts should interpret existing hearsay exemptions, including prior inconsistent statements, excited utterances, and statements of identification, to more readily encompass accounts of IPV victims recorded on BWCs. Second, legislators should enact a specific hearsay exception designed to admit these recordings. Together, the two reforms allow evidentiary doctrine to appropriately modernize with the burgeoning use of BWCs in IPV prosecutions.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence companions capable of simulating romantic attachment, emotional intimacy, and quasi-marital relationships are challenging the conceptual foundations of marriage law. This article examines the growing divergence between statutory definitions of marriage, which presuppose reciprocal legal capacity between natural persons, and the emergence of sustained human relationships with emotionally responsive AI systems. It argues that existing legal frameworks, including family law, consumer protection, data protection, and product liability, regulate only isolated aspects of this phenomenon while failing to address its broader institutional consequences. Using a comparative methodology encompassing the United States, the European Union, China, Japan, Brazil, and the Council of Europe, the article analyzes legislation, judicial decisions, regulatory enforcement, and interdisciplinary scholarship on parasocial attachment, digisexuality, and algorithmic governance. The analysis demonstrates an emerging international consensus that emotionally simulative AI presents distinctive governance risks, despite substantial divergence in regulatory strategies. Building upon these findings, the article proposes a Marital Substitution Governance Framework, integrating mandatory disclosure of dependency risks, fiduciary obligations for companion-AI providers, product-liability principles, and a narrowly tailored doctrine of non-recognition of human-AI marriages. Rather than asking whether machines can marry, the article reframes the legal inquiry around how law should regulate technologies that increasingly perform the social, emotional, and psychological functions historically associated with human spouses. It concludes that the future of marriage law will depend less on recognizing artificial partners than on governing the institutions that design, market, and monetize synthetic intimacy.

detail.abstract: Responding to the rise of hydraulic fracturing (HF) and risks to water quality, U.S. states mandated disclosure for HF wells. We study whether and how such targeting of corporate externalities with transparency regulation reduces environmental impact. We examine salt concentrations considered HF signatures and find significant reductions in surface water impact between 9-14%, mostly along the intensive margin. Consistent with that we document improvements in operator practices, including fewer wastewater spills. We unpack the transparency mechanism and show that transparency regulation enables social movements and increases public pressure, which in turn drives the documented changes in practices and water quality.

detail.title: Debt Heterogeneity and Leverage Measurement: The Role of Operating Leases
detail.abstract: Empirical work on capital structure typically treats debt as homogeneous. This paper examines that assumption by focusing on operating leases. Using data for U.S. firms from 2012–2023, I show that operating lease obligations constitute a substantial proportion of corporate debt and that firms substitute between operating leases, bank debt and public debt in ways that do not preserve leverage. Operating lease intensity is strongly negatively associated with the leverage gap (actual minus target leverage). A one standard deviation increase in operating lease intensity is associated with a 6–8% reduction in the leverage gap, suggesting that firms with greater reliance on operating leases appear under-levered under conventional leverage measures. These findings imply that aggregate leverage measures may omit information contained in debt composition. The analysis spans the pre- and post-ASC 842 periods, allowing operating lease liabilities to be measured consistently and validated against recognised lease liabilities.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how large-scale computing infrastructure investment shapes the functional distribution of income between labor and capital. Using China's “East Data, West Computing” initiative as a quasi-natural experiment, we exploit the geographic designation of eight national computing power hubs in a difference-in-differences design. We find that the initiative significantly increases labor income share, with gains driven entirely by non-executive employees and accompanied by a reduction in the within-firm pay gap. Three mechanisms account for this effect:technological advancement, financial facilitation, and human capital upgrading.Firms experiencing larger increases in labor income share further exhibit greater innovation, lower employee turnover, and higher employee productivity. Our findingsestablish computing infrastructure as a novel determinant of labor income share.

title: "Reconfiguring Land Governance in Jammu and Kashmir Post Independence"

detail.title: "Reconfiguring Land Governance in Jammu and Kashmir Post Independence"
detail.abstract:
Land has historically been constituted as one of the most complex and politically sensitive dimensions of governance in India, significantly influencing agricultural productivity, livelihoods, social equity, and economic development. Despite successive legislative and administrative reforms, challenges relating to land ownership, tenure security, and administration continue to shape policy reform debates. Within this broader landscape, Jammu and Kashmir presents a particularly significant case, owing to its distinctive trajectory in land governance since the pre-Independence period. During the Dogra rule, land ownership was characterized by highly concentrated estates, exploitative tenancy arrangements, and deeply unequal agrarian relations due to the benefits being usurped by the intermediary class comprising Jagirdars, Muafidars, and Chakdars, leaving cultivators with limited ownership rights and economic security. In the post-Independence period, the agrarian reforms introduced under the leadership of Sheikh Abdullah fundamentally transformed this structure by abolishing intermediary landlordism, redistributing land to the actual tillers, and establishing one of India's most comprehensive land-to-the-tiller regimes. These reforms were subsequently reinforced more strongly by the constitutional protections available under Articles 370 and 35A, which enabled the continuation of a region-specific land governance framework for several decades.

However, the abrogation of Articles 370 and 35A through the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act (2019) marked a significant departure from this historical framework through the restructuring of land laws, ownership regulations, and administrative institutions governing land in the current Union Territory. While these reforms have been justified on the grounds of economic integration, broader investment opportunities, administrative uniformity, and enabling national development, they have also raised important policy concerns relating to agricultural land tenure security, administrative discretion, changing land ownership patterns, and the long-term protection of cultivators' rights. Against this backdrop, the policy brief identifies the erosion of agricultural land tenure security as the primary policy challenge in the UT, which subsequently has led to land-related disputes, opportunities for fraudulent transactions, and declining confidence in public institutions. Drawing upon constitutional provisions, legislative instruments, government notifications, academic literature, and policy reports, the brief traces the historical evolution of the region's land governance, evaluates the implications of the post 2019 reforms through a stakeholder-centered framework, and proposes a phased three-pillar reform package comprising GPS-based cadastral demarcation, conclusive state-guaranteed land titling, and voluntary dematerialisation of land records to strengthen legal certainty, reduce land-related disputes, enhance administrative efficiency, and promote equitable and sustainable land governance.

title: Production of Commodities by Means of Parts: Generative Structures, Modules, and Productive Possibilities

detail.title: Production of Commodities by Means of Parts: Generative Structures, Modules, and Productive Possibilities
detail.abstract: Production theory records feasible input-output quantities. This paper develops a generative representation beneath that record. A commodity is defined as a structured functional object, and production is represented by directed generative structures that transform parts, operations, and knowledge into modules and final commodities. The paper defines generative length, minimal generative complexity, organizational gain, socially normal recipes, and execution labels. It proves that the standard production set is a projection of generative production space, that this projection loses dynamic information about future productive possibilities, and that recipe-space productivity improvements admit an exact mechanism decomposition.

detail.abstract:
Organizations increasingly rely on experimentation to navigate uncertainty. Yet scholars know little about how repeated experimentation becomes an enduring adaptive capability. This study addresses that gap. It examines how teams govern learning, rather than merely enact it, as they search for viable products and business models under uncertainty.

This study uses a two-phase qualitative design set within a highly structured experimentation environment, the U.S. National Science Foundation I-CORPS™ program. Phase 1 analyzes 40 semi-structured interviews through the Gioia methodology. Phase 2 triangulates nine complete cases using interviews, surveys, business model canvases, and archival artifacts.

The analysis yields an Input–Moderator–Process–Output (IMPO) model. In the model, founding mental models and contextual moderators shape an experimentation-as-search process. That process produces two distinct outputs: learning and behavioral, and venture value. Some teams move beyond single- and double-loop learning. They deliberately revise the rules that govern experimentation by redefining evidence thresholds, decision rights, and reflective practices. These revisions signal triple-loop learning and the formation of an adaptive capability.

The study introduces learning governance as a distinct construct and positions it as a microfoundation of dynamic capabilities. It explains how experimentation becomes a compoundable capability rather than a series of isolated tests. The model also travels beyond new ventures. It applies to corporate innovation teams, artificial intelligence implementation teams, deep-tech ventures, and biotechnology and medical technology firms, where organizations likewise govern experimentation under uncertainty.

detail.abstract:
Hong Kong built a complete legal and tax framework for sukuk more than a decade ago, and its
government issued three US dollar sukuk between 2014 and 2017. Yet no Hong Kong-listed
enterprise has issued a sukuk from Hong Kong, and the market has stayed dormant. This paper
argues that conditions have now changed in a way that earlier studies could not anticipate.
Global sukuk issuance reached a record US$264.8 billion in 2025, and outstanding ESG sukuk are
expected to exceed US$70 billion by the end of 2026. Hong Kong has meanwhile assembled a
green finance infrastructure that no Islamic finance centre matches: a sustainable finance
taxonomy extended to transition activities in January 2026, subsidy schemes for green and digital
bond issuance, and three sovereign tokenised green bonds, the latest a record HK$10 billion issue.
The paper examines Hong Kong's green sukuk opportunity through the lens of the First Five-Year
Plan for Economic and Social Development (2026–2030), whose consultation document promotes
green finance and Middle East engagement but does not mention Islamic finance. It identifies three
differentiators for Hong Kong: a common law system suited to the true-sale requirement of the
forthcoming AAOIFI Shariah Standard No. 62, proven tokenisation infrastructure, and the
offshore renminbi market. It then sets out a practical issuance playbook for Hong Kong-listed
enterprises and assesses the implications for the Hong Kong banking industry.
The paper argues that the convergence of regulatory reform, digital bond infrastructure, growing
Gulf connectivity and the First Five-Year Plan creates a policy window that did not previously
exist. It concludes with policy recommendations framed as a contribution to the Five-Year Plan
consultation.

detail.abstract:
Transition risk descends through a system, from capital, through portfolios, supply chains and markets, to the entities and communities at the end of the chain. It transmits as concentrated force from a few large nodes. This paper argues that the same architecture carries readiness in the opposite direction, and that the long tail of at-risk entities, the bulk of any value chain, is not peripheral to that reversal but its load-bearing structure. The proposition that value concentrates in a long tail of smaller actors rather than a short head of large ones has an established lineage: Anderson (2006) showed how falling distribution and coordination costs shift aggregate value toward many low-volume nodes. The readiness argument applies the same economics to transition capacity: as the cost of reaching and enabling small suppliers falls, the readiness of the tail becomes material and addressable. The thesis here is narrower and testable, specifying where in the tail readiness begins and what moves it. The architecture is shared in both directions but the mechanism is not: risk descends as concentrated force, while readiness ascends only by aggregation. From this the central position follows: the systemic risk institutions treat as diversifiable in fact resides in the long tail, so engaging it is not corporate charity but the management of an institution's own exposure. 

The paper's methodological contribution is four design principles for engaging the most constrained participant, their strength resting on convergence from two independent vantages, both grounded in practice. They emerge from the author's transformation work across many companies and fifty-two countries, and independently from years inside Google's Next Billion Users group, distilled by a practitioner co-author; they are corroborated by anti-deficit scholarship, which frames constrained populations by their capabilities, not their lacks. Applied through existing conduits, under trusted partners, with participant value visible and the architecture built to adapt, the principles reverse the cascade. What separates a just reversal from extraction is ownership of the value: the readiness, and the co-benefit dividend it earns, accrue at the long tail first, while the institutions above gain through the reduction of their own systemic exposure. WP-01 and WP-05 measure the exposure; this paper describes the architecture by which it is reversed.

title: Demystifying Mechanical Intelligence: "Autolligence" (A.L.) and the Illusion of Artificial Intelligence (A.I.) in Contemporary Education

detail.title: Demystifying Mechanical Intelligence: "Autolligence" (A.L.) and the Illusion of Artificial Intelligence (A.I.) in Contemporary Education
detail.abstract: The text critically examines contemporary Artificial Intelligence as a historical and ideological continuation of the industrial organisation of education, psychometrics, and techno-administrative control. Its central argument is that current algorithmic systems do not possess genuine intelligence, intention, or consciousness, but rather operate as mechanisms of statistical recombination of data; for this reason, the term Autolligence is proposed as a more accurate designation. Using a historico-hermeneutic approach, the paper traces the genealogy of these mechanisms from the factory-school model and teaching machines to learning and assessment systems based on standardisation, quantification, and algorithmic classification. It further argues that the integration of AI into education tends to reduce pedagogical autonomy, intensify surveillance, homogenise creativity, and reproduce inequalities. As an alternative, the paper advances a critical, biocentric pedagogical perspective, termed critical enbiagogy, which seeks to reconnect learning with living, communal, and non-anthropocentric forms of knowledge and practise.

title: Trading on Information versus Trading on Control in Event-contingent Markets

detail.title: Trading on Information versus Trading on Control in Event-contingent Markets
detail.abstract: Event-contingent markets trade claims on outcomes (court rulings, mergers, elections, platform-resolved events) that some traders can move, not merely forecast. This paper develops an equilibrium theory of this moral hazard, in which exposure precedes action and trades change the world. With rational dealers, an invariance theorem holds: trading intensity, informativeness, and calibration are unaffected by causal power, which is priced as an identified premium while hedgers finance unbounded real distortion. Manipulation pays only under mechanical liquidity or hidden power. Causal power is derived from governance, organized by a causal Gram matrix, and regulated best by severing feedback, not policing information.

title: When Peak Usage Becomes Capacity: Optimal Charging of Battery Swapping Stations Under Demand Charges

detail.title: When Peak Usage Becomes Capacity: Optimal Charging of Battery Swapping Stations Under Demand Charges
detail.abstract: Battery swapping stations provide a promising alternative for rapid electric vehicle (EV) refueling, but their charging operations must coordinate stochastic demand, renewable energy availability, battery degradation, and demand charge tariffs. We formulate the charging problem of a renewable-integrated station as a finite-horizon dynamic program and uncover a fundamental cost-capacity tradeoff: while peak grid usage level incurs demand charges, it also creates reusable charging capacity that can benefit future operations. We analytically characterize the optimal single-period charging policy and establish a two-threshold structure that separates aggressive, economic, and conservative charging regimes. This structural result provides a mathematical explanation for why optimal charging decisions can be non-monotone in the peak usage level and even exceed a no-demand-charge benchmark. To address the curse of dimensionality in multi-period settings, we leverage these structural insights to develop structure-informed heuristics and a structure-guided reinforcement learning policy. Using a case study of a NIO battery swapping station in the Netherlands, we quantify the financial impact of ignoring demand charges and demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed policies in improving operational performance.

detail.abstract: This Article argues that the critical minerals transition is increasingly governed through an "ESG truth-machine": traceability platforms, certification, vendor risk-scoring, automated audit triage, and, increasingly, generative systems that produce sustainability narratives from partial and asymmetric data. EU and transnational regimes present these techniques as technocratic solutions to supply-chain opacity. International legal scholarship, however, has been slower to treat AI-enabled compliance infrastructures as part of what due diligence is, rather than as implementation detail. The result is a structural mismatch between the normative aims of due diligence (prevention, mitigation, remedy) and the mechanisms firms use to demonstrate compliance (datafication, scoring, and disclosure optimization). Drawing on the growing empirical literature on due diligence implementation and on the EU's converging due diligence, reporting, batteries, critical raw materials, and AI instruments, the Article advances three doctrinal claims. First, disclosure regimes can manufacture credibility while hollowing out responsibility, enabling algorithmic greenwashing unless law disciplines the methods that produce ESG claims (provenance, assumptions, and contestability), not only their outputs. Second, compliance technologies can themselves generate adverse impacts, so dignity and equality constraints must attach to the tools that perform due diligence. Third, sustainability that ignores fiscal contribution risks legitimacy without redistribution: in extractives, tax practices shape state capacity, and state capacity is a precondition for environmental and labor governance. The Article also addresses the interstate dimension of these regimes, which producer states have contested as instruments of country-level exclusion, and closes with an architectural agenda for "algorithmic due diligence" centered on an ESG evidence chain, rightsrespecting technology governance, and fiscal coherence.

detail.abstract: This article examines the jurisprudence of the Bombay High Court on the unilateral deemed conveyance introduced into the Maharashtra Ownership Flats Act, 1963 by the amendment of 2008, and in particular the now-settled practice by which the Court, declining to interfere with the summary orders of the Competent Authority, relegates contested questions of title, area and entitlement to a civil suit. Avon Arcade Premises Cooperative Society Ltd., vindicates or defeats the beneficial purpose of the legislation. Proceeding doctrinally through the primary authorities, from Mazda Construction Company v. Sultanabad Darshan CHS Ltd. through the decision of Mohta, J., the ownership-versus-lease line culminating in Haresh Vijaysinh Bhatia, and the most recent pronouncements applying the Maharashtra Ownership Flats (Amendment and Validation) Act, 2025, the article advances a single thesis. The relegation doctrine is doctrinally correct but substantively incomplete: because the deemed conveyance transfers only the promoter's actual right, title and interest and binds no civil court, the statute delivers to the successful society a registrable title rather than a secure one. The article contends that the counter-line of interference is not a rival doctrine but the same principle policing the outer edge of a summary jurisdiction, that the distinction between questions of title and questions of the scope of the promoter's obligation is unstable in application, and that the 2025 Validation Act's bar on suits collides with the very civil-suit guarantee on which the entire edifice of deference rests.

title: AI Computing Demand and Energy Market Co-movement: Evidence from EGARCH-X and DCC-GARCH Models

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the expansion of AI-related computing demand has created a new financial linkage between major technology equities and energy infrastructure assets. Using 817 daily observations from March 2023 to July 2026, we estimate an EGARCH(1,1)-X model augmented with the MOVE Index as an exogenous variance regressor (Stage 1), and a bivariate DCC-GARCH model (Engle, 2002) on GARCH-filtered standardized residuals (Stage 2) for seven asset pairs spanning AI equities (NVDA, MSFT, SOXX) and energy infrastructure (URA, XLU). The MOVE Index coefficient δ is statistically significant for NVDA (δ = 0.023, p < 0.01), SOXX (δ = 0.030, p < 0.001), and XLU (δ = 0.018, p < 0.001), confirming macro-financial stress transmission to AI-equity volatility. DCC-GARCH estimates reveal a significant increase in NVDA-URA co-movement (Δρ = +0.175, p < 0.001) and SOXX-URA co-movement (Δρ = +0.108, p < 0.01) following July 2024, while the control pair URA-XLU shows no structural break (Andrews sup-Wald p = 0.597). These findings suggest an AI-specific, rather than broadmarket, origin for the documented co-movement increase. Policy implications for energy infrastructure investment and systemic risk monitoring are discussed.

title: Consumer Law Meets the New Company Store
affiliations: Temple University Beasley School of Law and

detail.title: Consumer Law Meets the New Company Store
detail.abstract:
Firms have discovered new ways to extract value from workers beyond traditional labor exploitation.  In labor markets increasingly characterized by monopsony power, platform work, and financialization, employers push a variety of financial products onto workers and establish surveillance systems that monetize worker data.  This Article introduces the Triple Extraction Model to explain how firms profit from workers through the three interconnected channels of labor productivity, financial products, and data commodification.  In turn, firms are turning the workplace into a modern company store.

Building on prior work establishing workers as “worker-consumers,” this Article proposes that workers facing the Triple Extraction Model turn to consumer law to complement traditional employment and labor law protections.  While treating workers as consumers faces typological and theoretical tensions, the worker-consumer framework offers legal tools that practitioners have already begun utilizing to rein in exploitation.  For instance, the Dodd-Frank Act’s prohibition of “abusive” practices, the Fair Credit Reporting Act’s (FCRA) requirements for treatment of personal data, and federal and state unfair and deceptive acts and practices (UDAP) laws offer mechanisms to challenge workplace financial practices.  In addition, even during a time of federal inaction, a little-known provision of the Dodd-Frank Act allows states to enforce the entire body of federal consumer financial protection law.

Consumer law works best for workers when it supports collective action.  The application of consumer law to the workplace can reduce surveillance that chills organizing and establish minimum standards that free up union bargaining capital for wages and other benefits.

As firms become more creative in monetizing their captive workforces, sustainable change requires both sophisticated legal strategies and shifts in workplace power dynamics.  This Article provides the theoretical understanding and doctrinal tools necessary to challenge the new company store, demonstrating how consumer law can complement employment and labor laws and ultimately encourage self-enforcement through unions.

title: Future Research Directions: Overcoming Key Bottlenecks in the Energy Transition – The Grid

detail.title: Future Research Directions: Overcoming Key Bottlenecks in the Energy Transition – The Grid

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The POLICY CLUB

detail.abstract:
The electricity grid has become the principal bottleneck to the energy transition. While renewable energy technologies continue to advance rapidly, today's electricity infrastructure was largely designed for centralised fossil-fuel generation and is struggling to accommodate distributed renewable energy, electrification, artificial intelligence and rapidly growing data-centre demand.

The next phase of the energy transition therefore depends not only on engineering innovation but also on the commercialisation of decentralised electricity systems. Microgrids, supported by micro-markets, offer a complementary pathway that can co-evolve alongside the modernisation of the conventional grid.

Building on recent policy developments, including the UK's Clean Power 2030 Action Plan, together with observations from industry, this article identifies the principal barriers preventing decentralised electricity systems from scaling and proposes a research agenda focused on governance, financing mechanisms and business models. Mobilising institutional capital towards decentralised electricity systems may become one of the defining challenges—and opportunities—of the next phase of the energy transition.

title: Monitoring with Multiple Parameters at the Boundary: The Chi-Bar-Squared Process

detail.title: Monitoring with Multiple Parameters at the Boundary: The Chi-Bar-Squared Process

declarations.funderStatement: There are no funding interests to disclose.

detail.abstract: When an inequality-restricted hypothesis is re-tested over an expanding sample, the monitored likelihood-ratio path converges to what we call the chi-bar-squared process: the squared norm of the projection of a multi-clock Gaussian process onto a convex cone whose geometry, measured in the evolving information metric, drifts with the sample fraction-so the classical chi-bar-squared mixture weights become deterministic weight paths. We establish this limit theory and prove three structural results that make it usable: an exact factorization with purely triangular cross-dependence for trend-level pairs; closed-form weight drift for non-orthogonal pairs; and full process independence of the trend and wrong-skew monitors at the singular boundary of the normal-half-normal frontier model, licensing a guarded joint procedure with exact size apportionment. A local power theory completes the analysis: a noncentral process whose signal accumulates like the square root of each coordinate's clock, leading-order minimaxity of the constant standardized boundary over all monitoringboundary shapes, guard costs bounded by size shares, local asymptotic normality in λ 3 at the singular boundary, and cluster robustness through a cubed Moulton factor.

title: Import tariff transmission in a production network
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank,  and Deutsche Bundesbank

detail.title: Import tariff transmission in a production network
detail.abstract: We find that whether US import tariffs have supply-side effects or demand-side effects on US manufacturing sectors depends on where the affected sectors are located in the US production network. Using local projections in a panel of US manufacturing sectors, we find that US import tariffs —including the 2018-19 tariff hikes— led to sectoral output contractions via two different channels: (1) Tariff increases act as negative supply shifters for sectors that use goods from tariff-facing sectors as input in production and thus face rising input costs. (2) Tariff increases act as negative demand shifters for sectors whose customer sectors suffer negative supply side effects due to tariffs and reduce their production. We show that these results are consistent with a stylized production network model featuring complementarities in production. Overall, our finding suggests that tariffs markedly reduce US manufacturing production and that the role of input–output linkages is key for understanding the transmission of import tariff shocks to output and producer prices.

title: The New Indentured Servitude
affiliations: Temple University Beasley School of Law

detail.title: The New Indentured Servitude
detail.abstract:
Workers across the United States are increasingly bound by employment contracts that courts, policymakers, advocates, and the workers themselves are calling “modern indentured servitude.” These “stay-or-pay” contracts require workers to pay thousands or tens of thousands of dollars if they leave before completing a specified term of employment. They take multiple forms, including Training Repayment Agreement Provisions (TRAPs) that require reimbursement for putative training costs, liquidated damages clauses triggered by early departure, and clauses demanding that the worker pay the employer’s “lost profits.” At least one in thirteen U.S. workers is bound by a stay-or-pay provision, which is frequently woven together with other restrictive covenants to trap a worker in a web of immobility.

The repeated invocation of “indentured servitude” runs through the litigation, regulatory enforcement, and legislative debates surrounding stay-or-pay clauses. The Article thus answers calls to extend Thirteenth Amendment scholarship into the modern labor context by analyzing examples of new stay-or-pay contracts through the free labor tradition. That tradition, though debated in its overall meaning, includes the positive rights to quit and to change employers. A stay-or-pay contract that functionally prevents a worker from quitting and changing jobs violates this free labor principle under the Amendment.

By the mid-nineteenth century, Americans came to view indentured servitude as incompatible with freedom. A similar normative evolution is underway today with stay-or-pay contracts, as there is a broad recognition that the formal right to quit is meaningless when exercising it can lead to financial ruin. Free labor theory combined with the “new indentured servitude” terminology is helping to move courts to deny enforcement of stay-or-pay contracts under trafficking theories, state legislators to ban the contracts ex-ante, and federal agencies to declare the contracts void. Likewise, advocates should consider pursuing Thirteenth Amendment-based challenges to stay-or-pay contracts as a manifestation of constitutional political economy.

title: Faithful Agencies
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School, Harvard Law School and UC Berkeley School of Law

detail.title: Faithful Agencies
detail.abstract:
For nearly a century, Congress’s primary instrument for insulating agencies from presidential control was “independence,” expressed, quintessentially, as for-cause removal protection for agency heads. That era is over. After the Supreme Court’s decision in Trump v. Slaughter, removal restrictions are presumptively unconstitutional, and the remaining hallmarks of agency independence, like staggered terms and partisan balancing requirements, are diminished as a result. Meanwhile, successive presidents have embraced a muscular conception of executive power, which the Trump administration has pressed to the limit.


This Article develops principles of institutional design for an era of presidential unilateralism. Even without removal protections, Congress has many tools at its disposal to help agencies resist an arrogating president. Congress can deploy these tools strategically, bundling and layering them, to hamper a president bent on derailing agencies from their statutory mandates. Canvassing the U.S. Code, we identify scores of statutory design features—many obscure and seldom considered together—that promote agency faithfulness to the enacting Congress’s objectives. We label these devices fidelity structures and organize them into a taxonomy of four categories: financing arrangements, personnel rules, internal architecture, and external linkages. We then map their presence across every executive department and nine major independent agencies, uncovering several striking patterns in their use—with implications for future institutional designers in Congress.


Fidelity structures, we argue, do more than build agency resilience: they vindicate the separation of powers. Because the laws the president must faithfully execute are overwhelmingly the work of past Congresses, the Take Care Clause is by its nature a command to abide by legislative bargains over time. This intertemporal check—yesterday’s legislature constraining today’s executive—is especially important now that party unity has weakened horizontal checks between the political branches.
