detail.abstract: This paper interrogates the persistence of institutional corruption in the Philippines through the lens of historical institutionalism, arguing against longstanding cultural and quasi-biological explanations that attribute graft to an essential national character. It contends instead that corruption is best understood as an institutional legacy: a path-dependent outcome of critical junctures established under Spanish colonial rule (1565–1898) and subsequently reinforced, rather than dismantled, by American colonial administration (1898–1946). Drawing on historical institutionalism, the extractive-institutions framework of Acemoglu and Robinson (2012), and the political marketplace approach to clientelism, the paper traces five interlocking institutional legacies: the transformation of pre-colonial elites into a landed and bureaucratic principalía; the conversion of indigenous reciprocity into a hierarchical padrino system; the consolidation of the hacienda economy and its attendant land inequality; the centralization of political and fiscal authority in "Imperial Manila"; and the enduring political influence of the Catholic Church. Employing comparative historical analysis of colonial administrative records and the secondary historiography of Philippine state formation, the paper demonstrates that American electoral and bureaucratic reforms were superimposed upon, rather than substituted for, pre-existing extractive arrangements, producing a hybrid political order that is democratic in form but oligarchic in substance. The analysis finds that these five legacies remain empirically traceable in contemporary political dynasties, patronage networks, land reform failures, regional fiscal dependency, and religious influence over policy. The paper concludes that anti-corruption reform premised on individual ethics rather than structural transformation is unlikely to succeed, and that policy must instead target the institutional architecture inherited from empire.

title: The Impact of Social Entitlements and Ethicality on the Perception of Impolite Encounters: A Contrastive Study of TrustPilot Reviews

detail.title: The Impact of Social Entitlements and Ethicality on the Perception of Impolite Encounters: A Contrastive Study of TrustPilot Reviews
detail.abstract: Among the most prevalent online communicative practices in the 21st century is the posting of online consumer reviews, often used as a channel for dissatisfied users. However, further research is needed into the psychosocial factors that lead customers to feel dissatisfied or disadvantaged. Against this backdrop, this study examines how social entitlements and ethical concerns shape perceptions of impoliteness in negative reviews posted on the outsourced platform Trustpilot. A corpus of 1,000 Spanishlanguage reviews was compiled, comprising 200 reviews for each of five companies differing in business model (business-to-consumer or peer-to-peer) and product orientation (good or experience oriented): Airbnb, Miravia, Ryanair, Wallapop and Zara. Our Quantitative coding identifies the frequency and distribution of rapport triggers related to sociality rights and ethical evaluations, while our qualitative analysis explores how these triggers are thematically realised and combined within the reviewers’ narratives. The findings show that costbenefit concerns and autonomyimposition issues are central to users’ negative evaluations across companies, but their relative salience and interactional framing vary depending on platform type and product orientation. Ethical judgements, often linked to perceived dishonesty, lack of transparency or neglect of customer welfare, cooccur with breaches of sociality rights and intensify the perception of impoliteness. Overall, the study demonstrates that perceived mismanagement of social entitlements and ethicality are crucial dimensions of rapport in online review discourse and offer insight into how users negotiate expectations of what is ”right” or ”wrong” in institutionalised service encounters on digital platforms.

title: Social Media Toxicity and Mental Health
affiliations: , University of Barcelona - Institut d'Economia de Barcelona (IEB),  and University of Warwick

detail.title: Social Media Toxicity and Mental Health
detail.abstract: We study whether content-level moderation that reduces exposure to social media toxicity, holding platform access constant, affects mental health. We deploy, for randomly assigned users, a cross-platform browser extension that hides posts and comments exceeding a prespecified toxicity threshold, and follow N = 664 desktop users over a six-week intervention across two waves-one during the 2024 U.S. election campaign and one outside of it. Contrary to basic intuition, filtering toxicity worsens mental health: treatment raises a standardized index of GAD-7 and PHQ-8 symptoms by 0.15σ, and the share of respondents above a moderate-symptom screening cutoff rises by about 12 pp. A QALY-based calibration implies a welfare cost of about $158 per treated participant. Heightened loneliness and a diminished relative moral self-view emerge as potential channels. We conclude that curbing toxic content can impose unintended psychological costs, even where it yields other social benefits.

title: Hybrid Staging and Gendered Access to Digital Equity
affiliations: University of Essex - Essex Business School,  and University of Bergamo

detail.title: Hybrid Staging and Gendered Access to Digital Equity
detail.abstract: Digital equity platforms are often viewed as alternatives to traditional entrepreneurial finance. We show instead that they frequently extend relationships formed in private capital markets. We develop the concept of hybrid digital staging, in which a venture enters its first equity crowdfunding campaign after one or more private equity rounds and with the continued involvement of prior investors. Using 789 initial campaigns launched on Crowdcube and matched to Beauhurst financing records, we find that 64% of classifiable ventures had completed at least one private round before entering the platform. Because platforms cannot negotiate individualized contracts with dispersed investors, information accumulated during the private phase may instead be reflected in campaign design. Conditional on pre-campaign observables, hybrid staging is associated with funding goals approximately two-thirds higher than those of otherwise comparable ventures. Goals also increase with the depth of the prior financing relationship: by about 22% for each additional private round and 27% for each additional year of staging history. This pattern is more consistent with information accumulated through repeated financing and monitoring than with a purely dichotomous certification effect. Access to this pathway is uneven and state contingent. Female-led ventures are about 10 percentage points less likely to enter crowdfunding with prior staging; this gap is indistinguishable from zero outside the COVID-19 period but rises to roughly 25 percentage points during it. Digital equity platforms therefore extend the reach of the private financing system, carrying both accumulated private information and inequalities in access into digital equity markets.

title: From priority ordering to scaling: A two-phase procedure for facility search in Japanese rehabilitation team interaction
affiliations: National Defense Academy of Japan

detail.title: From priority ordering to scaling: A two-phase procedure for facility search in Japanese rehabilitation team interaction
detail.abstract: Building on a line of inquiry that Sacks identified but left undeveloped—namely, the search for professional help—the present study draws on Bilmes’s frameworks of first priority response/mention and occasioned semantics analysis of scaling to provide a systematic account of the two-phase procedure through which suitable care facilities are identified in interprofessional discharge planning for stroke patients whose family caregivers are unavailable to provide care. Using naturally occurring conversational data from Japanese rehabilitation team meetings, it investigates: (1) how institutional criteria are occasioned as relevant and prioritized in interaction and (2) how participants manage the prioritized constraints through regrading. The analysis shows that, in the first phase, participants treat inflexible criteria—financial constraints and required care level—as first-priority matters before proceeding to more flexible criteria. Where necessary, they establish the procedural basis for the second phase through formulation practices, including maximal boundaries, scaling and contrast, and category attributions. In the second phase, participants accomplish facility selection by fitting placement options to the prioritized constraints through regrading. The analysis further demonstrates that, on some occasions, participants treat the prior non-mention of an inflexible criterion as accountable, showing that the relevance of the omitted criterion is displayed through participants’ actions. By providing a systematic interactional account of this two-phase procedure, the study extends Bilmes’s frameworks to interprofessional decision-making, demonstrating that priority ordering and scaling in discharge planning are institutionally constituted through participants’ ongoing collaborative actions.

detail.abstract: In a looped DeFi lending book, the figure a stress test flags as "at-risk" is liquidationeligible debt, and it is separated from the protocol's protocol bad debt by two distinct gaps that we measure separately. First, eligible debt is not executed volume: under a partial close factor a position is liquidated in parts and re-buffers, so at a 5% de-peg the $1.36B of eligible debt in the live loop cluster produces about $0.69B of executed repayment and $0.72B of seized collateral, not $1.36B of selling. Second, executed volume is not protocol bad debt: a loop is liquidated under the parameters of the mode it is held in, and when its liquidation threshold and bonus satisfy LT (1+b) < 1, a loop that crosses HF = 1 on a continuous price path is removed while its collateral still covers the bonus-grossed debt, so the protocol books no bad debt at any de-peg depth. Aave v3 satisfies this invariant in every e-mode category: the ETH-correlated category that carries the liquid-staking loops is LT 0.95 with a 1% liquidation bonus (the category bonus, read from the Pool contract, not the 6% wstETH reserve bonus), giving LT (1+b) = 0.9595; reaching the loss-on-crossing regime would require a bonus above 5.26%, five times what Aave sets, and all eight live e-mode categories carry a comparable margin. On one live Aave-v3 Ethereum block (17,419 borrowers, $6.5B debt), a 5% de-peg of the liquid-staking slice therefore flags $1.38B as liquidation-eligible while the continuous-path protocol bad debt is $0 (the pure-loop core carries $1.36B of that eligible debt at $0 bad debt; the 1.76% mixed-collateral remainder is discussed in the body). This $0 is not an empirical robustness finding but a consequence of the LT (1+b) < 1 invariant on an unbroken continuous path (a loop removed at its solvent crossing books nothing at any glide depth), so the load-bearing risk analysis is the boundary D * and the channels that break the path, below, not the depth of the de-peg. We characterize the boundary in closed form, D * = max 1-1/HF 0 , 1-(1+b)LT /HF 0 , matched to a cascade engine to one grid step; for the live e-mode anchor D * = 7.4%, and its median across the live slice is 6.9% (8.8% debt-weighted). Protocol bad debt appears only when something breaks the continuous path, and we size each channel on the live cluster: a discrete price gap (a jump no liquidator can step through) books $0.1M at a 5% gap but $47M at 10%; partial liquidation into a finite $2B pool books $3.0M at a 5% gap where full liquidation books $0; measured June-2022 oracle staleness adds up to $5M at an 8% gap; and secondary-market depth sets the magnitude past the boundary ($30M at infinite depth rising to $0.70B at a $1B pool for a 15% gap). A reflexive de-peg, in which the forced selling moves the peg itself, runs the peg to near-total collapse with the redemption queue frozen, yet still books $0 because the loops exit solvent as the peg runs away; a live withdrawal backstop is the control, not the threshold. Three real episodes are consistent with the invariant: pre-event Aave-v2 stETH/WETH (−6.8%) and the March-2023 USDC pin both reconstruct to $0, and the March-2026 Aave CAPO event liquidated ≈$26M of wstETH e-mode with no protocol bad debt. We are precise throughout that zero protocol bad debt is not zero economic cost: the same episodes transfer value to liquidators (the bonus), impose losses on the liquidated borrowers, and can trigger DAO compensation; our claim is about the protocol’s balance sheet, not borrower or third-party welfare. The operative controls are therefore oracle-deviation and heartbeat bounds, supply caps, and the withdrawal backstop, not the liquidation threshold. The directional-crash overstatement (6.53× at −5%) is a netting convention, not book risk. We formalize a mechanism recent Aave e-mode liquidations have already shown in the wild, not claim to discover it.

title: A Case Analysis of Judgment Update Deficiency: Taking Xiao Yan, Protagonist of Battle Through the Heavens, as the Research Subject

detail.title: A Case Analysis of Judgment Update Deficiency: Taking Xiao Yan, Protagonist of Battle Through the Heavens, as the Research Subject
detail.abstract:
(1) Research Purpose: Taking Xiao Yan, protagonist of Battle Through the Heavens, as a case subject, this study investigates Judgment Update Deficiency (JUD)-a cognitive dysfunction characterized by an inability to revise judgments based on new information. JUD is conceptualized not as a single bias but as a Self-Reinforcing Judgment Loop comprising four failed nodes: Initial Representation, Update Lockout, Consistency Maintenance, and Boundary Recognition Failure. 
(2) Research Design/Method: A case analysis of the full forty-volume text is conducted, comparing judgment behaviors across combat and non-combat domains. Analytical tools include Naturalistic Decision Making, Ecological Rationality, Signal Detection Theory, and Social Judgment Theory. The Yun Yun incident serves as the core case; the Medusa case delimits the theoretical boundary between Evaluation Update and Strategic Reclassification. 
(3) Research Results: The subject's judgment system operates as a closed loop: binary classification (Initial Representation), failure of new interpersonal information to trigger re-evaluation (Update Lockout), compensatory consistency maintenance, and cross-domain proliferation of combat logic (Boundary Recognition Failure). The Medusa case demonstrates that the loop permits Strategic Reclassification but precludes Evaluation Update. Sensitivity analysis shows that a single evaluation update event could reduce JUD by approximately 50%, yet none occurred across the forty volumes. 
(4) Limitations: Only one fictional character is analyzed; future research may expand the sample. 
(5) Implications: A four-node diagnostic framework is proposed for identifying JUD tendencies. 
(6) Originality: This study is the first to model JUD as a Self-Reinforcing Judgment Loop, to distinguish Evaluation Update from Strategic Reclassification, and to establish a replicable analytical pathway using a fictional case.

detail.abstract:
The global workplace is experiencing an unprecedented crisis of mental health, burnout, and disengagement, with significant implications for productivity, attrition, and human sustainability. Existing measurement frameworks-primarily annual engagement surveys and generic wellbeing assessments-are retrospective, fragmented, and illequipped to capture the multidimensional nature of human wellbeing. 

This paper introduces the Bharat Wellness Index (BWI), a novel composite framework grounded in the ancient Indian Panchakosha model-the five sheaths of human existence articulated in the Taittiriya Upanishad. The BWI operationalises the Annamaya (physical), Pranamaya (vital energy), Manomaya (mental-emotional), Vijnanamaya (intellectual-wisdom), and Anandamaya (bliss) sheaths into measurable indicators across organisational, campus, and state-level contexts. 

Drawing upon established research on composite wellness indices, the BWI integrates quantitative surveys, qualitative assessments, behavioural data, and predictive analytics to generate a dynamic, longitudinal score (0-100). The framework aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 3 and SDG 8), India's Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) requirements, and emerging global ESG standards. We present the conceptual architecture, methodological approach, and potential applications of the BWI for corporate organisations, educational institutions, and state governments. 

The paper positions the BWI as a foundational, India-first contribution to the global discourse on wellbeing measurement-bridging ancient wisdom with contemporary data science and policy impact.

detail.abstract: The global decline in aerosol pollution has produced a counterintuitive climatic effect: stronger heatwaves. While cleaner air improves public health, the reduction of reflective aerosols removes a temporary cooling shield, revealing the full warming force of greenhouse gases. This essay integrates climate physics, entropy-based development theory, entropic growth and development paradigm, and experimental microeconomics to analyse how autonomous civilisation emerges within legacy infrastructures. A game-theoretic model illustrates strategic interactions between states, industries, and planetary systems. The essay concludes that societies can achieve both clean air and reduced heatwaves by reducing greenhouse gases while maintaining low aerosol levels.

title: The Kinetic Mathematics of Institutional Navigation: A Formal Model of Resource Orchestration under Geopolitical Friction

detail.title: The Kinetic Mathematics of Institutional Navigation: A Formal Model of Resource Orchestration under Geopolitical Friction
detail.abstract: This working paper introduces a formal dynamic model to explain how multinational corporations (MNCs) navigate extreme institutional paradoxes and geopolitical friction. Mainstream strategic management literature typically relies on static compliance models, assuming that well-capitalized MNCs can overcome institutional distance through standardization and scale. We challenge this assumption, demonstrating that under conditions of extreme geopolitical friction, traditional compliance pathways inevitably fail. Instead, MNCs must adopt boundary-challenging resource orchestration strategies—traditionally associated with small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs)—to survive. We operationalize this theoretical proposition through a dynamic equation, Delta C_t = theta * (alpha * S_{t-1} / Omega), which defines geopolitical friction (Omega) as a quantifiable variable of organizational friction. Using Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) as an ultimate "stress test," we contrast its expansion trajectories in the United States and Japan. Empirical analysis indicates that facing immense institutional resistance, the rapid reconfiguration of satellite assets (S_{t-1}) and high organizational agility (theta) are the sole viable mechanisms for enhancing core capabilities (Delta C_t). This model establishes a scale-transcendent, universally applicable rule of institutional navigation, providing a quantitative tool for assessing corporate viability in an era of geopolitical fragmentation.

detail.abstract: Rare gases such as neon, helium, krypton, and xenon are indispensable inputs in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, yet they account for a negligible share of total production costs. This paper studies whether such hidden critical inputs generate meaningful supply-chain vulnerability under geopolitical stress. Using BACI bilateral trade data covering 2000-2024 and monthly Chinese customs records at the HS 8-digit level, I document three main findings. First, global rare-gas supply chains are highly concentrated and structurally differentiated across major semiconductor-producing economies, with Qatar and the United States jointly accounting for over half of world exports before the Russian-Ukraine war and the four largest industrial gas multinationals maintaining dense and overlapping affiliate networks across the same set of semiconductor-producing economies. Second, the 2022 Russia-Ukraine shock transmitted to the global rare-gas network primarily as a price shock rather than a quantity shock. Third, China's post-2022 adjustment followed a two-stage process: an immediate intensive-margin reorientation toward Russian supply and a surge in exports toward Korea, Taiwan, and Japan during the zero-COVID period. Crosscountry variation in price-shock intensity is closely related to pre-shock exposure to Ukrainian supply and to pre-shock sourcing concentration. The paper highlights how geopolitical fragmentation can propagate through low-salience but technically indispensable inputs, and documents the limits of customs-based trade statistics for assessing supply-chain vulnerability when production and distribution are organizationally concentrated within a small number of vertically integrated multinationals.

detail.abstract: Does matching loan repayments to expected cash flows raise take-up and the welfare impact of microcredit? We test this in a randomized controlled trial with Morocco's largest microfinance institution. The experiment introduces two new individual-liability loan products: a contract with a five-month principal grace period and a tailored contract with installments matched to expected revenues. Over 3,000 applicants are randomly assigned to an offer of one of the two new contracts or the standard loan. The new contracts attract distinct borrowers: agricultural households take up the grace-period loan, while entrepreneurs operating smaller, more capital-constrained businesses choose the tailored schedule. Most tailored-loan borrowers front-load their repayments, suggesting that demand for flexibility reflects cost minimization, not only liquidity management. The tailored loan raises sales and profits via non-agricultural business expansion and labor reallocation to self-employment. The grace-period loan shows similar but statistically insignificant effects. Neither product worsens repayment performance. We find no effects on investment or consumption. In a second stage, we randomize contract-specific information campaigns across 440 villages. Despite shifting stated preferences toward the advertised products, the campaigns do not raise take-up, consistent with supply-side frictions and a challenging macroeconomic environment.

detail.abstract: The specialised agencies of the United Nations have long occupied an ambiguous but consequential position in the architecture of international law-making. Bodies such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the International Labour Organization (ILO), the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the Universal Postal Union (UPU), and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) exercise what several scholars have termed a "quasi-legislative" function: the capacity to generate binding or quasi-binding norms through instruments-conventions, regulations, recommendations-that depart from the classical, consent-intensive model of treaty-making. This paper revisits that thesis and extends it to a domain the earlier literature could not have anticipated: the governance of artificial intelligence (AI). Drawing on UNESCO's 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, the WHO's 2021 guidance on the ethics and governance of AI for health, and ICAO's ongoing work toward a trustworthy-AI framework for civil aviation, the paper argues that specialised agencies are again functioning as first movers in a normative space that formal treaty-making has not yet reached-reproducing, in accelerated form, the same soft-law-to-hard-law trajectory earlier observed in public health and civil aviation regulation. The paper closes by examining the legitimacy costs of this pattern: the risk of institutional fragmentation, the weak enforceability of recommendations, and the disproportionate influence of a small number of technologically advanced states and private actors in shaping ostensibly universal norms.

title: Explaining the Productivity Paradox of Artificial Intelligence: A TAM/UTAUT-Based Study of AI Acceptance and Perceived Team Productivity in Industrial Work Environments
affiliations: Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU)

detail.title: Explaining the Productivity Paradox of Artificial Intelligence: A TAM/UTAUT-Based Study of AI Acceptance and Perceived Team Productivity in Industrial Work Environments
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are widely expected to raise organizational productivity, yet measurable gains remain inconsistent across firms and teams. This study extends the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) to examine how individual AI acceptance influences perceived team productivity in heterogeneous industrial work environments, using an industrial project team at a large German energy technology company as the empirical context. The proposed model adds two AI-specific constructs - trust in AI and verification effort - to established acceptance predictors, with AI usage intensity positioned as a mediator and perceived team productivity as the outcome. Data were collected from eleven team members through a structured seven-point questionnaire and analysed with descriptive statistics, reliability estimates, correlation, and exploratory regression. AI usage intensity was strongly associated with perceived team productivity, and a model combining usage intensity and perceived usefulness explained the majority of variance in the outcome. Contrary to expectation, verification effort was high but did not act as a statistical brake on perceived productivity; qualitative responses indicate that verification is experienced as a routine cost of use rather than a net productivity loss. Given the small sample, the study is positioned as an exploratory, model-building exercise that generates hypotheses for future large-scale research.

title: The End of the Free-Market Consensus

detail.title: The End of the Free-Market Consensus
detail.abstract: This paper argues that the post-Cold War free-market consensus is ending, driven by great-power competition with China and the structural inadequacy of market-led economies in confronting state-capitalist rivals. Using Margaret Thatcher's 1985 privatization of British Aerospace-and the "golden share" she retained-as an analytical entry point, the paper traces how governments on both sides of the Atlantic are now embracing equity stakes, veto rights, and strategic investment controls as instruments of modern statecraft. In the United States, the Trump administration has committed $26.7 billion to roughly 30 private deals since January 2025, acquiring preferred shares in U.S. Steel and Intel and stretching the CHIPS Act and Defense Production Act beyond their legislative parameters, without congressional authorization or defined exit strategies. In Europe, the EU's Economic Security Strategy, Germany's nationalization of Uniper, France's renationalization of EDF, Italy's expanded Golden Power regime, and Britain's seizure of British Steel's Scunthorpe works all reflect convergent pressures. The paper locates the systemic cause in China's model-pioneered under Premier Zhu Rongji-of concentrating industrial power into state champions, cornering critical mineral supply chains, and weaponizing economic dominance for geopolitical ends. It assesses the dangers of the new political economy: retaliatory nationalization, the erosion of the open investment order, and the absence of sunset clauses or congressional oversight. The analysis concludes that the competition with China offers no armistice and no natural endpoint, making temporary emergency measures the likely foundation of a lasting structural transformation in international political economy.

detail.abstract:
Introduction: National Health Service (NHS) failures at Mid-Staffordshire, Shrewsbury and Telford, and East Kent reached the same conclusion: leaders who fail to listen and understand put patients at risk. The NHS response has been to promote compassionate leadership. Yet, compassion often entails emotional merging, which can blur boundaries and lead to fatigue. By contrast, empathic leadership and curiosity-driven perspectivetaking, rather than emotional merging, offers a promising new way forward. Yet no practical method exists to teach empathic leadership. To fill this gap, we aimed to develop heuristics ('rules of thumb') for empathic leadership and create a course to teach them. 

Methods: 21 healthcare leaders attended a structured workshop. Using established heuristic development and curriculum design methods, participants generated, refined and prioritised heuristics for empathic leadership, then co-designed a training course to teach them. 

Results: The group produced 35 heuristics and prioritised 12, including 'Listen first, speak last', 'Say sorry', and 'Walk the shop floor'. A one-day interprofessional empathic leadership course was then co-designed, featuring experiential learning, role play and implementation planning. 

Conclusion: We identified and prioritized heuristics for empathic leadership and produced a course to teach them. The short course may support healthcare leaders to strengthen empathic leadership in practice.

title: Frequent, Systematic, Undefined: The MiFIR Review's Qualitative Turn and the Limits of Liquid Market Recalibration for Thin Equity Markets

detail.title: Frequent, Systematic, Undefined: The MiFIR Review's Qualitative Turn and the Limits of Liquid Market Recalibration for Thin Equity Markets
detail.abstract: On 1 February 2025 the European Union began operating a systematic internaliser regime with no quantitative content. Regulation (EU) 2024/791 and Directive (EU) 2024/790 deleted the arithmetic thresholds that had defined SI status since 2018 and left the statutory phrase "frequent and systematic" undefined, with no Level 2 specification beneath it. The prevailing account reads the reform as deregulatory simplification, and on its own terms that account is correct: the compliance burden was real, the underlying data was unreliable, and the new Designated Publishing Entity regime stripped the status of its old reporting function. This article argues that the qualitative turn nonetheless deepens the framework's oldest blind spot, its inability to see thin, small-economy equity markets. The old quantitative test was miscalibrated for such markets but legible; a firm at the bottom of the liquidity distribution could compute its status and prove it. Drawing on the consultation record, in which stakeholder objections to the thin-market calibration were raised and overridden, and on current capitalisation data from the Baltic regulated markets, the article shows that the reform converts a visible calibration failure into an invisible one. It names the resulting condition regulatory illegibility and locates the same structural pathology in other EU financial frameworks built on large-economy assumptions. The United Kingdom's contrasting choice under PS25/17 isolates the EU in an incoherent middle position. ESMA's April 2026 Call for Evidence opened the window through which a remedy could still enter.

detail.abstract: Scarce data hinders data-driven location optimization, as sample average approximation (SAA) can yield poor out-of-sample performance. While target data is limited in these settings, abundant related data may be available as a proxy. We study mixed-effects (ME) policies, which combine unbiased, noisy historical-data-based estimates with biased, low-variance proxy estimates, for facility location problems with small data. We analyze a stylized three-node example to derive insights into when ME policies outperform the gold policy (i.e., SAA using historical data) and extend our analysis to general location problems based on a softmax approximation. Our results show that ME policies are most effective in low signal-to-noise ratio domains where the proxy is sufficiently aligned with the target variable. Notably, even imperfect or seemingly low-quality proxies can be leveraged in ME policies to outperform the gold policy in both expected and lower-tail performance. A case study on locating critical care response units for response to major trauma incidents demonstrates that ME policies based on lower-acuity trauma as a proxy for major trauma outperform the gold policy in expected coverage and solution stability. Our work demonstrates that out-of-sample performance of location decisions in the small data regime can be strengthened by incorporating proxy information within the optimization framework. We provide analytical conditions and practical guidance on when proxies are valuable, and demonstrate through a case study that ME policies are straightforward to implement to improve expected performance and policy robustness.

title: A Hybrid Artificial Intelligence and Software Logic Framework for Recommending Custom Scan Rule Thresholds in Regulated Transportation Apps

detail.title: A Hybrid Artificial Intelligence and Software Logic Framework for Recommending Custom Scan Rule Thresholds in Regulated Transportation Apps
detail.abstract: The increasing deployment of automated scanning systems in regulated transportation applications-ranging from baggage screening at airports to cargo inspection at border checkpoints-demands high detection accuracy while adhering to strict regulatory compliance and operational safety standards. However, static threshold configurations for these scanning rules often fail to adapt to variable environmental conditions, evolving threat profiles, and device-specific performance degradation, leading to either excessive false positives that disrupt operations or dangerous false negatives that compromise security. This paper presents a hybrid framework that integrates artificial intelligence (AI) driven predictive modeling with a rule-based software logic layer to dynamically recommend optimal scan rule thresholds in real time. The AI component employs ensemble learning and reinforcement learning to analyze historical scan data, sensor health metrics, and contextual operational parameters, generating candidate threshold adjustments. The software logic layer then applies regulatory constraints, safety margins, and human-in-the-loop validation rules to filter, justify, and finalize these recommendations before deployment. We evaluate the framework using a large-scale dataset from a national transportation security agency, spanning over 18 months of multimodal scan operations. Results demonstrate that our hybrid approach reduces false alarm rates by 27.4% while maintaining zero regulatory violations, outperforming static baselines and purely data-driven methods. The framework also provides explainable audit trails for each threshold change, addressing regulatory requirements for transparency and accountability. This work offers a practical, deployable solution for balancing security efficacy, operational efficiency, and compliance in high-stakes transportation environments.

title: Virtual Reality-Based Job Interview Training Using AI Interviewers: Confidence Building, Stress Analysis, Body Language Assessment, and Intelligent Conversational Agents

detail.title: Virtual Reality-Based Job Interview Training Using AI Interviewers: Confidence Building, Stress Analysis, Body Language Assessment, and Intelligent Conversational Agents
detail.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) and artificial intelligence (AI) are converging on a long-standing problem in career development: how to help job seekers rehearse and master the high-stakes, anxietyprovoking social performance of the employment interview. Over the past decade, three largely separate research communities have advanced this agenda clinical and vocational rehabilitation scientists validating branching-dialogue VR simulators in randomized controlled trials (RCTs), affective-computing researchers building multimodal machine learning pipelines that infer hireability and confidence from facial, vocal, and gestural cues, and, most recently, humancomputer interaction researchers pairing large language models (LLMs) with embodied digital humans to generate open-ended, adaptive interview dialogue. This review critically synthesizes 61 peer-reviewed and indexed sources spanning 1985 2026, with emphasis on 2020 2026 publications, to determine what has been solved, what remains unresolved, and where genuine opportunities for high-impact contributions persist. We show that VR-based interview simulators produce replicated, clinically meaningful gains in interview skill, self-confidence, and anxiety reduction, particularly for autistic, justice-involved, and serious-mental-illness populations, but that this evidence base rests almost entirely on scripted or Bayesian-adaptive dialogue rather than generative AI. Conversely, the rapidly growing multimodal-assessment and generative-AI literatures report impressive technical benchmarks (fusion-model accuracies above 85 90% and correlation coefficients with human raters above 0.70) but are seldom evaluated inside immersive VR, rarely subjected to randomized trial designs, and almost never audited for demographic fairness in a training (as opposed to hiring) context. Physiological sensing (electrodermal activity, cardiac measures, and electroencephalography) has been shown capable of classifying interviewinduced stress with area-under-curve values approaching 0.95, yet no published system closes the loop by feeding these signals back into a generative interviewer's real-time behavior. We introduce an original taxonomy, an illustrative publication timeline, a technology-evolution ladder, a research-gap quadrant map, and a conceptual framework for a closed-loop, biofeedbackadaptive generative VR interviewer that integrates these currently disconnected strands. We conclude with 22 concrete, differentiated research directions spanning closed-loop adaptation, cross-cultural validation, fairness-audited feedback, panel-interview simulation, and privacypreserving on-device sensing that are positioned to yield Tier-1 contributions precisely because they combine elements that, to date, no single published system has combined.

title: Scaling as a Control Problem
affiliations: Frankfurt School of Finance & Management

detail.title: Scaling as a Control Problem
detail.abstract: Interventions that work in pilots often weaken when organizations scale them into routine programs. I argue that this attenuation is partly an accounting and control problem. A field experiment never tests an intervention on its own. It tests the intervention together with the bundle of budgets, measures, reviews, discretion, and audit that carries its working mechanism in the pilot. I call that bundle the control architecture, and I distinguish the architecture the researcher designs for the pilot from the inherited architecture a program runs on. When routine operation reproduces the nominal intervention but rebuilds the architecture around it, it can change the treatment that is actually delivered, even when population, site, and protocol are held fixed. I develop this pilot-to-program gap along five control functions and show how each produces a diagnostic prediction about where attenuation should appear.

title: Science versus Subjectivity in Environmental Research
affiliations: University of Wisconsin at Madison and University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: Science versus Subjectivity in Environmental Research

detail.abstract: Objective science aims to uncover truths about environmental conditions, including those related to emission trends, biodiversity loss, climate change, and their economic costs. When and why do scientists use subjective language to describe these conditions with bias, emotion, or advocacy? To shed light, we study determinants and trends in subjective language within the abstracts, introductions, and conclusions of over 170,000 peer-reviewed articles published during 1990-2023 in top economics and science journals. Using machine learning to label and score text by subjectivity, we find that subjective language is more prevalent in articles focused on environmental topics relative to non-environmental topics: by 12% in economics and by 42% in science. After accounting for factors such as article age, author experience, number of authors, and journal quality, higher subjectivity scores associate positively with future academic citations in both science and economics, especially if the article is focused on an environmental topic. These findings, which imply subjective language has been rewarded in the academy, are consistent with informal theory suggesting subjective language will be used more frequently by scientists when expected rewards are high and risks are low.

title: Relating Cognitive Skills and Personality Traits to Economic Preferences: Decision-Making under Cognitive Shocks and Guessing
affiliations: , Jinan University, University of Chicago - Department of Economics and Liaoning University

detail.title: Relating Cognitive Skills and Personality Traits to Economic Preferences: Decision-Making under Cognitive Shocks and Guessing
detail.abstract: Using rich data on Chinese schoolchildren, we study the relationships of IQ and personality traits with children’s risk preferences and how they affect the precision with which those preferences are measured. Our structural model separates preferences from deliberation noise and guessing, and relates guessing to deliberation noise. Psychological measures have weak direct influences on preferences but strongly affect deliberation noise and guessing behavior. Shocks to choice have persistent individual-specific components and are not independent. Socioeconomic background has little direct influence on preferences or deliberation noise once traits are accounted for. Background variables affect psychological traits, however. Risk preferences differ across and within genders. For small gambles, girls are less risk averse than boys, but the opposite holds for larger gambles.
